title: 5. Data Governance for AI
text:
5.10 Documentation
Every discipline in this chapter produces findings, whether on quality dimensions, provenance, representativeness, bias mechanisms, corpus governance, fine-tuning review, or privacy technique. Those findings are useful only if they are written down where a later reviewer, a regulator, or the organization’s own future self can find them. The standard structure for that record is the datasheet, a documentation format proposed by Timnit Gebru and colleagues in 2018 for the case where a dataset’s users are removed from its creators and have no other way to answer basic questions about what they are working with.
A datasheet organizes the record into categories that track this chapter’s sections, because they answer the same questions. Table 5.2 gives the categories and what each one records.
Table 5.2. Datasheet categories and their contents







Category
Contents




Motivation
Why the dataset was created and by whom


Composition
What the instances represent, whether any confidential or sensitive information is present, and what is known about gaps or absences of the kind section 5.6 treats as a bias mechanism in its own right


Collection process
How the data was acquired, tracking directly to the provenance discipline of section 5.4


Preprocessing and labelling
What transformations were applied and what was removed, again tracking section 5.4’s transformation question


Uses
What the dataset has been and could be used for, including uses the creators consider inappropriate


Distribution and maintenance
Who may access the dataset and who is responsible for it going forward, which is where corpus freshness and retirement discipline from section 5.7 get a named owner



Uses is where a fine-tuning set’s intended narrow purpose should be stated explicitly enough that a later team does not repurpose it for a use the original review never considered.
A datasheet filled in honestly, including what is unknown or unresolved, makes the rest of this chapter’s work last beyond the memory of the person who did it. Template 13, the Dataset Datasheet, carries the six categories above together with the representativeness assessment from section 5.5 and a field for every question that could not be answered.
Filled for MEDASSIST’s training data, as it should have stood before the community hospital deployments, it reads as follows.








DATASET
DS-2023-004 · Northfield deterioration cohort, v2


OWNER
L. Marsh, Director of Clinical Informatics


MOTIVATION
Built for this use. Assembled to train a deterioration prediction model for Northfield’s own inpatient population.


COMPOSITION
41,200 inpatient admissions, academic medical center only, 2019 to 2023. High acuity, dense monitoring, consistent documentation. No community hospital admissions.


SAMPLE
Not a sample of a wider population. It is the whole of one site, which is the finding, not a limitation of sampling.


COLLECTION
Extracted from the EHR under the clinical data warehouse agreement. Subjects consented to treatment, not to model training; Article 6(4) compatibility assessed, Article 9(2) condition identified separately.


PREPROCESSING
Cleaning and imputation applied before training. Specific steps not retained in a consultable form. Raw extract retained; the transformation between raw and training set cannot be reconstructed.


APPROPRIATE USES
Deterioration prediction for populations resembling the academic center’s.


INAPPROPRIATE USES
Deployment to a site with different case mix, vital-sign cadence, or documentation practice, absent a representativeness assessment for it.


REPRESENTATIVENESS
Academic center only. No community hospital population compared before deployment. Those sites differ materially on case mix, monitoring cadence, and documentation practice. Unfavourable, established after deployment rather than before.


UNKNOWN
The specific cleaning steps. Whether the 2019 cohort reflects pre-2021 guideline changes. Comorbidity coding consistency across the period.


BUILT ON THIS
MDL-2023-011, serving SYS-2023-008




Two fields carry the failure. PREPROCESSING records that the transformation cannot be reconstructed, which is a live gap rather than a completed entry. And REPRESENTATIVENESS names what the training population was never compared against. Neither field needed anything Northfield did not already know in 2023. The datasheet’s contribution is not new information. It is that the question appears on the form, so that deploying to a seventh hospital requires someone to write “not compared” in a place a reviewer will read. MEDASSIST’s community hospital failure was in part a documentation failure. Nothing was recorded, in a place anyone deploying to a new hospital would have consulted, that the training population was drawn entirely from the academic medical center. A representativeness assessment that is never written down has to be redone, imperfectly and from memory, by whoever eventually asks the question the first deployment never answered.

title: 5. Data Governance for AI
section: Case in focus: two data failures inside one system
text:
Case in focus: two data failures inside one system
MEDASSIST · Hypothetical, following the running case
Northfield Health trained MEDASSIST on ten years of records from its academic medical center, drawn from a large, high-acuity population with dense vital-sign monitoring and consistent documentation practice built up over a decade by a stable clinical staff. Validated against a held-out slice of that same population, the model performed well by every measure the validation exercise computed. It was then deployed unchanged across all seven of Northfield’s hospitals, including six community sites whose patient population, equipment, and documentation practice none of the validation work had touched.
The representativeness gap section 5.5 develops in full produced the first failure. Sepsis alerts at the community hospitals arrived late or not at all for patients whose deterioration, in retrospect, resembled patterns the model had learned to catch at the academic center. Their surrounding data did not match closely enough for the model’s learned pattern to fire reliably, since it carried a coarser vital-sign cadence, a different case mix, and documentation entered on a different schedule. No one had asked, before deployment, whether the training population resembled the deployment population on the dimensions the model actually relied on, and the gap was invisible to any test run against data from the training site itself.
Two years later, Northfield extended MEDASSIST with a generative documentation assistant that retrieves from the organization’s clinical guidelines and prior clinical notes to help draft admission summaries. The model itself was purchased, unmodified, from an external developer; nothing about it was trained on Northfield’s data. The corpus it retrieves from, however, was assembled by indexing a shared clinical-documents repository without preserving the access distinctions that governed who could read which notes when a clinician opened them directly. A nurse’s query could retrieve material from a note the querying nurse was never authorized to see under the hospital’s own access policy, and the assistant could reproduce that material in a drafted summary. This happened because the retrieval system operated on the index instead of the permission structure the original documents carried.
The two failures share a structure. Neither failure was a defect in a model. The predictive model performed as its training taught it to. The generative model retrieved what its corpus made available. Both failures came from data decisions nobody made before either model ran, namely a representativeness question never asked and a permission structure never carried forward into an index. A governance function that reviews model performance without reviewing the data underneath it, on the build path or the buy path, will keep finding failures that look like the model’s fault and are not.

title: 5. Data Governance for AI
text:
Summary
Data is one major source of AI risk, and treating it as a section inside model development instead of a discipline in its own right is how organizations miss where much of their risk sits. The governable data surface is broader than training data. It includes fine-tuning sets, retrieval corpora, and runtime data, and a system on the buy path, which describes most deployments, still has a data surface even when it has no training data at all.
Five quality dimensions, accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, and validity, turn a vague complaint about bad data into something a team can test for, and each produces a specific failure once trained on, not merely stored. Provenance and lineage make source, collection circumstances, transformations, and permissions traceable, which is what makes the other dimensions auditable rather than asserted. Representativeness asks whether a training population resembles a deployment population, a question testing against the training population’s own held-out data cannot answer by construction, as MEDASSIST’s community hospitals demonstrated. Historical, measurement, and selection bias are three distinct mechanisms requiring three distinct remedies, and diagnosing which is operating in a given dataset is analytical work a single word like “bias” cannot substitute for.
Retrieval corpus governance and fine-tuning data review extend these disciplines to surfaces that training-data governance has no native vocabulary for. Privacy-enhancing technologies each protect against a specific threat while leaving others open, so choosing among them depends on the threat at hand, not on a default setting. ## Review questions
COMPREHENSION

Explain why testing a model against a held-out sample from its own training population cannot detect a representativeness problem, and state what kind of evidence could.
Distinguish historical bias from measurement bias using the healthcare cost-proxy case, and explain why the remedy for one would not fix the other.

APPLIED

An organization purchases a language model and connects it to a retrieval system drawing on its internal wiki. Six months after deployment, a compliance review discovers that queries have returned draft HR investigation notes to employees outside HR. Identify which section of this chapter’s framework the failure traces to, and specify at least three controls that would have prevented it.
A fine-tuning set of four thousand customer service transcripts is assembled by pulling the most recent transcripts available. Explain two distinct ways this selection method could introduce bias, and describe how you would check for each.

SPOT THE RISK

A team preparing a dataset for a new credit model reports the following. All fields are populated, a manual review found no incorrect values, the schema has not changed in three years, and null values are rare. They conclude the data is high quality and ready for training. Identify at least four questions this assessment leaves unanswered, and for each, name the section of this chapter that supplies it.

COMPARE AND DECIDE

An organization must choose between differential privacy, applied to a dataset of patient interactions used to fine-tune a clinical assistant, and synthetic data generated to replace the real interactions entirely. State what each option protects against, what it does not, and what you would need to know about the intended use to decide between them.

RUNNING CASE

MEDASSIST Using the two failures described in this chapter’s case in focus, identify what a properly completed datasheet would have recorded for the training data, and explain specifically how having that record available would have changed what happened at deployment to the community hospitals.


A model trained on well-governed data and evaluated only against the population it was trained on has answered a narrower question than deployment requires. The next chapter turns to the model itself and to what an organization inherits when it builds one, fine-tunes one, or selects one someone else built. That choice closes off governance options long before the system sees any of the data this chapter covered.

title: 6. Model Selection and Development
text:
What you will be able to do
Meridian Financial’s model risk function had governed FAIRLEND’s original credit model for a decade. The model was a scorecard, a logistic regression over a small set of engineered variables. Every coefficient in it could be explained to an examiner in one sentence, stating how much weight it carried, in which direction, and why. When the data science team proposed replacing it with a gradient-boosted ensemble trained on a larger feature set, the performance case was not close. The new model separated good loans from bad loans measurably better, on the bank’s own validation data, than the scorecard ever had. The model risk function approved the replacement. Only after deployment did anyone outside the data science team ask the question the approval process had skipped. When an applicant asks why they were declined, what does the bank now say? Can it defend that answer to a regulator whose statute requires a specific reason and not a probability score?
The ensemble was better at the thing it was measured on. Meridian’s choice was between two goods that do not come bundled together, predictive accuracy and the kind of explanation an adverse-action notice requires. In practice, whoever picked the modeling approach made that trade, not whoever was accountable for defending the bank’s lending decisions. Selecting or building a model is a governance decision, and often the one that closes off the most options. Most of what a system can be made to do, and most of what can later be demanded of it, is set at this layer before anything else about the system exists.

Read a system card adversarially, focusing on what it omits, what a vague section signals, and what questions a thin card should generate before selection

Specify what a model bill of materials records and why an organization that cannot produce one cannot investigate its own system

7  6. Model Selection and Development

title: 6. Model Selection and Development
text:
6.1 Build, fine-tune, or select
Three nested lifecycles run underneath every AI system, at different cadences and under different ownership. The use case layer is the business process being served, such as hiring, lending, or clinical triage, and it outlives everything built to serve it. The system layer is what Part II governs. It covers the scoping, design, integration, deployment, operation, and retirement of a working system, which typically contains one or more models together with retrieval, tools, interfaces, and guardrails. The model layer is narrower still, and it is the fastest-moving and least visible of the three. A model is trained, validated, versioned, retrained, and eventually deprecated on its own schedule. One model can serve several systems, and one system can swap its model without changing what the system does from a user’s point of view. The three layers need to stay distinct, because a decision at the model layer, such as which base model a system is built on, can constrain the system layer for years without anyone at the system layer having made a choice.
Most organizations will not train a model from scratch. Three paths exist, and they differ in what they afford and what they foreclose.
Building from scratch means training a model on data the organization controls. It costs real data, compute, and specialized skill, and increasingly few organizations undertake it for a general capability. It remains common for narrow, well-specified predictive tasks, where a purpose-built model outperforms a general one and the organization has the historical data to train it. FAIRLEND’s original scorecard, and the ensemble that replaced it, both sit on this path. Full visibility into training data and the resulting model is the payoff, and full accountability for what the training data taught the model is the corresponding cost.
Fine-tuning means adapting a model someone else trained, adjusting its behavior toward a narrower task using a much smaller dataset than the base model required. This path inherits the base model’s properties wholesale, including properties the fine-tuning organization did not choose and frequently cannot fully inspect. A model fine-tuned to draft clinical documentation still carries whatever the base model learned during its original training, on data the fine-tuning organization never saw and cannot audit. Fine-tuning does not remove that inheritance. Depending on the method, it either adjusts the base model’s own weights, producing a new set in which the original training and the adaptation cannot be separated, or leaves the base weights frozen and trains a small set of additional parameters alongside them. The second can be versioned and removed separately. The first cannot, which is why the model bill of materials in section 6.8 asks which method was used. Section 6.3 sets out what that inheritance consists of.
Selecting means purchasing or licensing a model as-is, with no training or fine-tuning at all, and it is the path most organizations will be on. TALENTSCREEN’s resume-screening component sits here. Calloway licensed a model the vendor trained, on data the vendor has not disclosed, and Calloway’s governance function has no way to influence the training decisions that shaped it. Selection affords the least visibility of the three paths and forecloses the most. It means accepting another organization’s conclusions about what the model should and should not do.
Legal and governance obligation attaches differently on each path. A builder is accountable for what its training data taught the model, because it chose the data. A fine-tuner is accountable for what it added. It may also take on the base model developer’s obligations where fine-tuning changes its legal role, for example by rebranding the model, substantially modifying it, or changing its intended purpose. A regulation like the EU AI Act treats such a change as making the fine-tuner a provider in its own right. Fine-tuning alone does not automatically produce that shift. It depends on the role, system classification, market action, and modification tests the applicable regulation sets. Even a fine-tuner that does not become the legal provider can still carry contractual, product, or professional obligations toward the base model. This surprises organizations that assume responsibility flows entirely to the base model’s developer, whatever the fine-tuning changed. A purchaser is accountable for how it deploys a model it did not shape at all. That sounds like the lightest obligation of the three, until an incident occurs and the purchaser finds that “we didn’t build it” is not a defense available to a deployer under most of the frameworks this book covers. Obligation attaches to what a system does, not to who trained the model inside it (Chapter 2), and that principle becomes a selection criterion here.

title: 6. Model Selection and Development
section: 6.2 Model affordances and the control surface
text:
6.2 Model affordances and the control surface
Whichever path is chosen, the resulting model supports a specific set of behaviors, and a team that does not know them will invent a worse control than the one the model already offers. The most common example is a human review step layered on an automated output, which automation bias quietly hollows out (Chapter 1). A list of which vendor’s model does what this year goes stale within months. The axes persist even as models move along them, so the discipline is to ask, for each axis, what control it enables or forecloses.
Constrained and structured output determines whether a model’s output can be forced into a schema a downstream system can validate mechanically, instead of parsed hopefully from free text. A model that supports structured output lets a governance function write a machine-checkable gate, a field that must be one of a fixed set of values, or a confidence score that must exceed a threshold before an action proceeds. A model without that support pushes the same check into a fragile text-parsing layer that fails silently when the model’s phrasing drifts.
Tool calling with scoped permissions determines whether a model can request an action through an interface a surrounding system can constrain, instead of acting through an interface with no such structure. The scoping itself, which specific operations are permitted, is enforced mainly by the deployment architecture and by identity and access management around the model, not by the model. What the model contributes is whether it supports structured tool calls at all. What the deploying organization’s architecture contributes is whether those calls are bounded. Agentic controls depend on this axis, and Chapter 12 treats the enforcement layer, not the model property, in full.
Instruction hierarchy describes a model’s measured tendency to weight its developer’s and its deploying system’s instructions over instructions introduced later by a user or by content the system processes. It is not a dependable security boundary. Research and incident reports on prompt injection show that a sufficiently constructed input can still override instructions a model was trained to prioritize. A governance function should treat instruction-following strength as a behavior to test and monitor (Chapter 7), not as a control it can rely on in place of an enforced permission boundary.
Context handling determines how much material a model can hold and reason over at once, and it interacts with retrieval corpus governance (Chapter 5). A model with a short effective context forces aggressive retrieval filtering. A model with a long one tempts a system designer into dumping an entire corpus into context and calling it complete, which reintroduces the permission-inheritance failure from Chapter 5 at a different layer.
Confidence and abstention signals determine whether a model can indicate, in a form the surrounding system can act on, that it is uncertain or that a request falls outside what it should answer. A model that can abstain usably gives a governance function a lever, routing low-confidence outputs to a human or blocking an out-of-scope request outright. A model that cannot, or whose confidence signal does not track its accuracy, leaves the surrounding system no better placed to catch failures than a system with no signal. It can be worse, because a badly calibrated signal invites false trust.
Modality determines what kind of input and output a model handles, text, image, audio, and combinations of these, and it determines which governance controls apply. A control built around auditing generated text does nothing for a model that also generates images.
Latency and cost determine whether human review is operationally feasible. A model cheap and fast enough to run three times per request supports a self-consistency check. That check shows variance, not error, since a model that is confidently wrong will be consistently wrong. A slow, expensive model rules out even that check by economics, before anyone treats it as a governance question. A control that assumes a human can review every output before it ships has assumed away this axis. The assumption fails quietly once volume exceeds the assumed review capacity, as alert fatigue failed MEDASSIST’s nursing staff in Chapter 1.
Deployment options, hosted, private instance, or on-premises, determine what data may reach the model under the organization’s own data governance rules (Chapter 5) and under the sector-specific constraints in Chapter 2. A hosted model operated by a third party may be unusable for a workload involving the most sensitive data an organization holds, however well it performs on every other axis. Discovering this after selection is a recurring, avoidable failure. Check this axis first.






Figure 7.1: Figure 6.1. Affordance axes mapped to the controls each one enables




Figure 6.1 is a lookup table, not a ranking. No axis is more important than another in the abstract. Which axes matter most depends on what the system will do. A system that never takes an action can deprioritize tool-call scoping in favor of confidence calibration.
Deriving that priority from a use case takes three steps. First, name what the system will do, in the terms section 3.3 uses for the third trace. Does it produce text a person reads, a score a person acts on, or an action it takes itself? That answer makes some axes binding and leaves the rest as preferences, and Table 6.1 shows how.
Table 6.1. Binding axes by what the system does








System
Binding axes
Reason




Takes an action itself (agentic)
Tool scoping and instruction hierarchy
A model that cannot emit a bounded tool call cannot be made to later


Produces a decision a person must explain
Confidence and abstention
A score with no calibrated uncertainty gives the reviewer nothing to review


Handles regulated content
Deployment option
Where the model runs decides what leaves the organization



Second, score the candidates on the binding axes only, recording for each what is known, what the vendor asserts, and what is untested, which is the same three-way marking the bill of materials in section 6.8 uses. Third, compare accuracy among the candidates that cleared the binding axes. Taking accuracy first is what produces a shortlist of one, because the most accurate model is usually the one whose affordances nobody examined. Without these steps, a procurement decision is made on accuracy and price alone, and the control questions arise only after the contract is signed.

7  6. Model Selection and Development

title: 6. Model Selection and Development
section: 6.3 What you inherit from the developer
text:
6.3 What you inherit from the developer
Building a system on a model an organization did not train means inheriting a governance regime it did not write and cannot amend. This does not resemble ordinary vendor risk, which is why procurement practices built for ordinary vendor risk keep failing to catch it. An ordinary vendor relationship is a defined service against a defined specification, negotiated between two parties who can both amend the terms. A model developer’s governance decisions were made for a global customer base the deploying organization was never party to. Below a certain contract size, the deploying organization typically cannot negotiate them at all. Procurement teams tend to discover this only after signing.
Usage policies constrain what an organization may build on top of the model at all. A use the deploying organization considers legitimate can fall outside what the developer’s policy permits. Resolving such a conflict depends on facts specific to the use, but it has to be checked before the system is built, not after the developer itself discovers a policy violation.
Safety training decisions determine what the model will refuse, and a refusal shaped by the developer’s view of global misuse risk reaches the deploying organization’s own users as the deploying organization’s behavior. A clinical documentation assistant built on a general-purpose model can refuse to discuss a topic the developer’s safety training treats as sensitive across all use cases, even where the specific clinical context makes the refusal unhelpful. The deploying organization’s users experience that refusal as the deploying organization declining to help them, not as a decision made months earlier by an organization they have never heard of.
Deprecation schedules force migration onto whichever timeline the developer sets, and a forced migration is not a routine software update. It is a revalidation event, because a new model version can change behavior in ways the deploying organization’s original testing never covered. Chapter 7’s testing discipline applies to a forced migration with the same weight as an initial deployment. An organization that budgets a model migration as a configuration change instead of a revalidation event has under-budgeted it, and finds out at the worst time, immediately after the old version stops being supported.
Data retention and training-use terms determine whether an organization’s regulated data may touch the interface at all. These terms can differ across a single developer’s pricing tiers. An enterprise agreement may disclaim training use of submitted data where a consumer-tier agreement for the same underlying model does not. An organization that verifies these terms once at selection and not again when the tier or contract changes is assuming, not knowing.
Published safety frameworks, where a developer maintains one, determine which safeguards ship with the model and which the deploying organization must add itself. A developer’s safety framework is written to manage that developer’s risk across its entire customer base, not the risk profile of any one deployment. Gaps it leaves open are inherited by the deploying organization by default, unless it closes them itself.
System cards determine what the deploying organization can claim to know about the model it selected, and what a card leaves out is at least as informative as what it says.






Figure 7.2: Figure 6.2. Model supply chain layers, and where obligation attaches




Figure 6.2 shows roles with distinct duties, not a single chain of escalating blame. Table 6.2 maps each entry point to the role it carries and the duties attached to that role.
Table 6.2. Entry point, role, and attached duties








Entry point
Role
Duties




Build
Model provider
Carries the provider’s duties


Fine-tune
Fine-tuner
Adds the fine-tuner’s own duties on top of whatever the base model’s provider already owes. Takes on the provider’s duties as well where one of the Article 25(1) conditions is met

The three Article 25(1) conditions are putting its own name or trademark on a high-risk system already on the market, making a substantial modification to a high-risk system that the initial conformity assessment did not foresee, and changing the intended purpose of a system that was not classified as high-risk so that it becomes one. The third matters most to a fine-tuner, because it is designed to catch the organization working on a system that is not high-risk today. Each actor is responsible for the duties attached to its role. Entering the chain later changes which duties attach, but the deploying organization can still be held to account for its own use.
None of the six items above is boilerplate to accept at signature and never revisit. Each is a governance input, assessed with the rigor Chapter 16 applies to contracts generally, reassessed at each material change, and documented in the record Chapter 3 requires for every system the organization operates, on the buy path as much as the build path.

title: 6. Model Selection and Development
text:
6.4 Reading a system card adversarially
A system card is a developer’s own account of a model’s intended use, its training approach at whatever level of detail the developer chooses to disclose, its evaluated capabilities and limitations, and its known risks. The format traces to the model card structure Margaret Mitchell and colleagues proposed in 2018 for this purpose, giving a model’s downstream users a standard place to find answers to basic questions a developer would otherwise never think to volunteer. As of 2026, major developers of large general-purpose models generally publish something in this tradition, whether they call it a model card or a system card. The practice is a convention, not a uniform requirement, and its depth varies widely between developers.
Reading one adversarially means treating it as a document written by an interested party, because it is, and asking three questions a passive reading skips.
What does the card evaluate, and what does it not. A card that reports strong performance on a broad benchmark suite says nothing about performance on the deploying organization’s specific task unless that task resembles the benchmark closely. A card that does not state what it did not test has not demonstrated that the model performs well on the untested cases. It has left the question open, in a way that to an unhurried reader looks answered.
What does a vague evaluation section signal. A section that describes a testing methodology in specific, checkable terms (sample sizes, evaluator qualifications where humans graded, the actual metric computed) carries more weight than a vaguer one. A section that reports only a qualitative summary of “extensive testing” is the vaguer kind. The gap between the two signals what the developer is confident enough to make checkable. A thin section does not prove a thin evaluation, but it removes the deploying organization’s ability to tell the difference, which for governance purposes is the same thing.
Which claims does disclosed testing support. A card that reports the model resisted a red-team exercise for one category of harm supports a claim about that category and no other. A deploying organization that reads the resistance as evidence of general robustness has extended the claim past what the evidence covers. Chapter 7 treats that error as a specification failure in its own right.
A thin card, read this way, generates the deploying organization’s own pre-selection testing agenda instead of closing the question. MEDASSIST’s generative documentation assistant was selected on a general-purpose model whose card disclosed evaluation on general medical question-answering but was silent on clinical documentation specifically. That silence should have generated a testing requirement, before deployment, covering the gap the card left open, instead of being treated as an absence of concern. Chapter 15 applies the same adversarial discipline to a card the organization itself produces. Template 4, the Model Card, serves both directions. For a model the organization built, it is the card it publishes. For a purchased model, it is the structure in which to record what the vendor disclosed and what it did not, marking the undisclosed fields rather than leaving them blank. A governance function that can read a vendor’s card critically but cannot apply the same standard to its own has not adopted the discipline, only pointed it outward.

title: 6. Model Selection and Development
text:
6.5 Architecture and its governance consequences
A system card describes a model already built on one side of a tradeoff its developer made before the card was written. Accuracy and interpretability often trade against each other, so model selection should test the question and not settle it by assumption in either direction. For some tasks, a model simple enough that a person can trace how it reached a specific output is measurably less accurate than a more complex model trained on the same data. The complex model captures interactions between variables that a simple model’s structure cannot represent. This is not a universal law. Work on high-stakes prediction problems, in particular Cynthia Rudin’s argument in Nature Machine Intelligence in 2019, has shown that interpretable models can match or approach the performance of black-box alternatives. The finding is strongest for the structured tabular data that credit underwriting uses. It does not transfer automatically to perception or language tasks, where a black box’s added complexity may earn its keep. An organization cannot assume the tradeoff exists in its own case without testing for it.
The burden in this comparison falls on the complex model. The case for accepting a harder-to-interpret model should be made explicitly, with evidence. That means comparing the best viable interpretable model against the proposed complex model on the intended population and the operational metrics that matter, and stating the accuracy gain the complex model delivers after that comparison. It also means accepting the added complexity only when a material, reproducible benefit remains and the resulting explanation, monitoring, and recourse obligations can still be met. The case should not be assumed because the more complex option scored better on the metric someone computed first.
“The best viable interpretable model” is the interpretable model built with the same effort the complex one received, with the same feature engineering, the same tuning, and the same data. A logistic regression fitted in an afternoon and beaten by a gradient-boosted model tuned for three weeks has not lost a comparison. It has not been in one.
Run properly, the comparison can resolve either way. Northfield’s deterioration model went the other way from FAIRLEND. The interpretable baseline reached an area under the curve of 0.78 on the validation set, and the gradient-boosted model reached 0.86. The gain concentrated in the early-warning window where a clinician can still act. That is a material difference where the cost of a missed deterioration is measured in lives, not review time. The obligations still had to be met, and were. Northfield built a post-hoc explanation method into the clinical review interface, tracked performance by unit rather than in aggregate, and documented a route for a clinician to record disagreement with an alert. Northfield accepted complexity and wrote down why, which is what the burden asks for. Meridian accepted complexity and did not, which is why the two cases end differently. FAIRLEND’s ensemble scored better on the metric the data science team computed, and nobody made the affirmative case that losing interpretability was worth it for the obligation the loss bears on most directly, an explainable adverse-action notice. The tradeoff is not confined to the build path. A system built around a selected model, adding retrieval, chained calls, or an agentic loop with several decision points, accumulates the same cost even where the model itself never changes.

title: 6. Model Selection and Development
text:
6.6 Interpretability and post-hoc explanation
Two approaches answer the question of what a model’s reasoning was, and confusing them produces a recurring error, mistaking an explanation that sounds right for one that is right.
An intrinsically interpretable model is one whose structure is the explanation. A linear or logistic regression’s coefficients state how much weight the model places on each input, and in which direction. Reading them is reading the model’s own computation, not a separate account of it. FAIRLEND’s original scorecard had this property, which let Meridian answer an adverse-action inquiry by pointing at the coefficients themselves.
A post-hoc explanation technique is applied after the fact to a model whose structure does not reveal its reasoning. It produces an approximation of what drove a specific output, not a report of the model’s literal computation. SHAP, short for Shapley Additive Explanations, draws on a cooperative game theory concept. It assigns each input feature a contribution value for a specific prediction, computed by considering how the prediction changes as each feature is added to every possible subset of the others. A feature is never literally absent at inference, so absence is implemented by replacing it, either by marginalizing over a background dataset or by substituting reference values. That choice is the value function, and different choices produce different attributions for the same model and the same case. LIME, short for Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations, takes a different route to a similar goal. It perturbs the input around the case being explained and fits a simple, interpretable model to approximate the complex model’s behavior in that local neighborhood. It then reports the simple model’s coefficients as the explanation.
The distinction that matters for governance is between an explanation that is faithful and one that is plausible. A faithful explanation reflects what the model computed. A plausible one sounds reasonable to the reader, whether or not it matches the computation. LIME explains a local neighborhood through an interpretable surrogate fitted to perturbed inputs, so its fidelity depends on the perturbation and fitting choices behind the surrogate. It is an approximation by construction. SHAP is a family of feature-attribution methods, and the distinction is sharper there. Some implementations approximate Shapley values, while TreeSHAP can compute them exactly for supported tree-based models, under the value function and dependence assumptions it uses. Even an exact Shapley value, computed under a chosen value function, is not a causal account of what happened in the world. Nor does it guarantee that the attribution matches a person’s intuitive sense of “why.” Exactness under SHAP’s own assumptions is a different claim from faithfulness to a causal story. A reader who cannot check either method’s output against what the model computed, or against what the value function assumes, cannot tell by looking whether an explanation is faithful or only sounds right. Treating a post-hoc explanation as equivalent to an intrinsically interpretable model’s own structure, when defending a decision to a regulator or an affected individual, risks defending it with an account that was never verified to be true.

title: 6. Model Selection and Development
text:
6.7 Version control and reproducibility
Whether an explanation is faithful or plausible can only be checked against the model that produced it. A model that cannot be reproduced cannot be investigated. Reproducibility is a precondition for governance once something goes wrong, not a software-engineering nicety. It means being able to state which model version, trained on which data, with which configuration, produced a specific output under investigation. Where the model is deterministic, the pinned version can also be rerun to test the output directly. Many generative models will not return an identical result on rerun even from a pinned version. In that case the investigation relies on the traceable record of version, data, and configuration, not on an exact replay.
On the build path, this means versioning the training data, the code, and the resulting model weights together. A later question about a specific prediction can then be traced back to the conditions that produced it, instead of to a best guess at what the pipeline probably looked like. On the selection path, where the organization did not train the model at all, the analogous discipline is pinning the specific model version in production. The organization must be able to demonstrate, for any output under review, which pinned version produced it. A developer’s silent update to a hosted model between one request and the next can change behavior in ways that make a prior investigation’s findings inapplicable to the version now running. An organization that cannot answer “which version of the model produced this output” when an incident under Chapter 10’s response discipline requires the answer has failed a governance requirement, however sophisticated the model is.

title: 6. Model Selection and Development
section: 6.8 Provenance and model bills of materials
text:
6.8 Provenance and model bills of materials
A model bill of materials records what a model is made of, in enough detail that the record, not memory, can answer a later question about it. The starting minimum names the base model and its version, the specific weights in use, and the training data or the data used for any fine-tuning applied on top of a base model. It also names any adapters or fine-tuning layers added and by whom, and the software dependencies the model relies on to run. Each can carry its own vulnerabilities or licensing constraints, which the model’s governance record should surface instead of leaving them in an infrastructure team’s separate inventory. A record limited to that starting list is still incomplete. It should also carry hashes and identifiers sufficient to confirm exactly which artifact is in use, dataset versions and their own provenance, licensing terms for every component, intended and explicitly prohibited uses, and the evaluation evidence behind any performance claim. It also needs to carry the runtime environment the model depends on, upstream supplier and service dependencies, known limitations and vulnerabilities, the change history that produced the current version, and the deployment configuration it is running under. Each field should distinguish what the organization knows directly, what a supplier attests without independent verification, and what remains unavailable, since collapsing those three into a single populated-looking field misrepresents how much the organization knows.
This record extends the model record from Chapter 3. Template 3, the Model Inventory Record, establishes what a model is and which systems it serves. Template 14, the Model Bill of Materials, establishes what it is made of, and the two connect through the same model identifier. An organization that keeps only the first has a list. An incident asks which artifact produced an output, and only the second answers that. An inventory entry that cannot say what model version underlies a system, what it was fine-tuned on, or what dependencies it carries records that the system exists but not what is needed to govern it. TALENTSCREEN’s buy-path exposure shows the point. Calloway’s vendor controls most of the fields a full model bill of materials would contain, and Calloway’s own governance record can only state what the vendor discloses, which is frequently less than the full list above. That gap is itself a governance finding, one that belongs in Calloway’s record explicitly, not papered over by leaving the fields blank without comment. A blank field with no explanation looks, to a later reviewer, like a task nobody did rather than information nobody had.
Calloway’s record, filled honestly, shows what a buy-path bill of materials looks like. Every field carries how it is known.








MBOM
MBOM-2024-019 · TalentScreen scoring model · extends MDL-2024-019


BASE MODEL
Not disclosed. Vendor states a proprietary ensemble. UNAVAILABLE


VERSION
4.2, as returned by the vendor portal 11 September 2024. SUPPLIER-ATTESTED


WEIGHTS
Not in Calloway’s possession. No hash obtainable. Substitute: portal version string, endpoint region eu-west, service tier 2. UNAVAILABLE


TRAINING DATA
Requested 3 March 2024, refused as proprietary, escalated to procurement, unresolved. UNAVAILABLE


ADAPTERS
Vendor states none applied for Calloway’s tenancy. No means of verification. SUPPLIER-ATTESTED


DEPENDENCIES
Vendor-hosted. Calloway’s integration: ATS connector v1.4, internal. DIRECTLY VERIFIED


LICENSING
Master agreement clause 7, permits use for internal hiring only. DIRECTLY VERIFIED


PROHIBITED USES
Vendor terms prohibit use outside recruitment and any redistribution of scores. SUPPLIER-ATTESTED


EVALUATION
Vendor cites evaluation on general recruitment data. No disaggregated results supplied. No evaluation on warehouse or logistics roles. SUPPLIER-ATTESTED


CHANGE NOTICE
No contractual obligation on the vendor to notify a model change. Last notice received: none. DIRECTLY VERIFIED


VULNERABILITIES
None disclosed. Absence of disclosure is not evidence of absence. UNAVAILABLE


SERVES
SYS-2024-041




Read the right-hand column first. Four fields are unavailable, four rest on the vendor’s word alone, and three are things Calloway verified itself. That distribution is the governance finding, and it is legible at a glance only because the marking is there. The same record without it would read as a completed document. What it says is that Calloway cannot answer which artifact produced a given score, and would learn that during an investigation rather than before one.
The CHANGE NOTICE field is the one to raise at renewal. A vendor under no obligation to say when the model changed can change it between one hiring cycle and the next, and Calloway’s evidence from the prior cycle then describes a model that is no longer running.

title: 6. Model Selection and Development
section: Case in focus: two selections, two exposures
text:
Case in focus: two selections, two exposures
FAIRLEND and MEDASSIST · Hypothetical, following the running cases
Meridian’s data science team built the case for replacing FAIRLEND‘s scorecard on a single axis. The gradient-boosted ensemble separated good loans from bad loans more accurately than the model it would replace, measured on the bank’s own validation data. The model risk function that approved the replacement was staffed by people who understood credit risk and had governed the scorecard competently for a decade. The approval process they ran checked the ensemble’s accuracy, its stability across resampled validation sets, and its consistency with the bank’s existing risk appetite. It did not include, as a named criterion with its own accountable owner, whether the bank could still produce a specific, statute-compliant reason for an adverse action once the scorecard’s coefficients were no longer the mechanism generating decisions. The gap was not caught by the model risk function, which was not the function positioned to catch it. It was also not caught by legal, which was not consulted until a post-launch review flagged declined applicants’ adverse-action notices as vaguer than the prior model had ever required them to be. The fix Meridian eventually adopted, a post-hoc explanation layer generating per-decision reason codes, produced a notice that read as specific again. Nothing in the fix confirmed the reason codes were faithful to what the ensemble weighed, stable across similar applicants, or adequate under legal review, the same gap section 6.6 already warns a post-hoc explanation can leave open. That notice was produced after the fact, at additional engineering cost, for a gap that section 6.5’s affirmative-burden framing would have exposed before the model was ever put into production.
Northfield’s documentation assistant took the opposite path through the same underlying decision. The team selecting a model for it evaluated several general-purpose candidates on writing quality and cost, both reasonable criteria, and pulled each candidate’s system card before selecting, a step Meridian’s process for FAIRLEND had no equivalent of. The card for the model eventually selected disclosed evaluation on general medical question-answering and was explicit about not having evaluated clinical documentation drafting specifically, instead of staying silent on it. Reading that disclosure adversarially, per section 6.4, the team treated it as a testing requirement, not an absence of concern. It ran its own evaluation against a set of real admission-summary drafting tasks before deployment. That testing caught two behaviors that the vendor’s own testing had never had reason to look for, an overconfident phrasing pattern on uncertain diagnoses and a tendency to omit rather than flag missing information.
The two cases were run by capable teams inside organizations that both took governance seriously. They diverged on a single point, whether the model-selection decision was treated as a governance decision in its own right, with its own accountable owner and its own named criteria beyond the metric the selecting team happened to optimize, or as a technical choice that governance would review afterward if a problem appeared. Section 6.1’s point that selection closes off options before governance can weigh in is what happened at Meridian, and Northfield’s card-reading discipline was built to prevent it.

title: 6. Model Selection and Development
text:
Summary
The model layer moves faster and is governed less visibly than the system layer built around it. Most organizations will select a model instead of building one, so most of the weight falls on what selection inherits. Build, fine-tune, and select carry different visibility and different attachment of obligation. An organization needs to know which path it is on before it can know what it is accountable for.
The affordance axes, structured output, tool scoping, instruction hierarchy, context handling, confidence and abstention, modality, latency and cost, and deployment option, determine what controls a system built on a given model can support. Selecting a model an organization did not train means inheriting usage policies, safety training decisions, deprecation schedules, data terms, safety frameworks, and a system card, none of it boilerplate and all of it requiring the same governance rigor Chapter 16 applies to contracts generally. Reading a system card adversarially, for what it does not evaluate and what a vague section signals, turns the card into a testing agenda, not a closed question.
Whether architecture trades accuracy against interpretability is a question to test in the specific case, with the burden of justification on the more complex choice. Post-hoc explanation techniques like SHAP and LIME approximate a model’s reasoning without guaranteeing the approximation is faithful to what the model computed, and a plausible explanation is not automatically a true one. A model that cannot be reproduced cannot be investigated. A model bill of materials lets a later reviewer answer what a system is made of, on the buy path as much as the build path, even where the honest answer is that the vendor has not disclosed it.

title: 6. Model Selection and Development
text:
Review questions
COMPREHENSION

Explain why fine-tuning a purchased model does not remove the governance obligations attached to the base model, and state what it adds on top of them.
Distinguish a faithful explanation from a plausible one, using SHAP or LIME as the example, and explain why a governance function cannot tell the difference by reading the explanation alone.

APPLIED

An organization is evaluating three candidate models for a customer-facing chatbot that will occasionally need to escalate a request to a human agent. Using the affordance axes from section 6.2, identify which two axes matter most for this specific use case and explain what you would test for each before selection.
A vendor’s system card for a model an organization is considering discloses strong performance on general reasoning benchmarks and does not mention testing on multilingual inputs, while the organization’s intended use is multilingual. Write the pre-selection testing requirement this gap should generate.

SPOT THE RISK

A team reports that it selected a model for a new system based on its top ranking on a public leaderboard, confirmed the vendor’s usage policy permits the intended use, and is proceeding to deployment. Identify at least four gaps in this selection process, and for each, name the section of this chapter that supplies what is missing.

COMPARE AND DECIDE

An organization must choose between an intrinsically interpretable model with a measurable accuracy disadvantage and a more accurate model that would require a post-hoc explanation layer to meet a regulatory disclosure obligation. State what each option costs, what risk each carries, and what you would need to know about the specific obligation to decide between them.

RUNNING CASE

FAIRLEND Using the case in focus, identify the specific governance step that was missing from Meridian’s model risk approval process and name who should have owned it. Explain how you would build that step into a selection process so it applies before deployment instead of being discovered afterward.


The next chapter turns to verification. It covers how an organization tests a system whose behavior cannot be fully specified in advance, and why the fairness metrics that sound like they should agree provably do not. It also covers what it means to specify a property, like refusing to fabricate an answer, that resists direct specification.

title: 7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming
text:
What you will be able to do
Meridian is a bank. Its model FAIRLEND decides who gets a loan. FAIRLEND is an ensemble, which means it combines several models into one decision. Before the bank’s model risk team signed off, it ran three standard fairness tests. The first compared approval rates across protected groups. Protected groups are groups of people, such as groups defined by race, sex, or age, whom the law shields from unfair treatment. The second compared true positive rates across those groups. The true positive rate is the share of the people who would repay whom the model approves. The third checked the model’s predicted probabilities against actual repayment outcomes within each group. Every test passed, at an approval cutoff the review team considered reasonable.
Then one team member read the results side by side instead of one at a time. That person asked a question nobody had framed. Suppose the approval rate is equal across groups. Suppose the true positive rate is also equal. Suppose the groups differ in their base rates for actual repayment, the share of people in a group who repay. How can the false positive rate also be equal? A false positive here is an applicant who would not repay but is approved. It cannot be equal. Here is why. The equal approval rate fixes what share of each group is approved. The equal true positive rate fixes what share of each group’s repayers is approved. Because the groups differ in their share of repayers, the approvals that go to non-repayers must make up a different share of each group’s non-repayers. Different base rates then force different false positive rates. The team made no error. These properties cannot all hold when the groups differ in their underlying repayment rates.
The review had treated fairness as a checklist of properties a good model should all have. Fairness is a set of tradeoffs. Someone has to choose among them, on the record. That person must be ready to explain the choice. The audience could be a regulator, a plaintiff’s attorney, or an applicant who wants to know why the model treated their case as it did.
Testing an AI system means checking behavior that cannot be fully written down in advance. Chapter 1 showed why. A generative system’s output is a plausible continuation, not a verified fact. A rule learned from data is confident on cases it has never seen. Chapters 5 and 6 described what data and model choices set up before a system is ever tested. The FAIRLEND review above shows the problem. Every test passed, and a choice remained that no test could make. Generative systems and agents add other cases. A generative system produces new content, such as text, so its outputs often have no single correct answer. An agent is a system that takes actions, so its actions must be checked along the way. Some properties cannot be written as a rule. Refusing to fabricate an answer, meaning to make one up, is one. Such a property has to be turned into a requirement that a test can check.

title: 7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming
text:
Choose and defend a fairness metric for a specific decision, and explain to a skeptical reviewer why several widely used metrics cannot all be met at once when group base rates differ.
Design an evaluation set for a generative system, with a grading rubric and an inter-rater reliability check.
Explain benchmark contamination and the holdout discipline that survives it.
Recognize the documented failure modes of using a model to grade another model’s output.
Structure a red team exercise, including scope, team composition, and what happens to a finding afterward.
Decompose a property that cannot be directly specified into a verifiable proxy, a stated threshold, a verification method, and a named residual. The residual is the part the test does not cover.

8  7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming

title: 7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming
text:
7.1 Performance testing
A system must first do the narrow thing it claims to do. That is measured on data it has not seen during training, the stage where a model learns patterns from example data. A classifier is a system that sorts cases into categories, such as approve or decline. For a classifier, the right metric, the number that scores performance, depends on what an error costs. The wrong metric yields a model optimized for the wrong failure.
Two kinds of error matter. A false positive means the system says yes when the true answer is no. A false negative means the system says no when the true answer is yes. Take a system that screens resumes for further review. It can tolerate more false positives, which means letting through more candidates than necessary, because a false positive costs only a wasted interview. Now take a system that flags patients at risk of sepsis, a dangerous reaction to infection. It should weight false negatives more heavily, because a missed case can mean a preventable death. Accuracy alone, the share of all cases the system gets right, treats both errors as equally costly. It hides the distinction that matters for MEDASSIST, Northfield Health’s sepsis-alert system. For that system, accuracy would never have been an acceptable metric in the first place.
Other kinds of task need other choices. Regression tasks predict a number, such as a price. They need a choice between two kinds of metric. One kind penalizes large errors heavily, so one big miss costs far more than many small ones. The other treats every unit of error the same. Ranking tasks put items in order, such as a list of search results. They need a decision about which position in the ranked list drives the outcome a user experiences.
Held-out data, data kept away from training and used only for testing, underlies every number in this section. A model evaluated on data it trained on reports its ability to memorize, not its ability to generalize, meaning to work well on new cases. The gap is invisible unless the evaluation set was kept separate from training from the start. Sampling the set afterward does not achieve this, because the data may already have influenced the model through earlier iterations of the same pipeline, the chain of steps that builds and updates it. Section 7.5 covers a harder case. There the held-out set leaks into training through a channel the organization does not control.
A known correct answer is not always available when testing needs it, or in the form testing needs. Five things can get in the way.
Table 7.1. Five conditions that put a known correct answer out of reach







Condition
How it shows up




Delayed
A loan’s repayment is unknown until the loan matures years later


Selectively observed
A hiring model is checked only against people the organization hired, so declined applicants are never checked


Contested
Clinicians reviewing the same case may disagree about whether it was high risk


Affected by the intervention being tested
A fraud model’s flag changes what happens to a transaction, and so changes what outcome is recorded


A proxy
The recorded outcome is a stand-in for the thing meant



The proxy condition is the label problem that Chapter 5 raised for data, where a label is the recorded answer attached to a case. Testing inherits any flaw in that label directly.
Performance testing remains meaningful. The evaluation unit, meaning what each test item is checked against, is a labeled or otherwise justified reference outcome, where available. It is not a known correct answer. A test report has to state which of the five conditions applies to its outcome variable, the thing being predicted. The report must not present the comparison as though the reference were known.
crumbs: Part II: The AI System Lifecycle
8  7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming

title: 7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming
text:
7.2 Fairness testing
Fairness testing is where a technical choice becomes a values choice. Several widely used metrics can conflict with each other. Four of them are introduced below as a selected comparison, not an exhaustive list. They conflict under conditions that are mathematically settled. The conflict is not an open engineering problem.
Demographic parity requires that the proportion of each group receiving a favorable outcome be equal across groups. This holds even if the groups differ in the underlying rate of whatever the outcome is meant to predict. Applied to FAIRLEND, demographic parity would require the loan approval rate to be the same for every protected group.
Equal opportunity requires that among applicants who would repay the loan, the approval rate be equal across groups. This is narrower and more targeted than demographic parity. It does not require equal approval rates overall. It requires equal rates only among those who deserve approval by the model’s own definition of deserving.
Equalized odds requires equal opportunity’s condition and adds a second one. Among applicants who would not repay, the approval rate must also be equal across groups. In other words, it is equal opportunity plus an equal false positive rate. It is a strictly harder condition than either demographic parity or equal opportunity alone.
Calibration requires that a predicted probability mean the same thing for every group. Say a model scores a set of applicants at a seventy percent likelihood of repayment. Then seventy percent of them should repay. That must hold within each group separately, as well as overall. Calibration is what makes a risk score interpretable as a probability. A lender who prices a loan from the score relies on it, whether or not the fairness review named it.
Calibration is a property of the score, the number the model assigns to a case, here the predicted probability of repayment. Calibration holds or fails before any cutoff is applied. A cutoff, or threshold, is the score above which the model approves. Demographic parity, equal opportunity, and equalized odds are properties of a decision made by applying a threshold to the score. The distinction matters. A calibrated score does not settle what happens to the three threshold-based criteria once a cutoff is chosen.
The conflict among these metrics has a name, the impossibility result. Several researchers established it independently in the mid-2010s. The fairness literature now treats it as settled. It is narrower than “no two fairness criteria can coexist,” so it needs its conditions attached. The base rate is the actual proportion of the outcome being predicted. The result concerns imperfect, nontrivial risk scores. Imperfect means the score makes some errors. Nontrivial means the score separates cases instead of treating everyone alike. For such scores, when the base rate differs between two groups, calibration cannot generally be combined with equal balance for the positive and negative classes. The positive class is the outcome the model is built to find, here repayment. The negative class is the opposite outcome. Equal balance means the error rates for both classes are equal across groups. That is the condition equalized odds requires. Here, generally means in all but special cases. Related threshold-based criteria can also conflict with calibration under the same base-rate condition. Perfect prediction and other degenerate cases are exceptions. A degenerate case is an extreme or trivial one. The result does not show that every pair of fairness criteria is incompatible.
Treat the result as a proof, not a rule of thumb. A reviewer who treats it as a rule of thumb will keep looking for a clever fix to the tension between calibration and equalized odds. No such fix exists when the base rates differ.
Choosing which fairness property to prioritize, as FAIRLEND’s review had to do, is a decision about which kind of unfairness the organization will accept. It has no single correct technical answer. A decision of that kind needs a named, accountable owner and a documented rationale. A default inherited from whichever metric a data science team computed first does not meet that need.
Calibration leaves a further gap. A calibrated score may still yield unequal error rates after thresholding, especially when base rates and score distributions differ. Which threshold-based criterion ends up unequal is a question to measure in the actual decision outcomes, because calibration does not answer it.
Meridian’s eventual decision prioritized equal opportunity over calibration. The team measured the decision outcomes under each option. Keeping calibration meant a materially higher false negative rate for one group. The case in focus below works through that reasoning and the recorded dissent.






Figure 8.1: Figure 7.1. The four fairness metrics and where they conflict




Figure 7.1 maps one narrow conflict. It does not show four independent boxes to check off. Demographic parity and equal opportunity can coexist with each other, and with calibration, under conditions that review question 6 asks you to work out. They are not proven incompatible in general. The mid-2010s impossibility result proves one pairing incompatible, for imperfect, nontrivial scores when group base rates differ. That pairing is calibration and equalized odds. FAIRLEND’s review found this tension. Every comparable fairness review will find it if it looks, whether or not its documentation names it.

title: 7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming
text:
7.3 Robustness and adversarial testing
A model tested only on data resembling its training distribution has not faced the conditions most likely to cause a costly failure. Those conditions are often the ones furthest from what the model has seen. A distribution is the pattern of which cases appear and how often.
Distribution shift testing evaluates a model on data that differs from its training population along dimensions the deployment is likely to meet. Chapter 5 raised the representativeness question for data, meaning whether the data matches the cases the system will face. This test turns that question into an explicit test before release, instead of a hoped-for property.
Boundary behavior testing probes cases at the edge of a model’s decision categories. The decision boundary is the line where the model’s output switches from one category to another, such as from approve to decline. Near it, small input differences produce different outputs. A model that is accurate on average can be unstable at the boundary where a real decision is made. Ordinary accuracy metrics average that instability away.
Adversarial testing deliberately constructs inputs designed to cause a specific failure, instead of sampling from a natural distribution. Take a predictive fraud model, which flags suspicious transactions. It can be probed with inputs engineered to sit just inside the range of scores it treats as low risk. The test asks whether an adversary who understands where its decision boundary sits could exploit it.
Generative and agentic systems face a further category of adversarial input, which Chapters 11 and 12 develop. This category is the instruction-override input. It is crafted not to fool a classification boundary but to override the system’s own instructions. It does so by embedding a competing instruction inside content the system was only supposed to read. Testing for it requires the instruction-hierarchy evaluation, where the instruction hierarchy is the system’s ordering of which instructions win when they conflict. The evaluation checks whether that ordering holds when content the system reads tries to override it. Chapter 6 flagged that a vendor’s description cannot establish this capability. It has to be checked directly, with adversarial inputs built to probe it.

title: 7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming
text:
7.4 Evaluating generative systems
Testing a classifier asks whether one output matches a known correct answer. A generative system often has no single correct output to match. Its testing is a different discipline.
Evaluation design, often shortened to eval design, starts by decomposing a broad quality claim into specific, checkable tasks. Take the claim that a documentation assistant “writes good clinical summaries.” That claim cannot be tested as stated. Break it into parts. Does the assistant correctly extract the admitting diagnosis? Does it flag missing information instead of fabricating it? Does it use terminology consistent with the hospital’s documentation standards? Each part becomes a task that a specific evaluation item can check. Section 7.9 applies the same decomposition, task by task, to properties that resist specification even after decomposition.
Rubric construction turns each task into a graded standard, a written scoring guide, so that no pass or fail call is left to whoever is reading. The rubric for the missing-information task states what counts as correctly flagging an absence. It states what counts as fabricating a value absent from the source. It also states how to resolve ambiguous cases, so the rubric decides them and not the private opinion of a grader, the person or model scoring the output. Two graders applying an underspecified rubric to the same output will disagree. The defect lies in the rubric, not in either grader.
Inter-rater reliability is the degree to which different graders agree when rating the same outputs. It measures that disagreement instead of assuming it away. It depends on a workflow as much as on the final statistic. The rubric and its worked examples must be frozen before the scored sample is graded. Each grader produces an independent first rating before seeing any other grader’s rating or discussing the item. Only then does the settling of disagreements begin. The order matters. A grader who sees another’s rating first tends to anchor toward it, which manufactures agreement.
The statistic has to match the design. Each statistic named here is a statistical measure of agreement between graders.
Table 7.2. Agreement statistics and the designs they suit







Statistic
Design it suits




Cohen’s kappa
Two graders scoring categorical ratings, ratings that sort an output into classes such as pass or fail


Weighted kappa
Two graders scoring ordered categories, such as a one-to-five scale


Intraclass correlation
Continuous ratings, ratings on a numeric scale, where its statistical assumptions are met


Krippendorff’s alpha
Cases that need its added flexibility, such as more than two graders or a mix of rating types



A low agreement score is not automatically a personnel problem to fix by training graders harder. It often shows that the rubric has not resolved an ambiguity that different graders resolve differently. Low agreement can have other causes. The training may have been inconsistent. The thing being rated may be subjective, a matter of opinion with no one right answer. The mix of items may skew toward easy or hard ones. The evidence may vary in quality across the sample. Separate these causes before rewriting anything. Where the rubric is at fault, rewrite it and log what changed and why. Then retest agreement on a fresh sample before trusting the results.

title: 7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming
text:
7.5 Benchmark contamination
A public benchmark, a standard test used to compare models, is useful only if the model being evaluated did not see its answers during training. Keeping the answers unseen is increasingly hard to guarantee. A model trained on a broad scrape of public text, a large automatic copy of web pages, has probably met the benchmark somewhere in it. The model may also have met discussion of the benchmark, worked solutions, or both. This problem is called contamination. Contamination inflates apparent performance on the benchmark without improving the capability it claims to measure. The score cannot reveal this, because a contaminated model and a capable model produce the same high number.
The holdout discipline that survives contamination is a standing practice, not a one-time fix. The organization builds an evaluation set and keeps it private, shared only with a small group that needs it. A training process the organization does not control cannot contaminate such a set. This is why the sentinel check that section 7.9 proposes is a private, rotating set and not drawn from a public source.
Sometimes a public benchmark must be used. Then one warning signal is whether a model can complete a benchmark item word for word from part of the prompt, the text given to the model. Completion would be possible only if the model had memorized the item. So completion is evidence of exposure. Failure to complete does not show the benchmark was unseen. A model can be contaminated on a paraphrased or lightly modified copy that a word-for-word test misses. This test is one signal and not a contamination audit.
A more defensible check combines several signals.
Table 7.3. Signals a defensible contamination check combines







Signal
What it involves




Private held-out sets
Use private and rotating held-out sets alongside the public benchmark


Canary items
Plant made-up markers hidden in the benchmark text to detect scraping. If a model can reproduce the marker, that is a sign the benchmark text was copied into its training data


Timestamp and version record
Keep a record showing when the benchmark was published relative to the model’s training cutoff, the date after which the model saw no new data


Provenance statement
Get a training-data provenance statement, a record of where the data came from, where the developer has published one


Overlap checks
Run lexical and semantic overlap checks between the benchmark and known training sources. Lexical overlap means shared words, and semantic overlap means shared meaning


Reworded items
Repeat the evaluation on reworded versions of the same items



Finally, state the uncertainty explicitly where the training data cannot be inspected. Do not silently assume there is no contamination.
