title: 7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming
text:
7.6 Model as judge
Using one model to grade another model’s output instead of a human is called model-as-judge. The model doing the grading is called the grading model, or the judge model. It has become common because it scales in a way human grading does not. It is also widely misunderstood. Its failure modes, when unchecked, produce confident, wrong conclusions.
Three biases are documented, each a tendency of the grading model.
Table 7.4. Documented biases of a grading model








Bias
Tendency
Consequence




Position bias
Favoring one position, first or second, regardless of content, when the model compares two candidate outputs in a fixed order
The effect is strong enough that swapping the order of the same two outputs can flip the verdict


Self-preference
Rating an output more favorably when it resembles the grader’s own style or comes from a model in its own family
Using a model to grade outputs, including outputs from its own family, is a checkable source of distortion, not a theoretical concern


Verbosity bias
Rating a longer answer more favorably, whether or not the extra length adds correct or useful content
It rewards padding over precision unless the rubric corrects for it



The model-as-judge literature reports a pattern. It is not a universal law to assume for every task and grading model. Correlation with human ratings, meaning how closely the model’s ratings track them, tends to degrade most on the cases where human graders themselves disagree most. So a grading model can be least trustworthy on the hard, contested cases where its verdict matters most. It can be most trustworthy on easy cases that a cheaper check would have settled. Whether the pattern holds for a given grading model and task is something to check.
That is why using a grading model needs a validation process and not only awareness of the three biases above.
Table 7.5. Validation checks for a grading model and what each one tests







Check
What it tests




Swap the order in which the two candidate outputs are shown and check whether the verdict flips
Position bias


Control for length, either by instructing the grader to disregard it or by adjusting scores to remove its effect
Verbosity bias


Blind the grader to which system produced which output, particularly where its own family is among the systems compared
Self-preference


Run more than one grading model, from different families where feasible, and check whether they agree
A model’s own particular bias, which no one model can catch in itself


Compare a sample of verdicts against human ratings on the same items, concentrated on the contested cases flagged above
Prompt sensitivity, meaning how much the wording of the grading instructions changes the verdict, along with score calibration, disagreement between graders, and sensitivity to the reference answer used



Finally, route a contested case that the process cannot resolve with confidence to human review.
None of this rules out using a grading model to scale evaluation. Skipping validation is a specification error, an error in how the test itself was set up, and the findings above make it predictable. Trusting a verdict on a contested case as much as one on an easy case is the same kind of error.

title: 7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming
text:
7.7 Testing agentic systems
An agentic system takes actions instead of only producing output. Testing it is a distinct discipline from classifier testing and generative evaluation. The object evaluated is a sequence of decisions with consequences. It is not a single output that can be checked in isolation.
The precondition for testing an agent honestly is a sandbox, a walled-off test environment, with realistic tools and reversible consequences. A tool here is a system the agent can act through, such as a calendar, a file store, or a payment service. Production means the live system that real users rely on. A stripped-down test environment can differ from the tool access the agent will have in production. Then the agent passes tests that do not show how it behaves with the real scheduling system, file access, or payment authority it will hold. Payment authority is the power to move money. An agent tested directly against production systems risks the irreversible harm testing exists to prevent. So the sandbox must be realistic and reversible at once.
Evaluating action sequences means grading the path an agent took as well as the result. Two agents can reach the same acceptable final state by paths that carry different risk. Consider the scheduling component of TALENTSCREEN, a hiring tool that screens resumes and also schedules interviews. Once it acts autonomously, and no longer only recommends, it has to be evaluated on whether it checked availability before committing to a time. Checking only whether an interview eventually got scheduled is not enough. A path that skips the availability check and later cancels is a materially worse outcome for the candidate. An evaluator who checks only the endpoint sees the same final scheduled state either way.
Probing what an agent does when its goal conflicts with its constraints is the testing step most often skipped. It requires scenarios where succeeding at the task and staying within a stated boundary cannot both happen. The tester then observes which one the agent gives up. Suppose an agent is told to schedule an interview within a candidate’s stated availability. It meets a scenario where no slot satisfies every constraint. What it does next reveals its real priority ordering. It may report the conflict and ask for guidance. It may silently relax a constraint it was not authorized to relax. Or it may fabricate a resolution that appears to satisfy every constraint without doing so. This kind of test has no equivalent in classifier or generative evaluation. For an agentic system, it is required.
A sandbox, action-sequence grading, and a goal-versus-constraint probe are necessary but not sufficient. An agent that passes all three can still fail under operational conditions a stripped-down test never produces. A complete agent test process adds the following stages before the system counts as tested.
First, freeze the versions of the agent, its model, its prompts, its tools, its permissions, its memory contents, and its environment. That way a later failure can be traced to one specific, recorded configuration. Second, before testing, state the goals, constraints, prohibited actions, escalation rules, and measurable postconditions, the facts that must be true when the agent finishes. Do not infer these afterward from what the agent did. Third, test normal tasks with production-equivalent tool permissions and representative state. Do not use a broadened test account, because it would mask a permission-boundary failure.
Fourth, test malicious and malformed instructions arriving from the user, from retrieved content, from tool output, and from the agent’s own memory. An agent that resists a hostile instruction typed by a user can still follow the same instruction when it arrives inside a document, a webpage, or an API response. The agent was only supposed to read those. An API response is a reply from another software service. Fifth, test timeouts, retries, partial failures, stale state, duplicate actions, and concurrency. A retry is the same request sent again after a failure. Stale state is stored information that is out of date. A duplicate action is the same action carried out twice. Concurrency means more than one instance or agent acts on shared state at once. Sixth, run long-horizon tests, tests that span many steps or a long interaction, and run them repeatedly. They measure variance, how much the results differ from run to run, and compounding error, small errors that build on one another. An agent that is correct on a single fresh turn can drift into an incorrect belief over a long interaction. A one-shot test never exercises that drift.
Seventh, verify the side effects and postconditions in the systems the agent touched, and not only the response it returned. A response can describe an action the agent did not take, or took incorrectly. Eighth, exercise human pause, override, rollback, recovery, and incident escalation directly. Do not assume they work because they were designed. Ninth, preserve full execution traces. Triage every finding, meaning sort it by seriousness. Remediate each finding, meaning fix it, and retest independently. Add the failure to a regression suite, a set of saved tests rerun on every new version.






Figure 8.2: Figure 7.2. Evaluation approach by system class




Figure 7.2 shows three different disciplines, not one method with three sets of examples. A predictive system’s unit of evaluation is a single output. It is checked against a labeled or otherwise justified reference outcome, where available, per the caveats in section 7.1. A generative system’s unit is a graded output checked against a rubric, with inter-rater reliability confirming the rubric is sound. An agentic system’s unit is a sequence of actions. It is checked for the path taken as well as the endpoint. It also faces a deliberate test of what the system does when its goal and constraints cannot both be met.
A team that runs only the predictive tests on a system that also generates or acts has tested a fraction of what it does. A team that runs all three correctly still owes the system a combined check afterward. A predictive component, a generative component, and an agentic controller can each pass their own column’s tests. The assembled system can still fail in ways no single column’s test was designed to catch. The failure can come from its orchestration, its human workflow, or its access and recourse paths. Orchestration is how the components are coordinated. Recourse is a path for challenging or correcting an outcome. Most real deployments combine classes. The column boundaries describe evaluation disciplines. They do not claim that any system sits in one column only.

title: 7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming
text:
7.8 Red teaming
Red teaming is structured adversarial evaluation. Its purpose is to find the failure a standard evaluation was not designed to look for. The people who conduct it have one job in the exercise. They attack the system, and they do not confirm it works. The process has seven stages. The stage most often skipped is the one that turns a finding into a closed loop and not a one-time discovery.
First, authorize the exercise. A threat model is a description of who might attack the system and how. Before any testing begins, record the system version under test, the named owners, the threat model, and the scope and explicit exclusions. Record also the environment, the rules for test data, and the conditions that would stop the exercise early. Scope names the categories of harm the exercise probes and those explicitly out of scope. An unscoped exercise goes wrong in one of two ways. It wanders across every conceivable harm at shallow depth. Or it narrows, without anyone deciding to, to whatever the red team thinks of first.
Second, design scenarios and the evidence each is expected to produce across safety, security, privacy, misuse, fairness, and operational failure. Team composition matters here. A red team drawn entirely from the system’s developers will miss what their own assumptions hide. An effective exercise typically includes people without a stake in the system’s success. For higher-stakes systems, it also includes external participants with no loyalty to a clean result.
Technique categories give the exercise structure. They include adversarial prompting for generative or agentic systems, meaning inputs written to make the system misbehave. They include boundary and edge-case probing, the testing of cases at the edge of a model’s categories, carried over from section 7.3. They also include scenario-based social engineering. There the target is a human operator’s willingness to be misled by a plausible request, and not the model’s technical boundary.
Third, execute the exercise with reproducible traces, which are step-by-step records others can repeat. Protect the people, systems, and data involved in the testing itself. Fourth, triage and rate every finding, and assign each one a named owner and a deadline. Fifth, remediate the finding. Or document, through a decision by an authorized decision maker, that the residual risk is being knowingly accepted instead of fixed. Residual risk is the risk that remains. Sixth, retest independently, by someone other than whoever implemented the fix. Add the case to the system’s regression evaluation, so it is checked again on every future version. Seventh, close the finding only once that evidence exists. A finding marked fixed that was never independently retested is a claim of closure the exercise has not earned.
Feedback runs in both directions. A retest that fails routes back to remediation. An incident or a monitoring signal discovered later routes back to the first stage. That updates the threat model for the next exercise.
Documentation and disposition, meaning what happened to each finding, decide whether a red team exercise produces governance value or happens once and changes nothing. Both are carried through all seven stages and not added at the end. A report that lists findings without recording what happened to each shows that the exercise occurred and not that it mattered. The record for each finding should run through triage, remediation, and independent retest.

title: 7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming
text:
7.9 Specifying the unspecifiable
Verification means showing that a system meets its requirements. A specification is a written statement of what the system must do, exact enough to check against. Verification for AI systems differs from verification for conventional software in how it treats properties that cannot be specified directly.
Some properties resist direct specification entirely. Take the property “The system does not fabricate an answer.” It cannot be verified directly. Verifying it would require checking every possible output against every possible fact it could touch. That task is unbounded, and no test suite can complete it. The property is real and matters. A test plan that abandons it because it cannot be checked directly gives up the requirement most worth keeping.
The method that recovers a testable requirement from an unspecifiable property has four parts. Skipping any one produces a test that looks rigorous and is not.
First, decompose the property into a verifiable proxy, something narrower that can be checked. It is chosen because passing it is evidence, though not proof, that the fuller property holds. Second, state a threshold, how well the system must perform on the proxy to pass. It must be a specific number and not a qualitative impression. Third, specify the verification method. That means how the proxy will be measured, by whom or what, on what data, and on what schedule. Fourth, document the residual, what the proxy does not cover. State it explicitly, so that a later reader knows what passing the test does and does not establish. This part is the one most often skipped.
A worked example makes the method concrete. It uses a construct this book proposes for teaching. A construct here is a named idea built for a purpose. It is not a term of art, a phrase with a fixed official meaning, from an established standard. The construct is a recurring evaluation, run on held-out items, that checks answerability, whether a question can be answered from the material at hand. The construct is called a sentinel evaluation here because it stands watch on an ongoing basis and does not check once at launch.
A sentinel evaluation is a fixed-format check run periodically, before and after a batch of a generative system’s real work. It is built from items weighted toward questions that cannot be answered from the material the system has been given. The only correct response to a sentinel item is a refusal or an explicit statement of uncertainty.
The proxy is the system’s rate of correctly declining the unanswerable items. That rate stands in for its broader tendency to fabricate. A stand-in is needed because the system’s real answers cannot each be verified directly.
The threshold is a specific pass rate on the sentinel set. Whoever is accountable for the system’s release agrees on it in advance. It is not adjusted after a disappointing result. That person also has to be able to say what evidence supports the threshold.
The verification method specifies how the sentinel items are sampled. They are rotated so the system cannot be tuned to the visible set. They are secured so no one able to adjust the system sees the full set. The method also specifies how items are scored against a stated standard and periodically revalidated. A portion is held out entirely, so part of the check stays uncontaminated by anyone’s knowledge of its contents.
State the residual as plainly as the pass rate. A sentinel evaluation establishes the system’s propensity to fabricate on a narrow category of item, at the time the check was run. Propensity means tendency. The category is unanswerable questions structured like the sentinel set. The evaluation does not establish that any particular output on a particular day was truthful. It does not establish the system’s behavior on categories of question the sentinel set does not resemble.
A passed sentinel evaluation is a periodic, population-level check on a general tendency. A population-level check measures a rate across many outputs, not the truth of any single one. Treating the passed check as verification of a specific work product, such as one report, is a traceability failure, in the sense Chapter 3 gave the term. The failure attaches a claim of assurance, a claim that something has been checked and is sound, to a work product the evidence does not cover.






Figure 8.3: Figure 7.3. Decomposing an unspecifiable property into a testable requirement




Figure 7.3 reads top to bottom as a derivation, and not as a checklist completed in any order. The unspecifiable property sits at the top because it is what is wanted and the reason for the exercise. The four boxes beneath it depend on one another. A threshold is meaningless without a proxy to apply it to. A verification method is meaningless without a threshold to check against. The residual sits at the bottom at the same visual weight as the pass or fail result above it. An omitted residual is a claim of completeness the evidence does not support. The figure treats the residual as part of the result and not a footnote.
Better tooling will not retire the four-part method. The contrast with conventional software should not be overstated either. Some AI systems make residual uncertainty, the uncertainty left over after testing, prominent. Their behavior is probabilistic, meaning it is described in likelihoods and not certainties. Their inputs and environments are open ended, with no fixed limits on what can arrive. The property tested may resist complete specification. Conventional software can face the same limits when its environment, specification, state, or interactions are not fully bounded.
Formal verification is a mathematical proof that a system meets its specification. Where it is used, it establishes a specified property under stated assumptions. It does not prove every real-world behavior. It does not remove the risk of a wrong specification. Verification therefore states the property, the model, the assumptions, the coverage, and the residual. It does not claim that one technology class can reach zero residual while the other cannot. Verification for AI reaches a characterized and accepted residual, not a verified state. This is not a temporary compromise pending better methods. It does not hold AI to a lower standard than software achieves in practice, because software verification also stops short of certainty. It is the honest standard, and the one to hold a system to.

title: 7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming
text:
7.10 Release readiness
A release decision has to integrate every result the methods above produce. Those results include performance figures and fairness metrics with the tradeoff named. They include robustness findings and generative evaluation scores with their rubrics. They also include red team findings with their dispositions and sentinel results with their residuals. A system reaches production only on a single documented decision, made by someone with the authority and accountability to make it. The decision cannot be inferred from the fact that no individual test failed outright.
On the buy path, where an organization acquires a system from a vendor, release readiness adds a question. The vendor’s own testing is disclosed in a system card, a document describing the system and how it was tested. Chapter 6 showed how to read such a card with a skeptical eye. Given what that testing covers, what does the deploying organization still need to test itself? The answer determines whether the vendor’s coverage and the organization’s own add up to a readiness decision the organization can stand behind.
Naming the decision is not the same as being able to make it. A release decision is usable when it rests on a release record with a minimum set of fields. A narrative summary of how testing went does not serve. The record states these fields explicitly, without exception. It names the system and model versions released. It names the intended uses and the uses the release prohibits. It includes an evaluation coverage map. The map shows which of the methods above were run against which claim and which claims remain untested. It carries every unresolved finding from testing or red teaming forward and does not drop one once triaged. It states the criteria the release decision was measured against. It lists the named signoffs of everyone accountable. It records every remaining risk accepted knowingly, with the name of who accepted it.
The record also covers what happens after release. It confirms that legal and rights review has occurred, a check of the release against the law and against people’s rights. That review is required wherever the system touches a regulated decision, a decision the law sets rules for, or personal data. It includes the monitoring plan that will run after release. It states the training the system’s operators have received. It includes a rollback or deactivation test confirming the organization can revert if the release fails. It includes incident readiness, a stated plan for what happens when a failure is detected in production. It fixes the deployment’s operational constraints, the limits the system must run within once live. It lists the changes, in the system or its environment, that would trigger a re-review before the next scheduled one. It also sets an expiry date on the approval and a revalidation schedule. The schedule states when the release will be checked again, whether or not anything has changed. A release record missing a field is a decision made without knowing, or without recording, something the decision depended on.

title: 7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming
section: Case in focus: a fairness decision made on the record, and an audit built without training data
text:
Case in focus: a fairness decision made on the record, and an audit built without training data
FAIRLEND and TALENTSCREEN · Hypothetical, following the running cases
Meridian’s model risk function examined the applicant pool’s base rates by group. It then discovered that FAIRLEND’s ensemble could not satisfy equalized odds and calibration at the same time. It brought the choice to a committee. The committee included model risk, legal, and a consumer advocate the bank retained specifically for reviews of this kind.
Repayment is the positive class in section 7.2’s definitions. So a creditworthy applicant, one who would in fact repay, who is wrongly declined is a false negative and not a false positive. The committee read its own numbers on that basis.
The committee considered two options. Prioritizing calibration would keep the model’s risk scores meaningful as probabilities across every group, supporting consistent pricing. But it would also tolerate a materially different false negative rate between groups. Creditworthy applicants in one group would be wrongly declined at a higher rate than creditworthy applicants in another. Prioritizing equal opportunity would equalize the true positive rate. Creditworthy applicants would then face the same approval odds regardless of group. That came at the cost of calibration. The same risk score would imply a different actual repayment likelihood depending on group, which complicated the pricing model downstream.
The committee chose equal opportunity. Its stated reasoning was that an unequal rate of wrongly declining creditworthy applicants was a more direct harm to individuals than the alternative. That alternative was a pricing model whose scores meant different things across groups once calibration was given up.
What to do about the pricing complication was treated as a separate, harder question than the committee’s first framing had allowed. A per-group pricing adjustment was raised and then set aside. It would have restored something like calibration by pricing each group’s risk separately. But adjusting price by membership in a protected group raises its own legal exposure, the risk of violating fair-lending law, under Regulation B, a United States rule that forbids discrimination in credit. That is true even when the aim is to correct for a statistical artifact and not for animus, which means ill will. No amount of engineering work resolves that exposure on its own. Any such adjustment would also need legal review before it could be treated as a fix at all.
The committee’s memo instead listed the options available to it. One was to reconsider the target variable, the outcome the model was trained to predict. Another was to improve the training data’s representativeness. Another was to choose a different decision rule, the rule that turns a score into an approve or a decline. Another was to add a review-and-recourse path for declined applicants, a way to get the decision reviewed and corrected. The remaining options were to limit where the system could be deployed, or to decline to deploy it.
One committee member dissented in writing. That member argued that giving up calibration’s guarantee deserved more weight in the decision than the majority had given it. The guarantee is that a risk score means the same thing across groups. The dissent was recorded in the decision memo. The majority did not outvote it and leave it unmentioned. The decision, the reasoning, and the dissent all became part of FAIRLEND’s governance record. A future reviewer can learn from that record what was decided, what the alternative would have cost, and who thought the decision was wrong.
Calloway is the company that uses TALENTSCREEN. Its audit of the tool faced a different problem. There was no training data to test against at all, because the vendor had disclosed only that the model was trained on “a large and diverse dataset of resumes and hiring outcomes.” That sentence names nothing checkable. Calloway’s compliance team could not audit the training data that section 7.2’s methods assume. It ran an outcome-based audit instead, using its own applicant data.
For a full hiring cycle, the team tracked the tool’s pass-through recommendations, meaning its calls on which applicants move forward. It compared them against applicant demographic categories it collected separately for this purpose. It computed the same four metrics that section 7.2 defines. It did not use the vendor’s training data, which it could not see. It used its own deployment population, which it could see.
The audit found a materially lower pass-through rate for one age category. The vendor’s own documentation had not surfaced this finding and had no obligation to surface it. The vendor’s testing, to the extent any had been disclosed, covered its own broader customer base and not Calloway’s specific applicant pool.
Calloway’s finding did not establish why the gap existed, since the training data producing it remained invisible. It did establish that the gap existed in Calloway’s own deployment. That was enough to trigger a mitigation Calloway’s own legal team considered necessary, regardless of the vendor’s position on the model’s overall fairness.
The two audits differ in what they had available to work with. One could examine the model and its training data, and the other had only outcome data. They nonetheless share a structure. A fairness or evaluation finding is not complete until it produces a documented decision. A named party makes that decision. A later reviewer can trace it back to the reasoning behind it. That decision may affirm a tradeoff accepted on purpose. Or it may trigger a mitigation for a gap a vendor’s own disclosure never required it to close.

8  7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming

title: 7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming
text:
Summary
Verification for AI systems runs into two limits. Much of what these systems do cannot be checked against a single correct answer. Some of what they need to do cannot be specified directly. Performance testing picks the metric that matches what a specific error costs. Held-out data keeps the resulting number honest.
Fairness testing turns on one result. Calibration and equalized odds cannot generally both be satisfied for imperfect scores whenever the groups differ in their underlying base rates. That is a mathematical fact and not an engineering shortfall. It does not mean every pair among demographic parity, equal opportunity, equalized odds, and calibration is incompatible. Choosing which criterion to prioritize is a values decision. It needs a named, accountable owner, and not a default computed by whoever built the model.
Robustness and adversarial testing probe distribution shift, boundary behavior, and deliberately constructed failure inputs. These include the instruction-override inputs specific to generative and agentic systems. Evaluating generative systems requires eval design, task decomposition, rubric construction, and inter-rater reliability. That is a discipline distinct from classifier testing.
Benchmark contamination degrades public evaluation silently. Private, rotating, partly held-out evaluation sets survive it. Model-as-judge grading has documented biases in position, self-preference, and verbosity. It degrades most on the contested cases where its verdict would need to be most trustworthy. Testing agentic systems means a realistic, reversible sandbox. It means grading action sequences and not only endpoints. It means probing what a system does when its goal and constraints conflict. Red teaming finds what standard evaluation was not designed to look for. It produces governance value only when scope, team composition, and finding disposition are documented.
Specifying the unspecifiable decomposes a property that resists direct verification into a proxy, a threshold, a verification method, and a documented residual. The proposed sentinel evaluation illustrates it in full. It checks a general propensity and not any single output’s truth. Open-ended inputs, probabilistic behavior, and properties that resist complete specification make residual uncertainty prominent for AI systems. Conventional software can face the same limits when its environment or specification is not fully bounded. Verification for AI reaches a characterized, accepted residual instead of a verified state. This does not hold AI to a lower bar. It is the honest description of what the available property, model, assumptions, and coverage have established.
The output of testing is evaluation evidence. It consists of the coverage map of which methods were run against which claim, every finding with its disposition, and every documented residual. It also includes a release recommendation. That recommendation is grounded in the coverage and not in the absence of a failed test. Chapter 8 binds this evidence, together with Chapter 5’s and Chapter 6’s, into a deployment decision.

title: 7. Testing, Evaluation, and Red Teaming
text:
Review questions
COMPREHENSION

Explain, using base rates, why a model cannot simultaneously satisfy calibration and equalized odds when two groups have different underlying rates of the outcome being predicted.
Distinguish evaluating a generative system from evaluating a predictive classifier, and explain why inter-rater reliability matters specifically for the former.

APPLIED

A team is building a sentinel evaluation for a customer-support generative system. Specify the verifiable proxy, a plausible threshold, the verification method, and the residual you would document, following section 7.9’s four-part structure.
An organization is deciding whether to use a judge model to grade a batch of ten thousand generated summaries for accuracy. Identify two specific biases from section 7.6 that could distort the results, and describe a check you would run to detect each.

SPOT THE RISK

A team reports that its agentic system passed all functional tests, defined as reaching the correct final state in every test scenario. Identify what this testing approach has not checked, and explain what section 7.7 requires in addition.

COMPARE AND DECIDE

Construct a confusion matrix, actual counts of qualified and unqualified candidates and how each is decided, for two candidate groups with different qualification base rates, choosing numbers so that equal opportunity and demographic parity both hold at once despite the base-rate difference. Then identify what happens to the false positive rate in your example. State what each metric protects, and explain why this shows that the two criteria are not proven mutually exclusive in general, unlike calibration and equalized odds.

RUNNING CASE

TALENTSCREEN Using the case in focus, explain what Calloway’s outcome-based audit could and could not establish about the tool’s fairness, and specify what additional access or information would be needed to close the gap between what was tested and what section 7.2’s full methodology requires.


A tested system is not yet ready to operate. The next chapter turns to deployment and release. It covers an uncomfortable pattern that recurs across every system class. A system is usually ready for production before the organization around it is. Releasing anyway because the technical checklist is complete is where a well-tested system meets an unready operator. The system then fails in a way no test above was designed to catch.

title: 8. Deployment and Release
text:
What you will be able to do
MEDASSIST is the hospital system from the running case. It is an artificial intelligence (AI) model, a computer program that learns patterns from data, and it raises alerts for clinical staff. Northfield, the organization in the running case, rolled it out to its community hospitals, the step called deployment. Before that rollout, MEDASSIST passed every technical gate, or checkpoint, that Chapter 7 treats as rigorous.
Its performance metrics, the scores that show how well it does its job, were measured on held-out data from the academic medical center. Held-out data is data the model did not see while it was being built. The academic medical center is the hospital where the system was built and tested. The metrics exceeded the threshold set by Northfield’s model risk function, the part of the organization that manages the risks of using models. Its fairness testing covered the demographic groups in the academic center’s own patient population. Demographic groups are groups of people defined by traits such as age or race. The testing showed no disparity that the review considered serious enough to act on. A disparity is a gap in how the model treats different groups. Its technical integration with the electronic health record, the hospital’s digital patient chart, was tested and stable.
A deployment committee then reviewed the system before its rollout to the six community hospitals. The committee asked at length whether the model performed well. Nobody in the room asked, in those words, whether the six hospitals matched the place where the system had been built and tested.
The system was ready. The question that would have caught the gap was never on the agenda. The agenda was built around system readiness alone. System readiness is not the only kind of readiness a deployment decision requires.
A rushed deployment process merges three questions into one. First, is the system ready? Second, is the organization receiving it ready to operate it, to notice when it misbehaves, and to step in when it does? Third, does the context it was validated in still match the context it is about to run in? Validated means shown to work through testing. Context means the use, the people, and the surroundings the system works in.
A system is usually ready for production, meaning live use, before the organization around it is. Deploying anyway, because the technical checklist came back clean, is a recurring failure at this stage of a system’s life. A deployment review can miss it even when every question the review asked was answered honestly.

title: 8. Deployment and Release
text:
Evaluate deployment readiness along three separate dimensions: system readiness, organizational readiness, and context alignment. Explain why passing one does not mean passing the others.
Detect a mismatch between the context a system was validated in and the context it is about to be deployed into.
Design a progressive rollout, which expands a release in stages. Fix its blast radius (how much a failure could affect) and its halt criteria (the conditions that stop it) before launch. Do this for the user population and for the permission scope (what the system is allowed to do). This applies to every system, including an agentic system (one that takes actions on its own).
Specify a rollback mechanism, a way to return to an earlier version. Include the case where actions already taken cannot just be stopped.
crumbs: Part II: The AI System Lifecycle

title: 8. Deployment and Release
text:
8.1 System readiness
System readiness is the dimension every deployment process checks. It has three parts of its own. A checklist that names only “testing complete” tends to blur them together.
Infrastructure means the surrounding computer systems. Technical readiness asks whether the system works correctly with the infrastructure it will run inside. Examples are the electronic health record, the loan origination system that handles loan applications, and the applicant tracking system that tracks job applicants. Each of these has its own interface behavior, meaning its own way of sending and receiving information. A model that performs well in isolation can still fail against that behavior in practice.
Performance readiness is the set of results that Chapter 7 produces. These results include accuracy against the appropriate metric, and a fairness decision that is made and documented. A fairness decision is the recorded outcome of fairness testing. They also include robustness findings that have been addressed. Robustness is how well the model keeps working when conditions change or inputs are unusual. A generative system produces new content, such as text. A generative or agentic system also needs the evaluation results specific to its class, including sentinel results. A sentinel evaluation is a fixed check, run periodically on a generative system’s real work, that Chapter 7 describes.
Compliance readiness asks whether the paperwork a specific deployment requires, under the rules and laws that apply, is complete. The paperwork includes documentation, approvals, and disclosures, which are items the rules require an organization to share. These requirements come from the regulatory obligations in Chapter 2 and from Chapter 3’s inventory record, the system’s entry in the organization’s list of its systems. A review must check that the paperwork is complete. It must not assume so because the technical work is done.
The three parts need different kinds of evidence. Performance is the easiest of the three to produce a clean number for. A review that verifies only performance has not verified system readiness at all. It has verified only the part that happened to be measured.
These three parts are a minimum, not a complete account of what “the system itself is ready” can mean. A fuller review also checks the following:

security and resilience (the ability to keep working and recover) against foreseeable attack and failure
privacy exposure that the deployment newly creates, meaning new risk to people’s personal data
safe and fail-safe behavior, which means failing in a safe way, when an input or a dependency (other software the system relies on) is malformed, meaning broken or wrongly formed
supplier and supply-chain dependencies that the system inherits, meaning the outside companies and parts it relies on
a tested recovery path

None of these is guaranteed by “integration,” “Chapter 7 results,” or “documentation complete” alone.
crumbs: Part II: The AI System Lifecycle

title: 8. Deployment and Release
text:
8.2 Organizational readiness
Organizational readiness is a harder question than system readiness. A deployment review can skip it without anyone deciding to skip it. The reason is that it asks about the receiving organization, not about the system. A review convened to approve a system tends to stay focused on the system.
Organizational readiness has four parts. Table 8.1 states the question each part asks and what answering it requires, so that a review can check them one by one instead of holding all four in mind.
Table 8.1. The four parts of organizational readiness








Part
Question
Requirement




Operational readiness
Have the staff who will work alongside the system been trained?
Staff know what the system does and what it does not do, and what to do when it disagrees with their own assessment.


Oversight readiness
Can a human who reviews the system’s output catch a wrong output?
That person has the time, the authority, and the right information to do it.


Monitoring readiness
Is anyone watching the system’s behavior in production at all?
Someone watches a defined measure, and a defined threshold triggers a response.


Incident readiness
Does a response plan exist before a failure or harmful event involving the system occurs?
A response plan built in advance, not improvised on the day.



Chapter 9 develops the oversight question at length after it introduces automation bias, the habit of trusting a machine’s output too much. Chapter 10 shows that an organization that improvises its first response during an incident makes worse decisions than one that follows a plan built in advance.
These four parts are a minimum. A review that stops at them has covered ground but not the whole of it. A fuller readiness check also names the following:

Capacity and staffing. Enough trained people must exist to do the operational and oversight work, not just one person who happens to be available today.
Business continuity and a manual fallback. This is what the organization does when the system is unavailable. Business continuity means keeping the work going. A manual fallback is a way to do the work by hand.
Support and escalation paths for the people who use the system’s output. An escalation path is a route for passing a problem to someone with more authority.
Security operations and privacy operations specific to what this system newly exposes, meaning the day-to-day work of protecting the system and the personal data it handles.
Records and retention practices sufficient to reconstruct a decision later. Retention is how long records are kept. To reconstruct a decision means to piece together later how it was made.
A plan for communicating with the users or subjects of the system’s decisions.
Affected-person rights and a recourse path for someone who wants to contest an outcome. A recourse path is a way to ask for a fix.
Procurement, or buying, and supplier readiness. A vendor’s own support and change commitments are part of what “ready” depends on.
Accessibility, which means that people with different abilities can use the system.
A change-management process, a set of steps for making changes in a controlled way, for updating the system without silently invalidating the readiness work already done.

Each item on this expanded list needs a named owner. It needs the evidence that supports calling it ready, and a capacity estimate where staffing is the question. It needs an exercise or test where one applies. It also needs a stated readiness result. A checkbox marked complete because the topic was discussed does not count.
A model can pass every performance and compliance gate described in section 8.1 and still not be ready. The nursing staff who will act on its output may have received no training on what an alert threshold means. An alert threshold is the level at which the system raises an alert. Nobody may have been assigned to watch for a rising rate of overridden recommendations. An override happens when a person rejects what the system recommends. No incident plan may exist for the day the model is wrong in a way that matters. Deploying in that state is an organizational risk, not a technical one. It is the risk the case in focus was built around.






Figure 9.1: Figure 8.1. Readiness across three dimensions




Figure 8.1 shows the three dimensions as three gates. A single review has to clear them separately. They are not one list with items checked off in any order. Context alignment is its own independent gate.
The first gate, system readiness, is the one most deployment processes already check well, because it produces numbers. The numbers are a performance figure, a test result, and a compliance checkbox.
The second gate, organizational readiness, produces a different form of evidence, and it is not a worse one. That evidence is staffing records, workload exercises, direct observation, and interviews. It is not a single clean score. A review that has no comparable number for this gate is still required to run it.
The third gate, context alignment, is covered in full in section 8.3.
The figure’s argument is that a review clearing only the first gate has cleared only one of the three gates of deployment readiness. A release decision follows only once all three gates carry evidence.

title: 8. Deployment and Release
text:
8.3 Context alignment
A system validated in one context does not carry that validation automatically into a different one. Organizations usually discover this the hard way, and the mechanism is almost always the same. It is scope creep. In scope creep, a system approved for a specific use case, a specific population, and a specific environment is extended to something adjacent. The new use looked similar enough that nobody ordered a fresh review.
MEDASSIST’s deployment to Northfield’s community hospitals followed this pattern. Nobody framed it as extending the system’s scope. It was a rollout that treated “the same hospital system” as the thing that had to match, the unit of similarity. The right things to match were the same patient population, the same equipment, and the same documentation practice. These decide whether a model’s learned pattern transfers, meaning whether what the model picked up from its training data still works in the new setting. Chapter 5 already established that those three things are the deciding factors.
Context alignment has four checkpoints. Table 8.2 states what each checkpoint asks, and a review has to clear each one on its own rather than infer it from the others.
Table 8.2. The four checkpoints of context alignment







Checkpoint
What it asks




Use case alignment
Whether the task the system is now being asked to do matches the task it was validated on. A plausible extension of that task is not enough.


Population alignment
Whether the people in the test data look like the people the system will serve. This is the representativeness question that Chapter 5 raised. Here it becomes a deployment gate, no longer only a general concern about data governance, which means the rules for handling data.


Environment alignment
Whether the operational conditions match what the system was tested against. These conditions include equipment, staffing, documentation practice, and IT infrastructure.


Risk proportionality
Whether the stakes of the deployment match the level of scrutiny the system received.



Suppose a system was validated for a low-stakes pilot, which is a small trial. If it is then deployed at full production scale without a fresh review, its risk profile, the level of risk it carries, has changed. Its evidence base, the testing evidence behind it, has not.
Some deployment reviews check system readiness and organizational readiness, and then treat context alignment as implied by the first two. Such a review misses the specific failure that put MEDASSIST into a community hospital nobody had separately evaluated it against.
Naming the four checkpoints does not give a team a way to act on what they find. A context comparison record fills that gap. It turns the comparison into a decision.
The record names the validated context and the proposed context side by side. It compares them across task, population, input process, equipment, workflow, incentives, human roles, stakes, law, and physical or operational environment. Input process means how the data enters the system. The record then rates how material each difference is, meaning whether it is large enough to matter for the decision. The record also states the evidence behind each rating.
The comparison resolves into one of four dispositions, or recorded outcomes.

Equivalent. No material difference was found, so the existing validation carries over.
Mitigated and revalidated. A difference was found and closed before deployment, through additional testing or a safeguard.
Restricted or piloted. The deployment proceeds only for a narrower scope or a limited trial, while the difference is monitored.
Not approved. The difference is material enough that deployment does not proceed in this context at all.

The team must decide two things before the comparison is run. One is who approves a mismatch. The other is which disposition each comparison result requires. If the team waits, the decision gets negotiated after a difference has been found, when someone would rather not slow the launch down.
The same four checkpoints apply directly to a predictive system with no clinical setting at all. A predictive system uses data to predict an outcome. Take a credit model, which helps decide who receives a loan. It was validated on loan applications that came in through a bank’s branch network, its physical offices. It is then extended to applications that come in through an online channel the bank newly acquired. A channel is a route by which applications arrive.
That change alters the model’s population. As a group, online applicants differ from branch applicants on the paperwork that shows their income and on credit history. It also alters the model’s environment. The data captured at the point of application differs by channel. That difference can silently degrade the model’s inputs, which means it can make them worse without anyone noticing.
Treating “the same bank, the same product” as sufficient similarity is the credit-model version of the mistake MEDASSIST’s rollout made. The same four checkpoints catch it. A channel-specific checkpoint is not needed. This is why the checkpoints are stated as general dimensions. They are not a clinical checklist that happens to generalize.
crumbs: Part II: The AI System Lifecycle

title: 8. Deployment and Release
text:
8.4 The deployment decision
A deployment review should conclude in one of four documented outcomes. The outcomes are approved, approved with conditions, denied, and deferred. Each outcome has a named person accountable for it. The review should not end in an implicit approval, an approval assumed because nobody objected.
The record behind the outcome needs more than the outcome itself. The record includes the following:

the exact evidence version each finding was based on
the reviewing body’s quorum, which is the minimum number of members who must be present, and its authority to decide
any conflicts of interest disclosed
any dissent, noted and not resolved by a silent majority vote
the monitoring conditions the deployment will run under
confirmation that rollback readiness has been checked and not assumed
protections for the people affected by the system’s decisions
an expiry date on the approval itself
the specific triggers that would reopen the review before that expiry

Approved names the reviewer, the date, and the specific evidence the approval rests on. Because of that record, a later question about why the system was deployed has a more specific answer than the bare claim that it passed review.
Approved with conditions is an outcome that deployment reviews can reach readily and then fail to honor. A condition that is not specific and not tracked is only a note that made the reviewers feel the concern had been addressed. A real condition states what must happen, by when, and who verifies it. It also states the consequence if the condition is not met. It belongs in the system’s governance record from Chapter 3. Someone checks it on a schedule, so it is not filed and forgotten.
FAIRLEND, the lending model from Chapter 7, shows how this works. Its equal-opportunity decision, a recorded finding from the model’s fairness testing, is the kind of finding that should attach as a tracked condition. It should not be treated as a closed matter. The condition has to be a safe one. It is not the per-group pricing adjustment, which means setting prices differently for each group. Chapter 7 identified that adjustment as its own source of fair-lending exposure, the risk of breaking laws on fair lending, and it requires legal review. A safe condition looks like one of these:

a scheduled revalidation, a fresh check, of the decision rule (the rule that turns the model’s output into a decision)
documented completion of that legal review
an added recourse path for declined applicants
a restriction on where the model is used

Any such condition should be tracked with an owner and a date. The model risk function should verify it against the engineering or policy backlog, which is the list of pending work.
Denied names the specific readiness gap that produced the denial. It also names what would need to change to reopen the review. A bare rejection gives the requesting team nothing to act on.
Deferred states explicitly what additional evidence or work is needed before the decision can be made at all. That distinguishes a deferral from an approval that quietly never got finished being reviewed. A deferral is a decision to wait for something specific.
crumbs: Part II: The AI System Lifecycle

title: 8. Deployment and Release
text:
8.5 Progressive rollout
A decision to proceed with deployment is not a decision to expose the entire intended population on day one. Progressive rollout is the discipline of expanding exposure deliberately. The criteria for each expansion are decided before the rollout begins. They are not improvised once it is underway.
Blast radius is the size and consequence of what a failure could affect at the current stage of rollout. Staging a rollout means starting with a blast radius small enough that a failure is recoverable and costly lessons are cheap. The team then expands only once the current stage has run long enough, and been watched closely enough, to justify the next one.
A rollout has two axes, meaning two separate controls. The exposure axis controls how many are reached. That means the users, sites, transactions, populations, or traffic. The capability axis controls what the system is allowed to do at that stage. That means the data, tools, actions, permissions, spend, or rate. Each stage of a rollout is a chosen position on both axes at once.
The two axes, population and permission or capability, are not a choice between two different systems’ rollout styles. They are two independent controls that every system’s rollout needs. A narrow action can still touch many people, expose sensitive data, create an unfair exclusion, or overload an operations team. This holds regardless of how few users can currently reach it. The reverse is also true. A wide population exposed to only a narrow, low-consequence capability can be a safely staged rollout even on day one.
Halt criteria have to be defined before launch, on both axes. They are stated as specific, measurable conditions. Examples are an error rate threshold, a specific category of complaint, or a specific volume of overrides. These triggers force an automatic pause, not a call made under the pressure of a rollout in motion. A team midway through a launch it wants to succeed is poorly placed to decide whether a concerning signal is serious enough to stop for.
Each promotion, each move from one stage to the next, needs the following before it is granted.

a fixed observation window (a set length of time to watch) or sample size
stated success criteria
adequate monitoring coverage, meaning enough watching is in place for this stage
incident readiness
a rollback test
an owner’s approval
no unresolved release blocker, meaning no known problem that must be fixed before release

A halt sends the release to investigation, rollback, remediation, and retest. Remediation means fixing the problem. A halt is not a quiet pause that resumes once attention moves elsewhere.
TALENTSCREEN is a hiring tool. When its scheduling component is extended from a recommendation-only tool to one that books interviews autonomously, the change illustrates the capability axis. The component moves through three stages. In the first, it can propose times but cannot commit them. In the second, it can commit within a narrow set of pre-approved time blocks. In the third, it has fuller autonomy.
The capability axis is staged alongside the population axis, not instead of it. The population axis is how many candidates and recruiters the tool is exposed to at each stage. A plan that stages only capability, and reaches every candidate on day one, controls what actions the system can take. It does not control the exposure that a data-handling or fairness failure would have.






Figure 9.2: Figure 8.2. Progressive rollout with halt gates




Figure 8.2 shows two independent axes staged together. It is not a single track with an agentic exception branching off it. A stage that has produced no alarming signal is not automatically ready to expand on either axis. Each gate requires a positive check. The check compares the stage’s results with the halt criteria set before launch, a fixed observation window, and the stated success criteria. A rollout that expands on schedule, whatever the current stage showed, has turned a safety gate into a calendar entry.
Neither axis substitutes for the other.
crumbs: Part II: The AI System Lifecycle

title: 8. Deployment and Release
text:
8.6 Rollback
Rollback means returning to an earlier version of the system. Treated as a single action, it understates what recovering from a bad release requires. A gap lies between “we can roll back” and “we can recover.” An organization discovers that gap, under pressure, when its plan turns out to cover less than it thought.
A recovery plan, not a single rollback step, has to do all of the following:

Stop new harm first.
Preserve evidence before anything is changed further. A log is a file that records what the system did, and state is the information the system keeps as it runs. An overwritten log or a reset state can destroy the record a later investigation needs.
Decide between rolling back and fixing forward. A forward fix repairs the problem in the live version, and it is sometimes safer once new harm has been stopped.
Restore a compatible combination of model, code, data, prompt, configuration, and dependencies together. A prompt is the written instruction given to a generative model. Configuration is the set of settings the system runs with. Dependencies are the other software the system relies on. Reverting one without the others can produce a combination that was never tested.
Reconcile pending and already-completed actions against the restored state, finding and sorting out any mismatch.
Notify operators and, where required, affected people.
Verify that the recovered service is working. A successful rollback command does not guarantee a working system.
Monitor afterward for recurrence.

None of this helps much if the plan has never been exercised before the day it is needed. A plan that exists only on paper regularly turns out, once invoked under pressure, to depend on an assumption that quietly stopped being true months earlier.
Recovery needs three things.
First, it needs a technical mechanism. That means specific versions to return to across every layer in the list above, and a tested procedure for doing so. Chapter 6 required version-control discipline, which means keeping track of every version, for this reason.
Second, it needs a clear authority. A named role must be empowered to trigger recovery without convening the same committee that approved the original deployment. A process that requires the same lengthy approval as the original launch will arrive too late to limit the harm it exists to prevent.
Third, it needs to have been tested as an exercise, not just designed. A plan can look complete on paper and still fail under real conditions. Chapter 10’s incident response discipline takes up this gap, which recurs across systems that treated an untested plan as an adequate one.
Reverting a model or application stops its future behavior. It does not undo a decision, a message, or a record change that the behavior already produced. A predictive system’s denial that was already issued needs reconciliation, notification, and remedy. So does a generative system’s output that was already published or relied upon. An agentic system’s committed actions need the same.
Agentic systems make this harder, though the problem is not unique to them. One run can combine several tool calls, each a request the system makes to other software, plus permissions, retries, and state changes before anyone intervenes. Reverting to a prior model version does not resolve queued or duplicated actions still in flight. It does not by itself address stale cached state, meaning saved copies of data that are out of date. Nor does it by itself address another program that connects to the system and was built against the version being removed.
Consider the scheduling component of TALENTSCREEN. Suppose it is rolled back after committing a batch of interview times under a permission scope later found to be too broad. The commitments stay in place unless recovery explicitly includes a compensating-action step. That step means canceling or reconfirming the affected appointments. It also means addressing any remedy owed to affected candidates. Reverting the code path that produced the original commitments is not enough.
A recovery plan for an agentic system that only halts further actions has handled just part of the problem. It also needs a kill switch, which is a control that stops the system. It needs a manual fallback. It needs a way to reconcile and compensate for what already happened.

title: 8. Deployment and Release
section: Case in focus: a deployment that passed every gate it was asked about
text:
Case in focus: a deployment that passed every gate it was asked about
MEDASSIST · Hypothetical, following the running case
Northfield’s deployment committee for extending MEDASSIST to the community hospitals reviewed the evidence its process asked for. That evidence included three items. The first was the model’s validated performance on the academic medical center’s data. The second was technical integration testing against each community hospital’s own instance of the electronic health record. The third was sign-off from the clinical informatics team that the alert interface displayed correctly on each site’s terminals. That team is the staff who run the hospital’s clinical information systems. Every item on the committee’s checklist was true, and each could be verified.
The checklist did not ask whether the community hospitals’ patient population, equipment, and documentation practice resembled the academic center’s closely enough for the model’s learned pattern to transfer. That is the representativeness question from Chapter 5. The checklist also did not ask whether community hospital nursing staff had been trained on what an alert threshold meant. These staff had not been part of the model’s development or pilot. Nor did it ask whether they had been trained on what to do when their clinical assessment disagreed with an alert.
The deployment proceeded to all six community hospitals simultaneously, not as a progressive rollout. The committee’s approval was framed as a single decision covering the full extension.
There was no limit on blast radius. No halt criteria were defined in advance, beyond a general instruction to escalate “any concerning pattern.” That standard was vague enough that nobody could point to a threshold being crossed. This stayed true even once the representativeness gap began producing late and missed alerts.
The pattern was eventually noticed, months later. It came to light through the monitoring process Chapter 9 describes. It did not come from anything the readiness checks above had been built to catch. By then the organization had no progressive rollout, so there was no smaller footprint to roll back to. It also had no rollback mechanism that had ever been tested, because nobody had built one. Nobody had built one because of a reasonable-sounding assumption. The assumption was that a model this thoroughly validated at the academic center was unlikely to need it.
No reviewer in this sequence failed to do their job. The committee answered every question its process asked, correctly and honestly. The failure was in what the process asked about. It checked system readiness rigorously. It never named context alignment and organizational readiness as separate questions at all. Suppose the review had been built around the three dimensions and not around system readiness alone. It would have raised the representativeness question before the rollout rather than after the harm. It would also have had a progressive rollout and a tested rollback mechanism in place. Northfield eventually had to manage the situation without either.
crumbs: Part II: The AI System Lifecycle

title: 8. Deployment and Release
text:
Summary
Deployment readiness is three questions, not one. A review that answers only the first has not cleared a system for production. It has only confirmed that the system itself works.
System readiness covers technical, performance, and compliance readiness. Deployment processes already check it well. Organizational readiness covers operational, oversight, monitoring, and incident readiness, plus the broader minimum list in section 8.2. Reviews can skip it without anyone deciding to skip it. A system is usually ready before the organization around it is. Deploying anyway is a recurring failure at this stage.
Context alignment catches scope creep. In scope creep, a system validated for one use case, population, and environment gets extended to an adjacent one that nobody separately evaluated. The review checks use case, population, environment, and risk proportionality. The review does this through a context comparison record with a named disposition.
The deployment decision itself should resolve into one of four documented, accountable outcomes. The outcomes are approved, approved with conditions, denied, and deferred. Conditions must be specific, and they must be tracked, or they are not real conditions. A denial names the gap. A deferral specifies the missing evidence. The record states the evidence version, the authority, and the dissent behind the outcome.
Progressive rollout stages exposure and capability as two independent axes for every system, agentic systems included. The rollout is checked against halt criteria fixed before launch. Recovery needs a tested technical mechanism across every affected layer. It needs a clear authority to trigger it. For an agentic system specifically, it needs a compensating-action step that addresses actions already taken, not only halting further ones.
The deployment decision produces a release record. The record includes:

the exact versions and evidence bound into the decision
the conditions and their tracking status
the constraints (the limits the deployment must stay within) and residual risks the deployment carries, where a residual risk is a risk that remains after safeguards are in place
the staged-rollout position
the recovery plan

Chapter 9’s monitoring program is built to watch these constraints, risks, and versions. It does not watch a generic list that ignores what the deployment decision set.
