title: 8. Deployment and Release
text:
Review questions
COMPREHENSION

Explain why a system can pass every test in Chapter 7 and still not be ready for deployment, using the distinction between system readiness and organizational readiness.
Define scope creep. Then explain why treating “the same organization” as the relevant unit of similarity is not sufficient for context alignment.

APPLIED

A team is preparing to extend a fraud-detection model to a second payment channel that the organization considers similar. The model was validated on transactions from one payment channel. Using section 8.3’s four checkpoints, identify what would need to be verified before this counts as an aligned deployment instead of scope creep.
Design a halt criterion for a customer-support generative system’s progressive rollout. State it as a specific, measurable condition, not a general instruction to escalate concerning patterns.

SPOT THE RISK

A deployment committee approves a system “with conditions.” The conditions listed are to “monitor closely” and “review performance regularly.” Identify what is missing from this approval. Explain how you would rewrite it so the conditions are trackable.

COMPARE AND DECIDE

An organization must decide between two options. One is to deploy a validated model to its full intended population immediately, which captures the benefit sooner. The other is to stage the rollout, which delays full benefit but limits blast radius. State what each choice costs. Say what you would need to know about the system’s risk profile to decide between them.

RUNNING CASE

MEDASSIST Using the case in focus, identify the specific readiness question that was never asked. Name who should have been responsible for asking it. Explain what a properly designed progressive rollout would have looked like for the community hospital extension.


A system that is deployed is now generating the evidence that Chapter 9 needs to watch. The next chapter turns to operations and monitoring. The failure MEDASSIST produced at the community hospitals was invisible to every readiness check described above. It became visible only once someone was watching the system in production. Monitoring is a different discipline, with its own methods and its own blind spots. It also has its own hard problem. Some systems prevent harm, and when prevention works the harm leaves no trace.
crumbs: Part II: The AI System Lifecycle

title: 9. Operations and Monitoring
text:
What you will be able to do
MEDASSIST is a model, a computer program trained on data, that alerts hospital staff when a patient may be getting worse. It was validated, meaning tested and approved, at an academic medical center. It was then used at community hospitals. The gap between the two did not appear on any dashboard the day the model went live. A dashboard is a screen that tracks a system’s numbers. Going live means the system began real use.
The gap first appeared as a handful of nurses at one community hospital noticing a pattern. The model’s alerts seemed to arrive later than their own clinical instinct would have flagged a patient. None of them had the standing to raise this pattern as anything more than an impression. Standing means a recognized position to be heard. None of them had aggregated data either, meaning numbers pooled across many cases.
Months later, the gap appeared again in a retrospective chart review, which is a look back at patient records after the outcomes are known. A new clinical informatics director, a leader responsible for how a hospital uses clinical data and software, happened to commission it. The review compared alert timing against eventual outcomes across the academic medical center and all six community hospitals. That comparison is where the pattern first became a number, not a feeling.
In between those two moments, the model operated in production, which means real use, as opposed to testing. It generated a steady stream of alerts, most of them unremarkable, that is, ordinary and raising no concern. A small number were late or missing in the way that mattered. They stayed that way for as long as nobody was watching the specific thing that would have shown it.
Once a system enters production, its operation can continue long after its initial release. That operation produces evidence that no test run before release observed.
Development, release, monitoring, response, and change can overlap instead of running as one clean handoff. This is true for a system that is updated continuously. It is also true for a system retrained on a rolling basis, meaning trained again and again as new data arrive.
None of this assumes that every system follows one linear lifecycle, or that every risk first appears after release. Some material harms surface earlier, during data creation, training, evaluation, or predeployment testing. Chapters 5 through 7 have already shown several of them doing so.
crumbs: Part II: The AI System Lifecycle

title: 9. Operations and Monitoring
text:
Design a monitoring program across at least five core dimensions, and state what each one is mainly able to detect
Choose an approach to performance monitoring when ground truth, the real outcome a prediction tried to anticipate, is delayed, ambiguous, or absent
Monitor a generative system, one that creates new text, images, or code, that has no single correct output to check against, and a system that acts, not only outputs
Recognize automation bias, the over-trusting of an automated recommendation, from its operational signals and not from a reviewer’s stated intentions
Specify what a post-market monitoring plan, the written plan for watching a system after release, must contain as a documented artifact, and not only describe as an activity
crumbs: Part II: The AI System Lifecycle

title: 9. Operations and Monitoring
text:
9.1 Five monitoring dimensions
A monitoring program built around a single number will miss most of what goes wrong in production. That number is typically accuracy or its nearest proxy, a stand-in measure. Different failure modes surface through different signals. A dimension nobody is watching is a failure mode nobody will catch until it has already caused harm.
Each of the five dimensions watches a different signal, and Table 9.1 states what each one watches and what to know about watching it.
Table 9.1. Five monitoring dimensions








Dimension
Target
Notes




Technical
Whether the system itself is functioning. It tracks latency (how long the system takes to respond), error rates, uptime (the share of time the system is available), and integration failures with the systems around it
Most operations teams already do this well. It resembles conventional software monitoring, and it produces alerts through tools that predate AI systems


Performance
Whether the system’s predictions, generations, or actions remain accurate against whatever ground truth is available
Section 9.2 shows that this is harder than it sounds


Fairness
Whether disparities (gaps in how groups are treated or served) emerge across groups in production that pre-deployment testing did not reveal
Such gaps can emerge because the population in production shifts away from the population tested, well before the aggregate accuracy (the average over all cases) visibly degrades


Drift
Whether the statistical relationship between inputs and outputs is changing, that is, whether the pattern linking the two still holds
Watched whether or not the change has yet produced a measurable accuracy drop


Usage
How the system is being used, by whom, and for what, and whether that use matches the scope the system was deployed and approved for
Catches scope creep (the slow widening of use beyond the approved purpose) after release, in production, instead of only before deployment



Chapter 8 named scope creep as the central risk of context alignment, the fit between a system and the context it was approved for.
These five are a minimum view. They are the dimensions most monitoring programs should start with. They are not an exhaustive list, and they overlap instead of sitting in separate lanes. A security incident can show up first as an action-volume anomaly, an unusual jump in how many actions a system takes. A supplier’s silent model change, meaning an update an outside vendor makes without announcing it, is covered in section 9.6. It touches both drift and technical monitoring at once.
A fuller program adds more targets. One is human workflow and oversight, meaning how the people around the system work with it and check it. Section 9.8 develops this as its own monitoring target. It is not one of the five headline dimensions. A second is security and privacy monitoring specific to what the system newly exposes, the new ways it could be attacked or could leak personal data. A third is change and supply-chain monitoring, which tracks model, configuration, and vendor changes as their own signal. A fourth is impact or complaint signals from the people affected by the system’s decisions.
If a program gives one of these no dimension of its own, the plan should say which of the five covers it. The plan should not leave it uncovered by omission.
Every dimension, whichever list it comes from, needs a response loop. A response loop is a defined path from a triggered threshold to a next step. A threshold is a limit that, once crossed, calls for action. The next step may be triage, corrective action, revalidation, a deployment restriction, incident response, or a governance review. Triage means sorting problems by urgency. Corrective action means fixing the fault. Revalidation means testing again that the system still works as approved. A deployment restriction narrows where or how the system may be used. Incident response is the organized handling of a serious failure. A governance review is a formal look at whether the system should keep running as it is. A dimension that is watched but produces no defined next action is observed, not monitored.






Figure 10.1: Figure 9.1. Monitoring dimensions and what each detects




Figure 9.1 shows five watchpoints that overlap. They are not five separate readings of one and the same number.
A system can be technically healthy, performing accurately, and fair by every disaggregated check, meaning a check run separately for each group. Its usage may still have drifted well outside the scope it was approved for. Usage monitoring is well positioned to catch that failure. The other four dimensions are not built to.
A monitoring program that collapses all five into “is the model still accurate” is watching one dimension, not five. It will be surprised by whichever of the others moves first. A program that stops at these five has the same blind spot in a different place. That happens when it never asks where oversight, security, privacy, and supply-chain risk are being watched.
crumbs: Part II: The AI System Lifecycle

title: 9. Operations and Monitoring
text:
9.2 Ground truth problems
Performance monitoring assumes access to ground truth, the real outcome a prediction was trying to anticipate. This assumption fails in four distinct ways. They recur across the running cases. Each needs a different workaround, not one generic fix.
Delayed truth is the mildest version. The true outcome exists and will eventually be known. It does not arrive soon enough to inform a timely monitoring signal. A credit model’s ground truth is whether a loan was repaid. That answer arrives over the life of the loan, months or years after the decision.
So the monitoring of FAIRLEND, the running example of a credit model, cannot wait for full ground truth before acting on early warning signs. It has to rely on earlier proxy signals. Delinquency at ninety days, meaning payments ninety days behind, stands in for eventual default, a borrower failing to repay the loan. The team must stay explicit that the proxy is not the outcome itself.
Ambiguous truth is harder. The outcome exists and is knowable in principle. Reasonable evaluators still disagree about what it was. Content moderation, the work of deciding which posts a platform allows, has this problem built in. Whether a specific post violated a policy is frequently a matter of interpretation, not a fact.
A monitoring program built as though moderation ground truth were objective will treat evaluator disagreement as system error. The disagreement reflects real ambiguity in the task.
Absent truth is close to MEDASSIST’s problem but not identical to it. An intervention is the action taken because of a prediction, such as treating a patient early. When an intervention succeeds, the outcome it was meant to prevent never occurs. That leaves no trace to check the prediction against.
Take an alert for sepsis, a dangerous reaction to infection. Suppose the alert leads to early treatment, and the patient does not develop septic shock, a life-threatening stage of sepsis. That produces no confirmed case of the deterioration the alert predicted. A monitoring program cannot compare predictions to outcomes directly here. A correct, well-acted-upon prediction erases the evidence that would have confirmed it.
Intervention-affected truth is the hardest version. It is MEDASSIST’s real problem, stated in precise terms. The truth is absent. It is also unobservable in principle for the specific patient once the intervention has been taken. Unobservable in principle means no one could ever see it, no matter how they looked. Treating the patient changes what outcome gets observed.
The untreated counterfactual is what would have happened to this patient without early treatment. A retrospective chart review cannot look it up, because that outcome never happened. No record of it exists anywhere.
A usable signal can still be recovered, by several routes. One is trial design, meaning a planned experiment, where it is ethical and feasible. Another is phased or randomized implementation, which means rolling the system out in stages or by random assignment, so that a comparison group exists. Another is causal-inference methods, statistical tools for working out cause and effect, which model the counterfactual under stated assumptions. Two more are matched comparisons and careful process measures. A matched comparison pairs each treated patient with a similar patient who did not receive the intervention. Process measures evaluate whether the intervention was warranted and well executed. They do not try to score its outcome directly.
Every one of these methods carries its own assumptions. None of them reconstructs the individual counterfactual outcome for a specific treated patient with certainty. They estimate a population-level effect, meaning an average effect across many patients, or they evaluate the process. A monitoring program has to say which of those two it is doing. It should not present either as a direct confirmation of the original prediction.
Four approaches recur across these problems, and Table 9.2 pairs each with its own limitation.
Table 9.2. Four approaches to missing or imperfect ground truth








Approach
Method
Limitation




Sampling with human adjudication
Draws a manageable subset of cases for expert review, where a reviewer decides what the right answer is. A slower, more expensive, but more reliable human decision replaces the ground truth that is not otherwise available
Covers only a sample instead of the full population. In the intervention-affected case, the reviewers adjudicate the process and the available evidence, not a counterfactual nobody can observe


Proxy metrics
Substitute an earlier or more available signal for the true outcome, useful because the proxy is available sooner
The proxy’s known limitations must be stated alongside every number it produces, and the proxy should not be treated as equivalent to the outcome it stands in for


Delayed evaluation
Waits for ground truth to mature before drawing a conclusion
Gives up timeliness for reliability. Appropriate where a wrong early signal would cost more than a late correct one


Causal and comparison-based methods
Matched comparisons, phased or randomized rollouts, and causal-inference techniques, specific to the intervention-affected case
Answer a population-level question about whether the intervention helps on average, not a patient-level question about what would have happened to any one person



MEDASSIST’s community hospital gap was, in the end, confirmed as a performance problem only through a version of the first approach. That version was a retrospective chart review, which adjudicated a sample of cases by hand against the available process evidence. No proxy metric and no wait for later data could substitute for examining what happened to specific patients whose deterioration the model should have caught.
crumbs: Part II: The AI System Lifecycle

title: 9. Operations and Monitoring
text:
9.3 Monitoring generative output
A generative system, one that creates new text, images, or code, makes the ground truth problem worse instead of escaping it. It is not accurate to say a generative system has no ground truth at all. A generation can still be checked against the source documents it was supposed to be grounded in, that is, to draw its facts from. It can be checked against a citation it claims supports a fact. It can be checked against an executable test, which is a test a computer can run. It can also be checked against a task outcome that a user or a downstream process can confirm.
What is true is narrower. A single, universally correct output to match against is rarely available, as it is for a classifier, a model that sorts items into categories. Monitoring therefore has to shift. It moves from comparison against one correct answer to a family of narrower, partial, and task-dependent checks. In combination they cover more of the output than any one of them alone.
Table 9.3 sets out four such checks and the failure each one catches.
Table 9.3. Four checks for generative output








Check
Method
Failure caught




Rubric-based sampling
Extends Chapter 7’s evaluation discipline into production. The team draws a periodic sample of real outputs and grades them against the same kind of scoring guide, or rubric, that a pre-deployment evaluation used
Drift in quality that a static pre-launch evaluation cannot see, because production inputs are not the test cases chosen before launch


Groundedness checking
Verifies whether a generated claim is supported by the retrieved source material it was meant to be grounded in. Specific to a retrieval-augmented system, a system that looks up source material and uses it to write its answers
The system fabricating a plausible-sounding elaboration beyond what its own sources support


Refusal and over-refusal rates
Track when the system declines requests, in both directions. Watching only one direction misses the other
A rising refusal rate can signal the system declining to help with legitimate requests it should be handling. A falling refusal rate on requests that should be declined signals the opposite failure


User-reported failures
Rely on a reporting channel easy enough to use that a frustrated user uses it instead of giving up. An imperfect signal on its own
Categories of failure that no automated check was designed to look for



This list is a starting set, not the full range a production generative system needs watched. A fuller monitoring coverage map adds several checks. It adds factuality checks against whatever sources are available, citation validity, and privacy leakage in generated output. It adds harmful content, and prompt injection attempts (attempts to trick the system with instructions hidden in its input) and whether they succeeded. It also adds retrieval poisoning, which is tampering with the collection of documents a system draws from. It adds latency and cost, rates of users correcting or appealing an output, and task success where a downstream outcome can be observed at all.
Building the map starts from each system capability and risk. From each one, the team works to a specific signal. Each signal needs a data source, a sampling plan, a threshold, a named owner, and a defined response. The map should also state the blind spot that the signal does not cover. The team should not add checks piecemeal until the list feels long enough.
An aggregate check, one that averages over all outputs, can miss the failures that matter most. The sampling plan should deliberately oversample the categories most likely to contain one. A uniform random sample, one that gives every output an equal chance of being picked, dilutes them below the level an average can detect.
Aggregate quality metrics conceal the failures that matter, and the reason is built into how averages work. A metric like average output quality, or average groundedness score, is dominated by the large volume of ordinary outputs a generative system produces. The failures a governance function, the group responsible for oversight, needs to catch are rare and severe, not common and mild. A single fabricated clinical fact buried inside thousands of accurate summaries is an example.
Averaging across a population where failures are rare produces a reassuring number. It looks reassuring because of the way it is computed. A monitoring program that relies on an aggregate average has built a metric blind by design to the rare, extreme cases it most needs to see.
crumbs: Part II: The AI System Lifecycle

title: 9. Operations and Monitoring
text:
9.4 Monitoring agent actions
An agentic system takes actions toward a goal, such as tool calls, which are requests the system sends to other software to get something done. Its unit of monitoring, the basic thing its monitors watch, is the action it took, not the output it produced. Chapter 7 already made this distinction for testing. Operational monitoring has to carry it forward into production. A system that acts generates a different kind of record than one that only produces outputs.
Making the action the unit of monitoring does not mean ground truth stops mattering. Ground truth becomes one of several things to check alongside the action itself. A wrong result or a harmful effect can still occur even when every action taken was individually authorized and within scope.
Each action needs to be monitored along at least five questions. What was done? Under whose authority was it done? What outcome did it produce, and was that outcome correct or desired? What effect did it have? And did it fall inside the permission scope the system was granted, and meet the postconditions the action was supposed to satisfy? A postcondition is something that must be true after the action finishes.
These questions sit with monitoring on purpose, not with design. Monitoring is the layer of day-to-day operations that watches what a designed system does once it is running. Designing the permission boundary is a separate task, covered in Chapter 12. Designing the log format that records the action is separate too, and Chapter 15 takes it up.
Scope violation detection watches for an action taken outside the system’s permission boundary, the limit on what it is allowed to do. This detection catches a permission design that looked sufficient on paper. The design proves too permissive, or too ambiguous, once real users and real requests flow through it.
Unexpected tool use detection watches for a pattern of tool calls that, while individually within scope, forms a combination or sequence nobody anticipated when the scope was granted.
Action volume anomaly detection watches for a rate of activity that departs sharply from the pattern the system’s approved use case would predict. That signal caught an anomaly in the scheduling agent of TALENTSCREEN, a hiring tool in the running cases, in the case in focus below. It did so well before anyone had traced the anomaly to its specific cause.
None of these three substitutes for preserving a full trace of what the agent did. The trace covers the model’s own messages, and its tool calls and their results. It also covers its internal state, the permissions active at the time, the actions taken, and their outcomes. A scope check or a volume count computed after the trace has been discarded cannot be re-examined when a new question arises about what happened.
Section 9.3 warns that averaging hides rare, severe failures in generative output. Averaging across an agent’s action volume hides the same kind of failure. A monitoring program should instead sample and directly review the categories of action most likely to contain a serious failure. These include duplicate or irreversible actions, actions taken under an unusually broad grant of access, and actions taken just after a tool returned something unexpected. The program should not trust that a rare failure will show up in an aggregate rate computed across everything the agent does.






Figure 10.2: Figure 9.2. Monitoring approach by system class




Figure 9.2 shows three monitoring practices that differ in how they work. They extend the testing distinction Chapter 7 drew into operations. A real deployment can also draw on more than one of the three columns at once.
A predictive system forecasts an outcome. Its monitoring contends with ground truth that is delayed, selectively observed, contested, a proxy for what is meant, or affected by the intervention itself. It leans on sampling, proxies, delayed evaluation, or causal comparison, choosing whichever fits the kind of ground truth problem at hand.
A generative system’s monitoring rarely has one universally correct output to check against. It substitutes source checks, executable tests, rubric sampling, groundedness checks, human review, and outcome measures as the task allows.
An agentic system’s monitoring watches goals, plans, tool calls, permissions, state, actions, side effects, postconditions, outcomes, and recovery together. It does not watch actions to the exclusion of whether the result was correct.
Suppose a team builds one dashboard modeled on the predictive column alone, the column for systems that forecast an outcome. If it points that dashboard at a system that also generates or acts, it watches only a fraction of what that system does in production. A team whose system combines more than one class needs more than one column’s monitoring running at once.
crumbs: Part II: The AI System Lifecycle

title: 9. Operations and Monitoring
text:
9.5 Fairness monitoring
Fairness testing in Chapter 7 checked a snapshot. It tested the model as it existed at the moment of testing against the population available at that moment. Production is not a snapshot. A disparity that pre-deployment testing did not reveal, because the tested population did not yet show it, can emerge months into operation. It can emerge because the deployment population itself shifts. It can also emerge because edge cases, meaning rare and unusual situations, accumulate that a finite test set never sampled densely enough to catch.
Fairness monitoring is more than Chapter 7’s disaggregated analysis rerun on a schedule. Disaggregated analysis breaks results out by group. A monitoring program should be built on three things stated there. These are its precise fairness definitions, its distinction between the score a model outputs and the decision made from that score, and its impossibility conditions. Impossibility conditions are the proven limits on meeting every fairness measure at once.
Production also raises questions that a one-time pre-deployment test does not have to answer. What denominator is each rate computed against, and over what outcome window? The denominator is the total that a rate is divided by. The outcome window is the span of time in which outcomes are counted. How is the resulting number’s uncertainty treated, given a production sample that may be smaller than a curated test set, one built by hand? What minimum sample size is required before a computed disparity is trusted at all? Is the analysis run at the intersection of more than one protected characteristic, rather than one at a time? A protected characteristic is a trait, such as race or sex, that anti-discrimination law protects. An intersection is a group defined by two or more such traits at once. How is a delayed outcome handled without waiting silently for it? And how are feedback effects, complaints, and human overrides of the system’s own recommendations factored into what the numbers mean? A feedback effect is the system’s own past decisions shaping the data it now sees.
A production fairness monitoring plan states these items:

the favorable outcome, meaning the result a person wants, and the positive class, the category the model is set up to flag, that it is measuring against
the metric and the reason it was chosen
the groups being compared
the denominator, the observation window, and the minimum sample size
how uncertainty below that sample size is treated
whether and how intersectional groups, groups defined by more than one protected trait at once, are analyzed
how delayed outcomes are handled
the alert and investigation thresholds
the named owner
whether legal review is required before a threshold breach becomes public or actionable
the mitigation options available
the schedule on which the whole plan itself is revalidated

Setting the alert threshold in advance matters for the same reason a red team’s disposition process mattered in Chapter 7. A red team is a group that attacks a system to find its flaws. A disposition process is the agreed way of deciding what happens with each finding, fixed before the findings arrive. A threshold decided after seeing a concerning number is vulnerable to being rationalized away by whoever would rather not act on it. A threshold fixed before any concerning number appeared has no such vulnerability built in.

title: 9. Operations and Monitoring
text:
9.6 Drift
Drift is change in the statistical relationship a model was trained to capture. In plain terms, the pattern the model learned no longer matches the world that is sending it data. Telling input drift from concept drift is a useful starting diagnosis. It does not dictate a single response, such as a data fix for one and a retrain for the other. Retraining means training the model again on newer data. Treating the diagnosis as if it dictated one response oversimplifies a decision that needs its own process.
Input drift is a change in the distribution of the data a model receives, meaning how its values are spread. The underlying relationship between that data and the correct outcome does not change. Suppose a lending model starts receiving applications with a different income distribution than its training data. If the relationship between income and repayment has not changed, the model is experiencing input drift.
Not every input distribution change deserves the same response, and Table 9.4 lists what the change can turn out to be.
Table 9.4. What an input distribution change can be







Possibility
Description




Harmless
The model’s learned relationship holds across the new distribution too


Harmful
The model’s learned relationship does not hold across the new distribution


Temporary
The change corrects itself without intervention


Pipeline fault
A symptom of a fault upstream of the model, a break in the systems feeding it data, not a real change in the population


Population change
A genuine, lasting signal that the population being served has changed



A representativeness fix, one that makes the data representative again, is often the right response. But retraining on a distribution that turns out to be a temporary pipeline artifact can lock a problem in instead of solving it. Telling these cases apart is part of the work. It is not a detail to skip past on the way to a fix.
Concept drift is a change in the underlying relationship itself. The same input now predicts a different outcome than it used to. No amount of representative sampling will fix this, because the thing the model learned is no longer true.
Fraud is an example. Fraud techniques evolve past whatever pattern the model learned to recognize. In that case, retraining on data reflecting the new relationship is usually necessary. But even here retraining is one option among several. A real concept change can call for recalibrating the existing model, which means adjusting its scores rather than training it again. It can call for adding a new feature, an input that captures what changed. It can call for adjusting a decision threshold or rule. It can also call for restricting the system’s use while the relationship is investigated, rolling back to a prior version, or retiring the system. The choice depends on what changed and how much.
Detecting drift and deciding what to do about it are two different steps. Treating the two steps as one simple either-or rule overstates what either check can promise on its own. That rule says input drift shows up immediately, while concept drift shows up only once ground truth arrives. In practice, an input change can take time to accumulate to a detectable level. A concept change can sometimes be inferred earlier from a leading indicator, an early warning signal, before full ground truth confirms it.
A more accurate process has five stages:

Detect a candidate change. Use enough data, and make an explicit assessment of the statistical uncertainty or power behind the detection, so the team does not react to noise. Noise means random ups and downs in the data. Power is the ability to notice a change that is really there.
Diagnose the source. It might be an input distribution change, a change in the actual outcome relationship, or a change in how labels, the correct answers attached to the data, are produced. It might be a pipeline fault, a change in the rules or in the world around the system, or a model version change. The source might also be a prompt change, a change in the retrieval corpus, or a configuration change. These sources call for different owners and different fixes, even when the detected symptom looks similar.
Assess materiality, which means how much the change matters. Evaluate it against performance, fairness, safety, and the system’s actual use. Not every detected change needs action.
Choose the intervention. Match it to the diagnosis, and do not default to retraining just because that is the response most readily associated with “drift”. Options include recalibration, data repair, retraining, a threshold or rule change, escalation to a vendor, rollback, restriction, or retirement.
Validate that the intervention worked. Monitor for recurrence, and preserve the decision record.

One more source of change, a change made by the supplier of a purchased model, belongs in the diagnosis stage. It is specific to the selection path introduced in Chapter 6. The selection path is the route where an organization buys a system instead of building it. It should not be treated as a third category of data drift.
Take a purchased model. An apparent shift may not come from the deploying organization’s own population at all. The supplier may have updated the model or service underneath the deploying organization’s unchanged interface, the connection, often called an API, through which its software calls the model. This update is a model-version or configuration change, not a new kind of drift. It needs to be checked as its own diagnosis. It should not be folded into a catch-all label of “developer-side drift” as though it belonged in the same category as an actual population shift.
An organization that monitors only its own inputs and outputs may not track which model version is running behind its API calls. It can then misdiagnose a supplier-side change as its own population shifting, when nothing about its population changed at all.






Figure 10.3: Figure 9.3. Drift detection and response




Figure 9.3 shows a five-stage process that a detected change moves through. It replaces a two-row lookup table that matched input-versus-concept to data-fix-versus-retrain. Detection flags a candidate change with a stated confidence, not a certainty.
Diagnosis is where the real branching happens. It includes a possibility the two-row version omitted. What looks like a population shift can be a supplier silently changing the model or service behind an otherwise unchanged interface. That is a version or configuration change to check directly, not a third kind of drift.
Materiality assessment and the choice of intervention follow the diagnosis instead of a fixed input-versus-concept rule. Validation closes the loop. It confirms that the intervention worked, instead of assuming it did because it was applied.

title: 9. Operations and Monitoring
text:
9.7 Post-market monitoring plans
A post-market monitoring plan, the written plan for watching a system after it is released, is a documented artifact with defined contents. That requirement holds under the EU AI Act, the European Union’s law on AI, and in broader governance practice. The plan is not a description of an activity an organization asserts it performs.
Which organization holds which duty depends on a role. The plan has to state that role before it states anything else.
Article 72 places the post-market monitoring system and plan duty on the provider of a high-risk system. The provider is the organization that develops the system, or has it developed, and puts it on the market under its own name. High-risk is the Act’s own label for the systems it regulates most strictly. The provider must actively and systematically collect, document, and analyze relevant data across the system’s lifetime. This includes the system’s interactions with other AI systems where relevant.
Article 26 places a separate, narrower set of duties on the deployer, the organization that uses the system. These duties include operating the system according to the provider’s instructions. They include assigning competent human oversight with real authority and support, and monitoring the system’s operation. They include suspending use in specified risk circumstances, informing the provider or relevant authorities where required, and retaining logs the deployer controls. Article 73 adds serious-incident reporting on top of both.
An organization writing its own monitoring plan has to say first which of these roles it holds. It may be provider, deployer, or both for different parts of the same system. The contents required differ by role.
A provider’s plan documents continuous compliance analysis across the system’s lifetime, meaning an ongoing check that the system still meets the rules. It draws on deployer-reported data and other sources. It also documents the system’s interaction with other AI systems. It links to the technical documentation, the system’s required written record, and to serious-incident reporting. And it documents corrective and preventive action, meaning fixing problems and keeping them from coming back. A deployer’s plan documents operating within instructions, oversight assignment, its own monitoring, and its own reporting and log-retention obligations.
Article 72 originally called for an implementing act specifying a template for the plan, due by February 2, 2026. An implementing act is a follow-on rule issued by the European Commission, the EU’s executive body. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 replaced that power with Commission guidance, including a template, due by September 2, 2027. This was checked against two secondary sources on 2026-10-19 and has not yet been checked against the Official Journal text. A regulatory deadline can change again, so the status should be re-verified against the current official text before this section is relied on.
Beyond the legal roles, the plan needs the same defined contents whichever role is writing it. It must name which of section 9.1’s dimensions are being monitored. It must state the method, the schedule, the threshold that triggers escalation, and who is accountable for reviewing the results.
A plan that states an organization “monitors performance regularly” has not documented a post-market monitoring plan. It has documented an intention. The two are not interchangeable. This is true for compliance, and it is true for the more basic governance purpose of catching what section 9.1’s dimensions exist to catch.
A complete plan still establishes only design, not operation. These are two different layers of evidence, and a well-written plan cannot stand in for the second. An auditor reading the plan alone can determine what the organization committed to monitor, by what method, and on what schedule. The auditor cannot determine whether the collection, review, escalation, and response the plan describes happened.
That second layer needs its own operating record. The record holds the data collected, the analyses performed, the alerts reviewed and by whom, the decisions made, the actions completed, and any exception left unresolved. A plan that has never generated that operating record is design without operation, whatever its contents promise.

title: 9. Operations and Monitoring
text:
9.8 Human oversight in practice
Chapter 8 named oversight readiness as one dimension of organizational readiness, an organization’s overall preparedness to run its systems. Oversight readiness means being set up to supervise them. Oversight in practice is where a reviewer’s oversight either functions or collapses into a formality. The collapse has specific, detectable signals. A governance function should watch for them as its own monitoring target.
Meaningful oversight exists when a human reviewer has the time, the authority, and the information needed to catch a wrong output and act on it. Nominal oversight, oversight in name only, exists when a human sits in the review position but works, in practice, as a rubber stamp. The volume, the time pressure, or the framing of the task, how the job is set up and presented, has made real review impractical. This is true regardless of the reviewer’s intentions or competence.
The distinction matters because a human-in-the-loop control, a person reviewing the system’s outputs, can satisfy a compliance checklist while it has quietly stopped doing any real review. An organization can still point to that control. The checklist records that a reviewer is in place. It does not test whether the review still works.
Automation bias, introduced in Chapter 1 as the tendency to over-trust an automated recommendation, produces detectable operational signals. It does not remain a purely psychological phenomenon invisible to monitoring. Each signal is an investigation trigger, not proof of the underlying failure on its own. Every one of them has an innocent explanation alongside the concerning one.
The first signal is an approval rate approaching unity, meaning a rate close to its maximum of one. In practice, the reviewer agrees with the system’s recommendation in nearly every case. That pattern is at least as consistent with a reviewer who has stopped making independent decisions as it is with a system that has become extraordinarily accurate. It is equally consistent with an easy population of cases. It is consistent with a policy design that narrows the reviewer’s real discretion, the room to decide differently. It is also consistent with batching effects, patterns that come from handling cases in batches rather than one by one. And it is consistent with an appropriate degree of automation for the task.
The second signal is review times too short to plausibly support the evaluation the role requires. Timestamps a system already logs measure this directly. The third signal is absence of override, a reviewer setting aside the system’s recommendation and deciding differently. Absence of override means a reviewer has never once done so across a meaningful volume of cases.
None of the three should be treated as a finding until it has been validated. The validation has several parts:

Check a blinded sample, where the reviewer does not know which cases are being checked.
Compare against an independent human decision on the same cases, allowing for how hard each case was and how much time each review took.
Check the quality of whatever overrides do occur, not only their count.
Account for outcomes that are themselves delayed.
Where the pattern persists, interview or directly observe the reviewer. Look at the reviewer’s workload and alert burden, and whether the reviewer had the authority and the information the role assumes.

A governance function that treats an approval rate approaching unity as a finding, without running this validation, has replaced one unverified assumption with another. The first assumption is that the reviewer is engaged. The second is that the reviewer is not.
MEDASSIST’s alert fatigue, introduced in Chapter 1 as a governance concept, is related to automation bias. It is not automation bias running in the opposite direction. The two are distinct mechanisms whose signals happen to look like mirror images of each other. Approvals pile up in one, and dismissals pile up in the other.
Automation bias is over-trusting what a system recommends. Alert fatigue is attention worn down by too many alerts. It is an adaptation to volume and workload that can seem sensible from the reviewer’s side. It degrades attention regardless of how much the reviewer trusts the system. A nurse managing eleven patients and a high volume of alerts, many of them low-value, can learn to dismiss alerts quickly. The reason has nothing to do with how much she trusts the alert. The real driver is how many of them she has to process.
The detectable signal for alert fatigue is a dismissal rate approaching unity, not an approval rate. It comes alongside review times too short to have evaluated the alert’s content. It needs the same validation discipline as automation bias. Until validated, it is a hypothesis, not a finding.
Once validated, the two mechanisms call for different interventions. Automation bias calls for retraining the reviewers or restructuring incentives. Alert fatigue calls for workload and alert-volume management. The underlying operational discipline is the same. A governance function monitors dismissal and override rates, review timing, and the content of a validated sample of reviewed decisions. That function can catch either failure mode before it produces the specific missed case that first makes it visible. The alternative is waiting, as Northfield did, for a retrospective review to find it after the harm has already occurred.

title: 9. Operations and Monitoring
section: Case in focus: two signals a dashboard could have caught earlier
text:
Case in focus: two signals a dashboard could have caught earlier
MEDASSIST and TALENTSCREEN · Hypothetical, following the running cases
The retrospective chart review that eventually surfaced MEDASSIST’s community hospital gap was not the first opportunity to catch it. It was the first time anyone looked with the right method. Section 9.2’s absent-truth problem meant that no simple comparison of predictions to confirmed outcomes could have caught the gap directly. A prevented deterioration leaves no confirmed case to compare against.
But section 9.8’s alert fatigue signals were available. These were alert dismissal rates and review timing at each community hospital. They had been quietly diverging from the academic center’s pattern for months before anyone examined them. Nursing staff at the community hospitals received alerts calibrated to a population and workflow the model did not describe. They dismissed a higher proportion of alerts, and dismissed them faster, than staff at the academic center. A monitoring program watching dismissal rates by site would have flagged that pattern for investigation well before the retrospective review became necessary.
Nobody was watching that signal. The monitoring program in place tracked only the technical and aggregate-performance dimensions from section 9.1. It did not track human oversight. A program that covered only two of the five dimensions, with nothing on that target, caught nothing. The harm grew until it was large enough to trigger a review by other means.
Calloway, the organization that uses TALENTSCREEN, discovered an anomaly in the scheduling agent by a cleaner path. The signal that caught it was one the organization had in place. That signal was action volume anomaly detection from section 9.4.
A routine review of the agent’s weekly scheduling volume showed a sharp, unexplained spike at one regional office. The spike was well outside the pattern the tool’s approved use case would predict. Investigation traced the spike to a configuration event. The platform’s own access log had recorded the event, but nobody had reviewed it until the volume anomaly prompted the look.
A local hiring manager had granted the agent access to a broader calendar system than its approved permission scope covered. The manager intended a convenience. The platform accepted the change without an alert comparing the new effective access against the approved scope. Every scheduling action the agent then took passed its own runtime permission check. By that point, the broader access was what the system believed the agent was allowed to use. No single action, evaluated on its own, would have looked wrong. Each one was a normal scheduling decision correctly executed under the access it had.
The scope violation was real, and it was logged. But the log entry was made at the moment the access was expanded beyond what the deployment record approved, not at the moment any scheduling action ran. The action volume signal surfaced it a week later, because nobody had built an alert on the configuration log itself. The anomaly was visible only in aggregate. That is the argument section 9.4 makes for monitoring actions as a population, instead of only auditing them one at a time after a complaint arrives.
Both cases teach the same lesson from opposite directions. MEDASSIST’s harm went undetected because a dimension of monitoring, human oversight, was never built into the program. TALENTSCREEN’s anomaly was caught quickly because the corresponding dimension, action volume, was in place. A monitoring program is only as complete as the dimensions it covers. The gap between five dimensions in principle and two or three in practice is where harm accumulates unseen.

title: 9. Operations and Monitoring
text:
Summary
Operation is the longest phase of a system’s life. It is the phase where most of a system’s risk materializes. A monitoring program built around a single accuracy-like number will miss most of that risk.
Five core dimensions are technical, performance, fairness, drift, and usage. They are a minimum. They are not an exhaustive or mutually exclusive taxonomy. A fuller program also names where human oversight, security and privacy, change and supply-chain, and complaint signals are being watched. A program that reduces everything to performance monitoring alone has narrowed its watch to one dimension without noticing it did so.
Ground truth can be delayed, ambiguous, absent, or affected by the very intervention being evaluated. Four approaches recover a usable signal from these situations. They are sampling with adjudication, proxy metrics with stated limitations, delayed evaluation, and causal or comparison-based methods. MEDASSIST’s intervention-affected problem is the hardest of these cases. It is an unobservable individual counterfactual, which goes beyond absent truth.
Generative systems rarely have one universally correct output to check against. That is not the same as having no ground truth at all. Source checks, executable tests, rubric-based sampling, groundedness checking, human review, and outcome measures each cover part of the gap. A fuller coverage map adds factuality, citation validity, privacy leakage, harmful content, prompt injection, retrieval poisoning, and user-correction signals. Sampling should favor the rare, severe failures that an aggregate average conceals.
Agentic systems require monitoring of goals, plans, tool calls, permissions, state, actions, side effects, postconditions, and outcomes together. Monitoring actions alone, without checking whether the result was correct, is not enough. That means watching for scope violations, unexpected tool combinations, and volume anomalies. It also means preserving full traces and directly sampling the categories most likely to contain a severe failure.
Fairness monitoring builds on Chapter 7’s method. It adds what production requires beyond a snapshot test. These additions are a stated denominator, observation window, minimum sample size, intersectional analysis, delayed-outcome handling, and named ownership. All of them run against thresholds fixed before any concerning number appears.
Drift detection and response is a five-stage process. The stages are detect, diagnose, assess materiality, decide the intervention, and validate. It is not a two-way lookup between input-drift-means-data-fix and concept-drift-means-retrain. A supplier silently changing a purchased model behind an unchanged interface is a version or configuration change to diagnose directly. It is not a third category of drift.
A post-market monitoring plan is a documented artifact. It names dimensions, methods, schedules, thresholds, and accountability. It is not an asserted activity. It has to state first whether the organization holds the EU AI Act’s provider duties, deployer duties, or both, since the required contents differ by role.
Human oversight can collapse from meaningful to nominal in detectable ways. The signals are an approval or dismissal rate approaching unity, review times too short to support real evaluation, and an absence of override. Each is an investigation trigger requiring validation, and none is a finding on its own. Alert fatigue is a related but distinct mechanism from automation bias, and it is not its mirror image.
Evidence carried forward. Monitoring watches the constraints, residual risks, versions, and human workflow that Chapter 8’s release record specified. Residual risks are the risks that remain even after fixes. It does not follow a generic checklist independent of what was decided. It is where a finding gets its first disposition, meaning the first decision about what to do with it. The options are triage, corrective action, revalidation, a deployment restriction, an incident, or a decision to roll back or retire the system. Chapter 10 picks up from one of those dispositions, incident response, when monitoring surfaces something that needs more than a routine correction.

title: 9. Operations and Monitoring
text:
Review questions
COMPREHENSION

Explain why MEDASSIST’s ground truth problem, a prevented deterioration leaving no trace, cannot be solved by any of the four approaches in section 9.2 without modification, and describe which approach, in what modified form, the case in focus shows being used to find the gap.
Distinguish input drift from concept drift, and explain why a monitoring program that detects only the first will still miss certain failures.

APPLIED

Design a monitoring plan for a generative customer-support system with no ground truth available. Specify at least three of the methods from section 9.3 and what each is intended to catch.
A monitoring dashboard for an agentic system tracks only whether individual actions fall within the agent’s permission scope. Using section 9.4, identify what this dashboard would miss and specify the additional signal needed to catch it.

SPOT THE RISK

A team reports that its human review process shows a 99 percent agreement rate between reviewers and the system’s recommendations, and treats this as evidence the system is highly accurate. Identify the alternative explanation section 9.8 requires the team to rule out, and describe how you would investigate which explanation is correct.

COMPARE AND DECIDE

An organization detects input drift in a fraud-detection model’s incoming transaction data but has not yet observed any change in the model’s actual error rate. State the case for retraining immediately versus waiting for concept drift confirmation, and what you would need to know to decide between them.

RUNNING CASE

TALENTSCREEN Using the case in focus, explain why the action volume anomaly was detectable even though no single scheduling action looked wrong in isolation, and specify what change to Calloway’s permission-scope monitoring would have caught the underlying cause sooner.


Monitoring tells an organization something is wrong. It does not, by itself, fix anything. The next chapter turns to what happens after that moment. It covers how a response is classified, staffed, and executed, and what reporting obligations attach and on what timeline. It also covers how a root cause analysis, a method for finding a failure’s deeper causes, reaches the systemic factors that the case in focus above already illustrates. It does not stop at the first proximate cause, the nearest and most obvious one, that a rushed investigation finds convenient to blame.

title: 10. Incident Response and Remediation
text:
What you will be able to do
Chapter 9’s case in focus was MEDASSIST’s community hospital gap. MEDASSIST is an AI system that alerts hospital staff to sepsis, a life-threatening reaction to infection. The gap was that the system performed worse at the community hospitals it served than at the academic medical center where its validation cases came from. The gap did not end when a retrospective chart review confirmed it. A chart review looks back through patient records to see what happened.
Confirmation was the beginning of a different kind of work. Someone had to decide how serious the finding was, and who had the authority to act on it in the next hour, not the next committee cycle. Someone had to decide whether any regulator, a government body that enforces rules, needed to hear about it, and on what clock. Someone had to decide why the gap existed, in a form deeper than “the model performed worse at six hospitals”. And someone had to decide what would change afterward, so the same pattern could not go unnoticed for months a second time.
All of these questions belong to incident response, the work of handling a failure once it is found. The case in focus below shows how Northfield, the organization behind the system, answers these questions. Its answers decide whether the community hospital gap ends as a contained, documented, corrected episode or becomes the first chapter of a worse one.
Response is a discipline with its own structure. It is not an improvisation that begins once monitoring or a user report produces a bad enough number. Systems fail. How the organization responds is a separate variable, and the organization controls it. That response decides whether a failure stays a governance success story or becomes real harm. Governance means the rules, roles, and checks an organization uses to control its AI systems.

text:
Identify the detection channels (the ways an incident comes to light) that monitoring alone will not cover, and explain what each can find that planned monitoring did not expect
Apply a severity classification scheme, which sorts incidents into levels called tiers, and state what response each tier triggers
Carry out the full incident response lifecycle, including the duty to fix effects already produced and the extra checks that the lookback for an agentic system (one that takes actions on its own) requires
Identify which incidents must be reported to a regulator, and by when
Conduct a root cause analysis, a search for why an incident happened, that reaches systemic factors (weaknesses in the organization’s processes) and does not stop at the first proximate cause

11  10. Incident Response and Remediation

title: 10. Incident Response and Remediation
text:
10.1 Detection channels
An organization learns about an incident, an event in which an AI system fails or causes harm, through one of several channels. The channel that surfaces a given incident is rarely the one the governance program was built to rely on.
Detection channels are broader than the handful a governance program tends to build first. Table 10.1 sets out seven channels, where each signal comes from, and what each can surface.
Table 10.1. Detection channels








Channel
Where the signal comes from
What it can surface




Automated internal signals
Monitoring, the routine tracking of how a system performs and the subject of Chapter 9
What monitoring’s dimensions, the specific aspects of behavior it tracks, are built to watch, and no more


Human internal reports
People inside the organization, from a frontline employee’s direct observation to internal audit, security operations (the team that watches for attacks on the organization’s systems), safety surveillance (the routine watch for safety problems), and an employee escalation or whistleblower report made through a channel built for that purpose
A problem staff observe directly. In the MEDASSIST case, nurses noticed that alert timing felt wrong well before any combined number confirmed it


Affected-person and customer channels
The people a system’s decisions land on, not the staff operating it
A complaint, a request for explanation, or litigation (a lawsuit), often long after the organization’s own channels should have caught the same pattern


Supplier and partner notifications
A vendor, an outside company that supplies a product or service, or an outside service the system relies on
A disclosed problem in a purchased component, or an upstream service incident, a failure in an outside service, that spreads into the organization’s own system


Assurance activity
Scheduled checks, such as a test, an audit, or an evaluation
A problem outside the check’s original purpose. Those findings are a detection channel too


Regulators and legal processes
A regulator’s inquiry or a legal claim
An incident the organization did not report first


Public external discovery
A journalist or academic who examines the system from outside, with no obligation to notify the organization before publishing
A contained internal matter turned into a public one, on a schedule the organization does not control



A whistleblower is a person who reports wrongdoing or danger inside their own organization.
Every channel needs the same support to work. It needs accessible intake, meaning a way in that a person can find and use without specialized knowledge. It needs a named triage owner who reviews what comes in and sorts it by urgency. It needs correlation across channels, meaning someone connects related reports, so that a pattern several channels hint at separately gets recognized as one thing. It also needs acknowledgment to whoever raised the concern, and protection against retaliation, which is punishment for raising the concern. Where appropriate, it needs feedback on what happened as a result.
Some might claim that the channel an organization did not build is the one most likely to find the next incident. That claim has no evidence behind it. Channels an organization did not build can reveal failures that designed monitoring did not anticipate. This is a reason to build several channels and to treat none of them, including monitoring, as enough on its own.
Consider a governance program that is confident in its monitoring dashboard. It may provide no accessible channel for a nurse’s informal observation or an applicant’s complaint. That program has optimized detection for the failures it already expected. Every other way of failing is left to whichever of these other channels happens to notice first, or to none of them.

11  10. Incident Response and Remediation

title: 10. Incident Response and Remediation
text:
10.2 Severity classification
A severity scheme sorts an incident into a tier, a level of seriousness, the moment it is identified. The tier determines who responds, how fast, and with what authority. Without a scheme, those decisions would be negotiated fresh under the time pressure each incident brings.
A workable scheme needs criteria specific enough that two different reviewers classify the same incident the same way. That rules out a scheme built only on adjectives, such as labels that call an incident “serious” or “minor” without saying what makes it so. The scheme must also avoid the opposite failure. A rule can be too blunt in two ways. It can treat any health, safety, or fundamental-rights outcome as automatically critical, whatever the scale. Fundamental rights are the basic rights that law protects. Or it can treat an anomaly with no confirmed harm as automatically low tier, however fast it is accumulating. An anomaly is an unusual pattern.
Either version creates the same two failures. It will overclassify a minor, reversible event, which means rating it too high. A reversible event is one whose effects can be undone. It will also underclassify other events, which means rating them too low. These include a serious near miss, which is an event that almost caused harm. They include an active security compromise and a large but not yet confirmed exposure. They also include a risk accumulating so fast that waiting for confirmation would be its own mistake.
The classification a severity scheme produces at the moment of detection is provisional, meaning open to change, because the facts available at that moment are incomplete. The scheme has to be built around that fact. Table 10.2 lists the factors the scheme should assess and weigh.
Table 10.2. Factors a severity scheme assesses







Factor
What the scheme asks




Harm
The actual and credible potential harm, and which affected right or domain (area of life, such as health or hiring) is involved


Population
The scale and vulnerability of the population involved, meaning how many people are affected and how easily they can be hurt


Reversibility and duration
How reversible the harm is and how long it lasts


Spread
How far the harm has spread, geographically or across systems


Exposure and detectability
Whether exposure is ongoing and how detectable the problem is


Legal threshold
Whether a legal threshold is involved, meaning a point at which a legal duty begins


Data compromise
Whether data has been compromised


Operational criticality
How operationally critical the affected function is, meaning how much the organization’s daily work depends on it


Uncertainty
How much uncertainty remains in the assessment itself



Uncertainty is a reason to escalate immediately and not wait for it to resolve. A provisional severity assigned under uncertainty is expected to be reclassified, upward or downward, as better evidence arrives. It is not a one-time decision locked in at detection.
Once assigned, each severity level maps to a fixed set of commitments. These are a response time, an authority empowered to act, and containment options. They also include a communication obligation, a legal assessment requirement, and a review cadence. Containment means stopping harm from continuing or spreading. A review cadence is how often the incident is reviewed.
Classifying an incident is therefore, immediately, an instruction. It is not the start of a debate about what to do next. A scheme that sorts incidents into tiers without committing each tier to this full set has built only a taxonomy, a sorting list. A sorting list says what kind of incident something is, but it does not make anyone respond. The scheme has not built an incident response capability.

11  10. Incident Response and Remediation

title: 10. Incident Response and Remediation
text:
10.3 Response procedures
A short version of incident response names five procedures. They are notification, assessment, containment, communication, and documentation. Once an incident is classified, a fuller lifecycle runs than those five. Naming only the five omits stages a real response cannot skip.
One missing stage is declaring the incident and assigning a named commander. Another is protecting people and stopping active harm as its own step, before broader containment. Another is preserving evidence before anything else changes it. The response must also correct or eradicate the active cause, and not only contain it. To eradicate is to remove the cause completely. It must recover service through a validated path, meaning one that has been checked before use, and then verify that recovery worked. Last, it must define a closure authority, the person or role with the power to declare the incident over. Without one, the incident has no formal end. It fades when attention moves elsewhere.
The lifecycle applies to every system class. A system class is a kind of AI system. Predictive systems score or decide cases, generative systems produce content, and agentic systems take actions on their own. In sequence, the lifecycle runs as follows.
The response team first receives and acknowledges the triggering signal, and it preserves the evidence around the signal. It then triages the incident, formally declares it, and assigns an incident commander, the person in charge of the response. It sets the provisional severity from section 10.2. Next it protects people and stops active harm. Then it contains the system, the data, the access, and, where relevant, the supplier path. The supplier path is the vendor’s link into the system.
At the same time, the team assesses the scope. It checks whether the cause is still active, who is affected, what legal duties attach, and what communication is needed. Notification reaches the required internal and external parties on each party’s own clock, which is the deadline that applies to that party. A decision log is kept throughout. Alongside this, the team corrects or eradicates the active cause. It also remedies prior effects for every system class, not only the agentic one.
Recovery follows. It happens through a validated system, a restricted service, or a manual fallback, which means doing the task by hand. The team verifies that recovery worked, watches for recurrence, and updates severity and scope as new evidence arrives. Root cause analysis and post-incident review, from sections 10.5 and 10.6, run while communication and documentation continue. Communication and documentation do not wait for that work to finish. The incident closes only once the technical, human, legal, and process actions each have evidence and an owner.
These stages are not strictly sequential for a severe incident. Several run in parallel. New evidence at any point loops back to update severity, scope, containment, communication, or the legal assessment. It does not only feed forward.
Containment is a set of layered options, running from small targeted steps up to full shutdown, and not a single lever to pull. The team chooses options for the specific incident and does not default to the same response every time.
The options include local access revocation, which removes permissions. They include credential rotation, which replaces passwords and keys. They include isolating a specific integration, which cuts one connection to other software. Other options are stopping a data feed, restricting which users can reach the system, and invoking a vendor’s contractual suspension right. Others are a feature flag, which is a switch that turns one feature off, and a rollback to a prior version. The last two are a manual fallback process and full shutdown.
The right choice is the least disruptive option that controls the credible harm within the time the severity tier requires. Credible harm is harm that could realistically happen. The choice comes from comparing three things. They are the harm, the uncertainty still remaining about its cause and extent, and the fallback that is available. The choice does not come from a rule that says one system class always has narrower containment options than another. Suppose a policy treats continued availability, meaning keeping the system running, as the default to protect. Suppose nobody has written down a comparison of that default against the credible harm. Then the policy has traded harm against uptime by default and not by decision. An example is a faulty alert system. Keeping it online means its faults keep causing harm, while turning it off removes the alerts that some people still need. A real decision compares both harms, in writing.
Take a purchased system. The deploying organization, the one that uses the system, may not control the vendor’s infrastructure. Even so, its containment is not limited to a contractual disable right. The deployer can typically still revoke local access and rotate its own credentials. It can disable its own integration and stop sending data to the system. It can also restrict which of its own users can reach the system. An organization should confirm which of these options exist, and on what timeline, before an incident makes the question urgent. That confirmation is part of building the containment capability. It is not an afterthought for when the vendor relationship becomes the bottleneck.
For every system class, containing future harm is a different question from remedying harm already done. To remedy is to set right. A response that stops at containment has not finished the job. A predictive decision that wrongly denied an applicant leaves effects after the system is contained. So does a generative output that disclosed sensitive data or published false content. So does an agentic action. Each needs its own lookback, notification, correction, recourse, or remedy for whoever was affected while the system was misbehaving. A lookback is a review of past outputs and actions to find who was affected. Recourse is a way for an affected person to seek a fix.
An agentic incident carries additional checks specific to its own record. These are the tool actions taken, transactions initiated, commitments made, and messages sent. They also include state changes recorded (changes to stored data) and any downstream automation the agent’s actions triggered. Each of these needs its own assessment of whether it can be reversed. Where it cannot be reversed, it needs a compensating action, a new action that offsets the harm. The underlying discipline is that stopping future behavior is not the same task as addressing past effects.
TALENTSCREEN is a hiring system used by a company called Calloway. Its scheduling agent is an AI agent that schedules job interviews. In Chapter 9’s case in focus, the agent was caught by an action volume anomaly, an unusual jump in the number of actions it was taking. Halting the agent the moment the anomaly was confirmed stopped it from scheduling further interviews through the broader calendar access it should never have had. But halting left open the separate question of what to do about every interview already scheduled through that access. Some of those interviews needed to be reviewed, and in a few cases unwound, meaning undone, before the response could be considered complete.
Communication keeps affected parties informed. They may be internal stakeholders (people inside the organization with a stake in the outcome), regulators, or the people harmed. The cadence and level of detail are proportional to the severity tier. Communication is distinct from any regulatory notification, which has its own legal form and timeline.
Documentation records what was known, when, and what was decided. It does this in real time and not in a reconstruction made afterward. A reconstruction written after the fact tends to describe the response the organization wishes it had run, rather than the one it ran.
Decision authority under time pressure is the procedural detail most incident plans get wrong by omission. A plan may name a response but not a specific person or role empowered to invoke it at three in the morning. Such a plan has not built a response capability. It has only described one, and that description depends on improvised authority when improvisation is least reliable. The severity scheme from section 10.2 should already have answered the authority question before any specific incident makes it urgent.







Figure 11.1: Figure 10.1. Incident response flow with decision points



Figure 10.1 shows a ten-stage lifecycle with two timeline branches, standard and emergency. The same severity decision point gates both branches. The figure is not five boxes with a single emergency path. It marks the feedback loops that carry new evidence back, rather than flowing in one direction only.
The correct-or-eradicate-and-remedy stage applies to every system class. The agentic-specific checks are tool actions, transactions, commitments, messages, state changes, and downstream automations. They are additional detail within that same universal stage. They do not show that only an agentic incident needs to look backward at what already happened.
The TALENTSCREEN case shows the same obligation on the containment side. A response plan that treated halting the agent as the end of containment would have closed the incident while several of its consequences were still live.
An organization can license a system instead of building it. This is the buy path, the path of buying instead of building. The buy path adds a specific option to confirm in advance, not a specific limitation to assume. TALENTSCREEN is licensed rather than built, and Calloway does not control the infrastructure the agent runs on. A full shutdown may therefore require invoking a contractual right to disable functionality, instead of flipping a switch that Calloway owns. That does not mean the vendor holds the only lever. Calloway’s own local access revocation, credential rotation, and integration isolation remain available, whatever the contract says about a full disable. Integration isolation here means Calloway cutting the connection between the system and its own software.
A response plan for a purchased system confirms in advance which of the layered containment options it controls itself, and which depend on the vendor and on what timeline. The confirmation should also cover evidence access, log retention (how long records are kept), and the vendor’s contractual duty to cooperate with the organization’s own investigation. A disable right alone does not establish what happened or satisfy a reporting obligation.
A generative system’s containment has the same full range of layered options as any other system class. Which option is right depends on the incident’s harm, uncertainty, and available fallback. No rule says that generative incidents default to narrowing over shutdown. Narrowing is not automatically better than a fuller restriction.
A generative incident is often a pattern of bad outputs rather than a single confirmed decision. So restricting capability, disabling a specific feature, or routing outputs through mandatory human review is frequently sufficient and less disruptive than a full disable. But where the credible harm is severe enough, or too uncertain to limit with a narrower control, shutting the capability down entirely is the correct choice. The framework should not be read as discouraging it.
