title: 13. Organizing the Governance Function
text:
13.4 How federated governance fails
Federated governance fails in three predictable ways. A program that has not been warned about them tends to discover all three at once. The first is classification drift. Two business units facing comparable systems classify them at different risk tiers. Without a shared calibration mechanism, a shared way to compare and align decisions across units, federated decisions can drift further apart over time. They do not come back together on their own.
The drift itself is not automatically a defect. A hiring screen and a credit screen can be built on the same underlying model architecture, meaning the same basic design of model. They can legitimately land in different risk tiers. Their intended uses, affected populations, and consequences of error differ. A program that flags every difference as inconsistency would punish sound decisions that fit each unit’s own context. It would not catch a real failure.
The failure to catch is narrower. Two units may face the same use, the same population, and the same stakes. They can still reach different classifications because the reviewers weighed identical evidence differently. Neither reviewer knows the other’s classification exists. No recorded rationale lets either one compare their reasoning with the other’s.
Calibration tells the two cases apart. It means sampling classifications across units. It means comparing the recorded rationale and not only the tier assigned. It also means updating shared guidance where the comparison reveals unwarranted variation, meaning differences with no good reason behind them, and not a defensible contextual difference, one that context justifies. In both cases, the drift stays invisible until that comparison happens or an audit or incident forces it.
The second failure is capture, where a reviewer comes to serve the interests of the group it is meant to check. Local governance is captured by the business it serves. A reviewer embedded in the same business unit whose deployment they are reviewing faces continuous pressure to approve. They share the unit’s incentives and its relationships. Independence erodes gradually, not through any single compromised decision. The reviewer does not experience this as compromise. They experience it as sound decisions made under time pressure by someone who understands the business. That is why capture is hard to detect from inside the arrangement that produces it.
The third failure is lost aggregate visibility. Nobody holds a view of the whole organization. This failure is serious. At least some regulatory reporting obligations attach to the deploying organization, or to a specific provider or deployer role under it. They do not attach to a business unit in isolation.
Under the EU AI Act, Article 26 places monitoring, suspension, and notification duties on the deployer. Article 73 places serious-incident reporting duties on the provider, duties to report serious harmful events. Either duty holder needs a view across whatever business units its own systems span in order to meet the duty. A federated program with no central aggregation point cannot answer that kind of organization-wide or role-wide question. This is true even when every individual business unit could answer its own piece correctly.
An organization should be able to say how many AI systems it operates and how that scope was defined. That is the standard set by the inventory obligation in Chapter 3. Specific sector regulation or supervisory guidance can separately impose that same answer as its own legal recordkeeping duty. An organization has no answer at all if its inventory lives in a dozen disconnected spreadsheets instead of a single record. This holds however well each business unit tracks its own piece.
crumbs: 14  13. Organizing the Governance Function

title: 13. Organizing the Governance Function
text:
13.5 Roles and responsibilities
A governance decision needs four explicit answers. Who is responsible for doing the work? Who is accountable for the outcome? Who must be consulted before the decision is made? Who needs to be informed after it is made? Together, these answers form the RACI structure, named for the four roles: responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed. It is borrowed from broader risk practice. Here it is applied to AI-specific decisions and is not left as a generic template.
Take a deployment decision under Chapter 8’s readiness dimensions, the conditions a deployment must meet to count as ready. The deploying business unit might be responsible for assembling the readiness evidence. It might also be accountable for the underlying use decision. A central AI governance function might hold required concurrence, an approval without which a deployment cannot proceed. The model risk function and legal would then be consulted before the decision. The executive sponsor, the senior leader who backs the deployment, would be informed once it is made.
Required concurrence is a second-line control right. It does not mean that AI governance owns the deployment decision itself. Section 13.6 develops why keeping this distinction sharp matters. A second-line function needs independence to challenge a first-line decision.
Written this specifically, a RACI assignment resolves what a vaguer “governance reviews deployments” leaves open. It states how deployments get reviewed. It states with what authority a reviewer can block one. It states who is left holding responsibility when a deployment goes wrong.
An incident response RACI follows the same logic as the deployment RACI, with different names filling the roles. It is drawn from Chapter 10’s ten-stage lifecycle. It needs one correction that the deployment-decision RACI does not need.
Legal and privacy review cannot sit ahead of notification as a sequential gate, a step that must finish before the next one can start. For a deployment, “consulted before the decision” works as such a gate. For an incident it does not. Chapter 10 names two regulatory clocks, the deadlines for reporting to a regulator. They are Article 73’s provider outer limits, the longest a provider may take to report, and Article 26’s deployer duties. These clocks are not yet in force for most systems. The obligations tied to the high-risk uses listed in the Act’s Annex III take effect 2 December 2027, checked against the consolidated EU AI Act as of 2026-09-12. Only from that date do both clocks run. They run from the moment of awareness, the moment the organization learns of the incident. They do not start when an internal consultation finishes.
Different incidents also route to different legal actors and jurisdictions. The route depends on the organization’s role and the incident type.
Table 13.3 states how the four roles then divide for an incident.








RACI role
Who
What they do




Responsible
The team operating the system
Runs the containment step, the step that stops the harm from spreading. They are the ones positioned to halt the system. For an agentic system, they can trigger the circuit breaker that Chapter 12 described, the control that stops the agent.


Accountable
The AI governance function
Confirms the provisional severity classification, the first rough rating of how bad the incident is. Signs off on the owned, dated remediation from the post-incident review, the review done after the incident is over. Each fix in that remediation carries a named owner and a due date.


Consulted
Legal teams and, where personal data is involved, privacy teams
Work in parallel with containment and investigation, not ahead of them. Identify the applicable legal role and jurisdiction. Prepare whatever notification the clock requires. That includes an initial report that is incomplete, a first report filed before all the facts are in, where the rules allow it. They do not wait for a complete investigation to finish first.


Informed
The executive sponsor and, for the most severe tier, the board
Informed once containment is underway, both at the same point. Neither waits for the investigation to close.



Table 13.3. The incident-response RACI. Consultation and notification run beside containment, not ahead of it.
The same four-role structure applies to a deployment decision and to an incident response. The timing differs. RACI states who does what. It does not, by itself, state when. An organization applying it needs to recognize where the incident-response version’s timing constraints differ from the deployment version’s.
crumbs: 14  13. Organizing the Governance Function

title: 13. Organizing the Governance Function
text:
13.6 The three lines model
The three lines model comes from risk management in general. Here it is mapped onto AI governance. The model used is the current statement of it from the Institute of Internal Auditors (IIA). The statement was updated 8 July 2026 and checked against that update on 2026-09-12. It describes roles and not department names.
The IIA is explicit that the “lines” name complementary roles and relationships. They operate at the same time. They are not a rank order. They are not an org chart. They are not a sequence of checkpoints that one decision passes through in turn. That framing holds even where an example, like the deployment sequence in section 13.5, shows roles acting at different points in time.
The first line owns and manages risk directly. It is the teams that build, select, and deploy AI systems. They make the day-to-day decisions that earlier chapters describe. They bear primary accountability for those decisions being sound.
The second line provides oversight, standards, and challenge. It does not take over the first line’s underlying decision. An AI governance function occupies this line. It sets standards. It reviews deployments against them. It holds a required-concurrence right where section 13.5 assigned one. It maintains the aggregate visibility that section 13.4 showed a federated program can otherwise lose. It often does this alongside a model risk management function. That function handles the technical validation piece specifically.
A concurrence right that can stop a deployment is a second-line control. It is not evidence that the function has moved to the first line. The two lines stay distinguishable. One owns the underlying business decision. The other can block it on risk grounds. In the Meridian case below, the deploying business unit stays the first-line owner. The governance function’s sign-off is a second-line control. A governance program that treats “has veto power” as a signal of first-line ownership has lost the independence that the second line’s challenge role depends on.
The third line provides independent assurance to the board and senior leadership. Assurance here means confirmation that the first two lines are functioning as designed. It comes from internal audit. Internal audit tests the governance program itself and not any individual AI system. Its mandate is independent of both the teams deploying systems and the function governing them.
Two functions that sit side by side are not automatically “the two lines.” This applies to a model risk management function and an AI governance function. Whether they occupy the same line or different lines depends on each one’s actual role in a given decision. That role needs to be stated explicitly and not assumed from the function’s name.
Agentic systems add pressure to this allocation of lines. The pressure already exists. Agentic systems increase its frequency, speed, and scope. They do not invent it from nothing.
Predictive systems already require ongoing first-line monitoring and outcomes analysis, the study of the results a model’s decisions produce. Current model risk management guidance calls for both. Drift, misuse, and process overrides can all surface after deployment. Drift here means a change in how the model itself performs, a different thing from the classification drift above. A process override happens when someone bypasses a required step. None of these problems waits for a scheduled review.
What changes with an agentic system is the timing of design. Chapter 12’s permission scope, the set of actions the agent may take, and its runtime intervention, the ability to step in while the agent runs, have to be designed before the agent acts. They cannot be reviewed after a single output. A first line that owns day-to-day operation of an agent is, in effect, exercising a risk decision every time the agent takes an action within its granted scope. That happens at a frequency a predictive system’s periodic monitoring cycle does not approach.
The second line’s job shifts correspondingly. It moves from periodic deployment review toward two tasks. One is setting standards for which permission scopes are acceptable. The other is auditing the action logs that Chapter 12 required, the records of each action an agent took. A governance program that has not adjusted its second-line practice for this shift will review agentic deployments with the same pre-deployment checklist. That checklist was built for systems that only ever produced a discrete output to review.
Chapter 11 and Chapter 12 name controls along different axes. The difference matters for tracing a specific control back to a specific owner. Without that tracing, the connection between a technical safeguard and the role accountable for it gets lost.
Table 13.4 sets the three classification vocabularies side by side.








Vocabulary
Basis
Categories




Chapter 11
Classifies a control by its effect
Reducing likelihood, detecting, containing before release, correcting, and transferring residual risk


Chapter 12
Classifies a control by where it sits in the pipeline, the chain of steps a system’s work passes through
Inline enforcement, near-real-time detection, aggregate monitoring, and retrospective audit


A third vocabulary
Names controls
Prevent, detect, contain, intervene, recover, verify, and learn



Table 13.4. Three vocabularies that classify the same controls.
An inline enforcement point, for instance, can carry a preventive effect, stopping a problem, a detective one, finding a problem, or both. It depends on what it is configured to do.
The underlying obligation is the same, whichever axis names the control. Each control still needs a first-line owner who runs it. It needs a second-line function that sets its standard and challenges it. Where the control failed and the failure was material, it needs a third-line assurance check that the standard itself is working.
Chapters 11 and 12 describe controls such as a registry record, a permission scope, and a claim-verification step. Any of these left without a named role is one of the decisions that the RACI and three lines structure has to assign. That structure does not tolerate leaving it unassigned. The gap is the one the structure exists to close.
Which operating model an organization picks determines who ends up in which line for a given decision. It does not only shape how authority is drawn on an org chart. Table 13.2 returns to the operating-model choice that section 13.1 opened. The roles and lines now give that choice concrete stakes.









Operating model
What it does well
Risk to control
Better suited when




Centralized
Consistent standards; a single point of aggregate visibility
Becomes a bottleneck once deployment volume outpaces one team’s review capacity; can lack the local business context each deploying unit has
Deployment volume is modest relative to the central team, and standards consistency matters more than local responsiveness


Federated
Responsive to local context; judgment suited to each business unit’s own conditions
Classification drift across units, capture by the business a reviewer serves, and lost aggregate visibility (section 13.4)
Business units differ substantially in context, and deployment volume exceeds what a central team could review itself


Hybrid
Combines central coordination on one dimension with local judgment on another, tracking where a defect actually originates
Requires a deliberate, explicit split (sections 13.2 and 13.3), not an accidental one, and most individual decisions the split touches remain cross-layer rather than exclusive
An organization can name a specific dimension, layer, risk tier, or system class, along which authority should split, and is willing to design and maintain that split on purpose



Table 13.2. Three operating models compared by what each does well and the risk each puts on the organization to control. This is not a ranked or validated comparison. It is this book’s own synthesis of the tradeoffs that sections 13.1 through 13.6 developed. The table rests on a contingency principle, meaning an idea that the right answer depends on circumstances. Here the principle is that no single structure fits every organization. That principle follows the Federal Reserve/OCC/FDIC’s SR 26-2 supervisory guidance on model risk management (issued 17 April 2026, superseding SR 11-7, checked 2026-09-12) and the GOVERN function, the part that covers governance, of NIST AI RMF 1.0 (checked 2026-09-12). The Federal Reserve, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) are U.S. bank regulators. NIST is the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the AI RMF is its AI Risk Management Framework. Neither source validates this specific three-model taxonomy, this way of sorting the models into three types, or ranks the models against each other. Read the “risk to control” column across all three rows before choosing any one model. Do not read any row as a fixed or guaranteed outcome. Every operating model carries a predictable risk. The choice is which risk an organization is best positioned to control given its own scale and deployment speed. It is not a search for a model with no risk at all.
crumbs: 14  13. Organizing the Governance Function

title: 13. Organizing the Governance Function
text:
13.7 Governance bodies
A governance body is a committee convened to review or approve AI systems. Composition, mandate, and decision rights are the necessary starting point. A body needs more than these three stated, however, if it is to function as a governance mechanism and not as a discussion group.
Composition names who sits on the body and why. It ensures that the perspectives a decision requires are present. These are technical, legal, and business perspectives, and, where relevant, representation for the people a system affects. These perspectives should not be assembled from whoever was available. Mandate states what the body is empowered to decide. This is distinct from what it is only invited to discuss. Decision rights specify whether the body’s decision is binding, advisory, or escalates to someone else.
Consider a committee that spends an hour debating a deployment. Then it watches the business unit proceed regardless. That committee has decision rights of zero, however substantive its discussion was.
Naming these three does not yet make a body able to operate on an ordinary working day. A working governance body needs rules for what comes in, rules for how it decides, and rules for what happens after a decision. Table 13.5 lists that operating detail, grouped by stage.








Stage
Element
Requirement




What comes in
Intake criteria
Say what reaches the body and what is handled below it


What comes in
Quorum requirement
Sets how many members must be present to decide


What comes in
Conflict-of-interest check
Covers members with a stake in the specific decision


What comes in
Evidence pack
Assembled by a submitter, the person bringing the proposal, before the meeting


How it decides
Decision standard
Must be stated


How it decides
Minutes
The written record of the meeting. Must record dissent as well as the outcome


How it decides
Conditional-approval option
Approves a system on stated conditions, with a stated exception duration, meaning how long the exception lasts


How it decides
Escalation path
A route that sends the matter to a higher authority, for when the body cannot reach a decision


After a decision
Appeal route
For a submitter who disagrees with the outcome


After a decision
Action tracking
For anything the approval was conditioned on


After a decision
Re-review trigger
For a material change to the approved system


After a decision
Emergency route
For a decision that cannot wait for the body’s normal cadence, its regular meeting rhythm


After a decision
Periodic review
Of whether the body’s own decisions are holding up in practice



Table 13.5. The operating detail a working governance body needs beyond composition, mandate, and decision rights.
A committee may have a charter that names its composition, mandate, and decision rights. Without this operating detail, it still functions ceremonially, meaning for show. It approves whatever evidence happens to be presented to it. It does not govern the decision.
One documented illustration shows a governance body being stood up at close to this level of structural specificity. It does not reach every element listed above. It comes from outside banking. The White House Office of Management and Budget issued Memorandum M-25-21 on 3 April 2025. It rescinded, meaning withdrew, the prior administration’s earlier memorandum, M-24-10. The memorandum requires the head of each U.S. federal agency to retain or designate a Chief AI Officer within sixty days. A Chief AI Officer is the official in charge of an agency’s AI work.
The memorandum separately requires each agency covered by the Chief Financial Officers Act to convene an AI Governance Board within ninety days. The requirement does not cover every federal agency. An existing governance body may serve that function. The memorandum specifies the board’s chair, vice-chair, and required functional representation. Alongside these, a cross-agency Chief AI Officer Council coordinates AI governance across the federal government as a whole. OMB itself convenes the council (checked 2026-09-12).
The memorandum states a requirement. It does not prove that every covered agency met it. The U.S. International Trade Commission’s own AI page reports that it re-designated its Chief AI Officer and retained its AI Governance Board. The page names the board’s thirteen member positions. This is direct evidence that the requirement was implemented and not only imposed (checked 2026-09-13). Neither source specifies the quorum, evidence-pack, or dissent-recording detail that a body needs in order to function. That is the gap between naming a governance body and operating one.
crumbs: 14  13. Organizing the Governance Function

title: 13. Organizing the Governance Function
text:
13.8 Acceptable use and sanctioned tooling
Unapproved AI use means employees using AI tools that the organization has not reviewed or approved. It often happens because a sanctioned alternative, a tool the organization has approved, is slower or less capable. Sometimes no sanctioned alternative exists at all. An acceptable use policy, the document telling employees which AI uses are allowed, exists to address this practical problem.
Current government guidance on this pattern was published 7 September 2026. It recommends four steps: understanding what need drove the unapproved use, building a positive security culture, meaning a workplace culture that supports secure behavior, offering an approved alternative, and taking direct steps that reduce the risk. It does not treat a written prohibition as sufficient on its own. A prohibition may be necessary for particular data, tools, or uses. That does not mean every prohibition backfires. Consistent with that guidance, policy text alone rarely creates the visibility or the safe alternative an organization needs. A prohibition with nothing else beside it risks losing visibility into use the organization cannot detect. It does not eliminate the use itself.
A fuller acceptable use policy combines these parts:

Clear use rules, with an approved tool that meets legitimate needs where one can be provided.
Access and data-loss controls in proportion to the risk. Data-loss controls are tools that stop sensitive data from leaving the organization.
Procurement and security review of new tools before they spread informally.
Awareness training and a reporting channel for tools employees want but do not have.
Monitoring consistent with law and internal policy.
A defined response path for discovered unapproved use that does not default to discipline alone.
Periodic measurement of how much unapproved use remains, so the policy’s effect can be assessed and not assumed.

Combining all of this into a policy still leaves an individual employee needing one place that states these things concretely. That place should state:

Which tools and accounts are approved.
Which tasks and data are permitted, restricted, or prohibited by classification. Classification here means how sensitive the data is.
Where human review of AI output is required before anyone relies on it.
How output accuracy gets verified.
How intellectual property, confidentiality, and privacy obligations apply to AI-assisted work.
What security requirements attach to an approved tool.
What records the employee must keep.
What disclosure the organization owes a counterparty or regulator about AI-assisted output. A counterparty is the other side of a deal or contract.
How to report an incident or a tool the policy does not cover.
How an exception gets requested and granted.
What happens when the policy is violated.
How often the policy gets checked against the tools employees are asking for.
crumbs: 14  13. Organizing the Governance Function

title: 13. Organizing the Governance Function
section: 13.9 Conflict with incumbent functions and executive engagement
text:
13.9 Conflict with incumbent functions and executive engagement
Where a model risk management function already exists with real authority, a new AI governance function arrives as a structural competitor and not a blank slate. This was the situation at Meridian. Its model risk management function had real authority for a decade before FAIRLEND’s AI governance function was chartered. Pretending otherwise produces unresolved friction.
The boundary a new function should draw is not the one an assumption of empty incumbent territory would suggest. Current U.S. federal banking supervisory guidance on model risk management was issued April 2026 and supersedes the prior 2011 guidance. It directly addresses model purpose, intended and actual use, limitations, misuse, validation, and monitoring. It also addresses aggregate exposure, meaning risk viewed across models together rather than one at a time, and third-party models, those built by outside vendors. So an incumbent function governed by that guidance already has a real, if partial, mandate over questions of use appropriateness, meaning whether a model is appropriate for a given use. Its mandate is not limited to technical accuracy. A new AI governance function that assumes otherwise is working from an outdated picture of what model risk management is built to check.
That guidance leaves four gaps. It does not cover these:

Fundamental-rights obligations, covering the basic legal rights of people, and disclosure obligations.
Contestability, which is the ability of affected people to challenge a decision.
Affected-party requirements broader than model performance.
Governance of the system classes outside the guidance’s stated coverage.

It leaves those gaps for two reasons. It addresses model risk specifically and not every AI-specific legal or social-impact question. It also explicitly excludes generative and agentic models from its own scope.
The correct starting point is therefore a joint-responsibility analysis. The analysis has three steps. It maps what the incumbent mandate already covers. It identifies the AI-specific duties the mandate does not cover. It assigns explicitly the decisions that fall in both territories. This is different from a new function asserting or conceding a three-question territory, a patch of ground marked out in advance by a fixed list of questions. Neither the incumbent’s actual mandate nor its actual gaps line up with that territory.
This specific conflict is banking-specific, and so is the supervisory guidance that resolves its boundaries. A nonfinancial organization can face the same structural pattern. A new AI governance function may meet an established data governance board or cybersecurity risk committee. That body has its own reporting line and its own settled scope. The organization runs the identical joint-responsibility analysis described above. No comparable federal supervisory framework, the set of rules a government supervisor applies to the bodies it oversees, already dictates what the incumbent function’s mandate covers. For that reason, the analysis itself transfers. The specific banking citations do not.
Executive and board engagement depends on regular reporting that answers four matters. The first is the aggregate picture that federated governance can lose. The second is the specific questions to ask of any significant deployment. The third is whether the readiness dimensions that Chapter 8 requires were evaluated. The fourth is whether an incident this year exposed a systemic gap and not an isolated failure.
What a board’s oversight duty requires depends on the entity’s jurisdiction and legal form. But reporting built to answer these questions is what lets a board exercise whatever oversight duty applies to it. Without it, the board receives reassurance dressed as reporting, regardless of which duty governs.
Cadence, how often reporting happens, matters as much as content. No single cadence is the correct one for every board. A board may rely on annual reporting alone, with no operational monitoring or event-driven escalation underneath it. Such a board can learn about a systemic gap long after it opened and not while it is still forming. That lag is too slow for a governance function whose own inventory Chapter 3 requires to be current continuously. Annual reporting paired with the continuous monitoring and escalation triggers described below does not carry the same lag. So the problem is the missing pairing. The annual cadence is not the problem by itself.
Quarterly reporting is one cadence some boards already use for other risk reporting. A similar rhythm for AI governance can let a function surface three things. One is a drifting classification pattern. Another is a rising rate of near-miss incidents, meaning incidents that almost caused harm. The third is a business unit consistently pushing deployment decisions past the readiness bar. The function can surface these while the pattern is still a trend and not an already-realized failure.
Whatever the routine cadence, it needs to be paired with event-driven escalation. Event-driven escalation sends defined triggers to the board or the relevant committee immediately. The triggers are a serious incident, a threshold breach, meaning a measure crossing a set limit, and a material change. They do not wait for the next scheduled report. A board relying on a fixed cadence alone learns about an urgent problem only as fast as its calendar allows.
The report itself should name what changed since the last one. It should not restate the program’s structure every cycle. A board that reads the same description of the operating model repeatedly has learned nothing new about whether the model is working.
crumbs: 14  13. Organizing the Governance Function

title: 13. Organizing the Governance Function
section: Case in focus: a mandate that had to be negotiated, not assumed
text:
Case in focus: a mandate that had to be negotiated, not assumed
FAIRLEND · Hypothetical, following the running cases
This continuing fictional scenario illustrates the conflict pattern that section 13.9 describes. It does not report an event that occurred at any specific organization.
Meridian’s board chartered its AI governance function with a mandate spanning fairness, transparency, and risk review across every AI system in the organization. On its face, the charter read as complete. The model risk management function governed FAIRLEND’s credit models under a supervisory framework it had operated under for years. It read the same charter as an intrusion into territory that was already its own. The function had held that territory without dispute since before “AI governance” was a phrase anyone at Meridian used.
The first several deployment reviews under the new charter produced that pattern. Both functions showed up to review the same model. Each was unclear on whose decision controlled the outcome. Each carried a different picture of what the other’s mandate already covered.
The resolution followed a joint-responsibility analysis. Neither function conceded, and neither asserted exclusive territory. Meridian first mapped what its model risk management function’s existing mandate already covered for FAIRLEND. That mandate was governed by current supervisory guidance. It covered technical validation. It also covered model purpose, intended use, and monitoring for misuse. This was a broader mandate than the AI governance function had initially assumed.
AI governance then identified the specific gaps that the mandate did not close. There were two. The first was whether the population that a proposed lending-product extension would newly reach matched the population that FAIRLEND’s fairness testing had covered. The second was whether Meridian could satisfy the adverse-action explanation duties that Chapter 2 introduces and produce the decision-level evidence that Chapter 15 develops. Adverse-action explanation duties are the duties to explain to a customer why a lender turned them down. Chapter 8 makes both matters conditions of deployment readiness. It is not the source of the underlying legal duty. Both questions required AI-specific and legal expertise. The model-risk mandate did not claim to provide that expertise.
Meridian did not assign these questions as separate, walled-off territories. It required both functions’ sign-off on any deployment touching either question. Model risk management’s validation evidence fed directly into the readiness record. AI governance’s concurrence decision required that record.
Part of the resolution was working out which line each function occupied in the three lines model. Meridian did not assume the two functions were automatically “the two lines” because two functions existed. Both turned out to sit in the second line for FAIRLEND’s deployment decisions. One provided technical challenge. The other provided AI-specific and fairness challenge. In both cases, the deploying business unit remained the first-line owner of the underlying decision.
A stalled product launch forced this mapping into being. It carried a cost that the board tracked directly. The cost had three parts. The first was the delayed launch. The second was that a business unit sponsor, rather than repeat the experience, learned to route around both functions on the next deployment. The third was that the boundary existed on paper only because a deployment had already stalled to force it into being.
Meridian drew a lesson from this, and it is the right lesson to draw. The joint-responsibility mapping should happen before the first contested deployment and not during it. A boundary drawn under the pressure of a stalled launch is drawn worse than one drawn in advance. It carries more resentment on both sides. It gets less attention to whether the mapping tracks what each function’s mandate does and does not already cover.
crumbs: 14  13. Organizing the Governance Function

title: 13. Organizing the Governance Function
text:
Summary
Centralized, federated, and hybrid operating models are design patterns and not a performance ranking. The right choice depends on organizational scale, existing risk maturity, deployment speed, risk concentration, and independence requirements. The choice must be tested against an organization’s own conditions. It must not be assumed from any one pattern’s general reputation.
The operating model choice recurs at every governance decision point. It is not made once on an org chart. An organization that has not noticed this is often centralized on one axis and federated on another by accident and not by design.
One candidate split divides authority by layer. It is federated at the system layer, where local context matters most. It is centralized at the model layer, where a defect needs to be caught once and not rediscovered independently. Most individual decisions this split touches are cross-layer processes. They need a decision-rights matrix and not a two-column allocation.
Federated governance fails through classification drift, capture by the business a reviewer serves, and lost aggregate visibility. The last is a serious failure. At least some regulatory reporting obligations attach to the organization, or to a specific provider or deployer role, and not to a single business unit.
RACI applied to governance decisions makes responsibility, accountability, consultation, and information explicit and not assumed. An incident-response RACI needs one adjustment. Its consultation step runs in parallel with containment and investigation. It is not a sequential gate ahead of a regulatory notification clock.
The three lines model, fully mapped onto AI-specific functions per the IIA’s current statement, separates three roles. The first line owns. The second line provides oversight and challenge. This includes a required-concurrence right that does not by itself make the second line an owner. The third line provides independent assurance.
A governance body needs composition, mandate, and decision rights stated explicitly. It also needs operating detail that makes it function and not only exist. That detail includes intake criteria, quorum, evidence pack, dissent record, escalation, and re-review triggers. An acceptable use policy addresses unapproved AI use only by combining a sanctioned alternative, where one can be offered, with access controls, monitoring, training, and measurement. A written prohibition alone does not do this.
Conflict with an incumbent function like model risk management is structural. It cannot be avoided. Resolving it requires a joint-responsibility analysis and not an assumed empty territory. An incumbent function governed by current supervisory guidance may already have real authority over use appropriateness and not only technical validation. The first step is to map what its mandate already covers. The second is to identify the AI-specific duties it does not cover. The third is to assign the overlap explicitly. Neither function concedes or asserts exclusive ground.
crumbs: 14  13. Organizing the Governance Function

title: 13. Organizing the Governance Function
text:
Review questions
COMPREHENSION

Explain why the operating model choice is not a single decision made once on an org chart, and give two specific governance decisions where an organization might reasonably choose different models.
State the federated-at-system, centralized-at-model pattern, explain why it follows from the two-record inventory Chapter 3 established, and name one organizational condition under which a different split would fit better.

APPLIED

Design a RACI assignment for a deployment decision under Chapter 8’s readiness dimensions, naming who is responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed.
An organization discovers extensive unapproved AI use despite a clear written prohibition. Diagnose what a prohibition alone cannot provide, and specify at least three additional controls a fuller acceptable use policy would add.

SPOT THE RISK

A federated governance program reports that every business unit’s own AI review process is functioning well. Identify the failure mode this chapter warns is invisible from that vantage point, and what evidence would actually reveal it.

COMPARE AND DECIDE

State the case for centralizing AI governance authority versus federating it, for an organization with twelve business units each deploying AI at a different pace and level of maturity.

RUNNING CASE

FAIRLEND Using the case in focus, explain why Meridian’s resolution started by mapping what the model risk management function’s existing mandate already covered, rather than assuming a boundary and negotiating from it, and name the specific gap AI governance identified once that mapping was done.


Structure alone does not decide what a governance function does with its authority once organized. The next chapter turns to the substance of that work. It begins with the assessment process that a governance function runs on every system it reviews. That process includes the stakeholders that standard assessment methods cannot reach.
crumbs: 14  13. Organizing the Governance Function

title: 14. Risk Assessment and Management
text:
What you will be able to do
Consider a constructed scenario that continues the running TALENTSCREEN case. Calloway Industries ran an impact assessment on TalentScreen when it first licensed the tool for hiring on its manufacturing floor. An impact assessment is a written review of how a system could harm the people it affects. On its own terms, Calloway’s assessment was competent. It named a risk called disparate impact. Under Title VII, the US law against workplace discrimination, a hiring practice such as screening applicants with this tool can cause disparate impact. That means the practice hurts one group more than another without a job-related reason. The assessment assigned a control, which is a safeguard meant to reduce a risk. It also documented who accepted the risk that remained. But no one on the assessment team thought to consult a single applicant the tool would screen.
Eighteen months later, Calloway extended the same tool to its logistics job family, a set of related jobs treated as one group. It did not redo any of that work. The logistics applicants were a different population. The assessment that would have caught this difference was never run. The first assessment had not failed. The second one never happened.
An impact assessment has to be more than a form filled out once and filed.

title: 14. Risk Assessment and Management
text:
Build an impact assessment from its five components, ending in a documented decision with named accountability instead of an open-ended list of risks. Named accountability means one named person answers for the risk
Use real methods to hear from stakeholders (the people a system affects) when standard interviews and workshops cannot reach them, and say honestly what each method stands in for and what it cannot recover
Score and prioritize risk without false precision, which means without making a number look more exact than it is. Force the explicit tradeoff, the choice of what to fix first, that a claim of “everything is critical” is designed to avoid
Choose controls by naming what each one does (prevention, deterrence, detection, containment, correction, recovery, or compensation) instead of using a bare reduce-or-detect label. That label says only whether a control reduces or detects a risk. Name the changes that should trigger reassessment before an organization discovers them the way Calloway did

title: 14. Risk Assessment and Management
section: 14.1 The five components of an assessment
text:
14.1 The five components of an assessment
An impact assessment needs at least five components. An assessment that lacks one of them is missing something a reviewer will eventually ask for. Treat the five as a management spine, which is a basic structure for managing the work. The spine is not a complete, legally sufficient assessment on its own, meaning one that meets everything the law requires.
ISO/IEC 42005:2025 is the current international standard for AI system impact assessment, a published set of agreed rules from the standards bodies ISO and IEC. The standard was published in May 2025. It covers effects on individuals, groups, and society across the system lifecycle, which is the whole life of the system (checked 2026-09-13). The five components below are this chapter’s own minimum synthesis. They do not summarize that standard. An organization that wants to conform to ISO/IEC 42005 needs to read the standard itself, not this chapter.
Some laws require a specific type of assessment. Two examples are a data protection impact assessment under GDPR Article 35 and a fundamental-rights impact assessment under Article 27 of the EU AI Act. GDPR is the European Union’s data protection law, and the EU AI Act is the European Union’s law on artificial intelligence systems. A data protection impact assessment reviews the risks that data use creates for people. A fundamental-rights impact assessment reviews the risks to people’s basic rights.
Each legally required type adds its own required elements, and the spine does not supply them. They include necessity and proportionality, a test that asks whether the use is needed and in balance with its effects on people. They include named affected groups. They include human-oversight design, which is a plan for how people watch over the system and can step in. And they include a complaint mechanism, a way for affected people to raise a problem. In some cases they include a duty to consult a supervisory authority, the public body that enforces the law, before going ahead. So the first task of any assessment is to find out which legally required type, if any, applies. The team then adds that type’s requirements to the spine below. The spine alone is not enough.
System description comes first. It states what the system does, who it affects, and in what context. It must be specific enough that a reader unfamiliar with the deployment could still evaluate the risk analysis that follows.
Risk identification names the risks. It uses categories set out earlier, not a third scheme made up here. The first set is the harms taxonomy from Chapter 1, which is the book’s list of kinds of harm. The second set is the classification factors from Chapter 3. Those factors were used to place the system in a risk tier, a level of risk a system is sorted into, in the first place.
Mitigation, meaning the steps taken to reduce a risk, states the control assigned to each significant risk. Residual risk names what remains once the control is applied. A control rarely removes a risk completely. A documented decision, with named accountability, closes the assessment. Someone specific accepted the residual risk that remained, on a specific basis. That acceptance is recorded, not assumed.
Every class of AI system carries the full set of harms in the Chapter 1 taxonomy. These include privacy, security, safety, accessibility, intellectual property, and the rest. No class is exempt from any of them. Systems fall into three classes.
The three classes differ in which risk category needs the sharpest extra attention in the risk identification component. That attention comes on top of the shared core. Table 14.2 names each class and the emphasis its assessment adds.
Table 14.2. Assessment emphasis by system class









System class
What the system does
Assessment emphasis
What the assessment asks or tracks




Predictive
Estimates or scores something, such as how likely an outcome is
Error and disparity, an uneven result across groups of people
Tracks false positive and false negative rates and checks whether either rate falls unevenly across groups of people


Generative
Produces new content, such as text or images
Content and misuse
Asks what the system might produce, make up, or be directed to produce outside its intended use


Agentic
Takes actions, such as using tools or software on its own
Action and scope
Asks what the system can do, not only what it might say, and how far its granted permissions reach



A false positive is a case the system wrongly flags. A false negative is a case the system wrongly misses.
Suppose a team builds an assessment template for one class’s emphasis and applies it unchanged to another class. The template will underweight the other class’s sharpest risk in the risk identification component. This holds however well the other four components are carried out. The difference between the system classes is one of degree and of design timing. Design timing here means when and how often risk decisions come up as the system runs. It is not a difference of kind. Chapter 12 explains that a business or use owner operating an agent makes risk decisions at a pace that a predictive system’s periodic monitoring cycle does not match. For this reason, a template built for periodic review needs an agentic-specific overlay, which is an added layer of checks.
crumbs: 15  14. Risk Assessment and Management

title: 14. Risk Assessment and Management
section: 14.2 Engaging stakeholders whom standard methods cannot reach
text:
14.2 Engaging stakeholders whom standard methods cannot reach
Standard consultation methods assume a participant who can be identified and reached. The participant might be reached through an interview, a workshop, or a survey sent to a known group. For some of the people an impact assessment most needs to hear from, that assumption fails. It does not fail automatically, though.
Before looking for a substitute, the team does a documented reachability and safety analysis. The analysis asks whether the organization can build a safe, lawful channel to the affected group before it concludes that it cannot. It checks more than whether people can be found. It also checks whether they could take part without an unreasonable burden, meaning too much effort or cost. It checks for a language or accessibility barrier. And it checks for a realistic fear of retaliation, which is punishment for speaking up.
Some groups look hard to reach but can be reached through others. A union, an advisory panel, a civil-society organization, or an ombuds service may represent a group. A union speaks for workers. An advisory panel gives advice. A civil-society organization is a nonprofit or community group. An ombuds service handles complaints on behalf of a group. A group that one of these represents is not unreachable just because its members are spread out. A public notice, a purposive sample of people chosen because they fit the situation, or a worker representative can sometimes reach applicants that a one-to-one interview never could. A public notice is an announcement posted where affected people can see it.
TalentScreen’s applicants are a group for which this analysis can come back negative. They never interact with Calloway in a way that would let anyone interview them. Most do not know that a resume-screening tool evaluated them rather than a hiring manager. Calloway had no worker-representative or advisory channel through which applicants could be heard, and it used none. Where the analysis does come back negative, the honest response is a different method entirely. A more diligent version of the same method will not work. The recorded analysis is what separates a truly unreachable group from one the assessment team did not try hard enough to reach.
Direct and representative engagement comes first wherever the reachability analysis allows it. Worker representatives, unions, advisory panels, civil-society organizations, ombuds services, accessible public notices, and purposive recruitment can all bring an affected voice into the process. Sometimes they bring a trusted representative of that voice instead.
Where none of that is feasible, several further approaches exist. Each one stands in for engagement in a specific and limited way. None of them is engagement itself.
Table 14.3 sets out the five approaches by what each one draws on and what each cannot recover. The first two stand in for engagement. The last three are evidence, not engagement, and should be named that way.
Table 14.3. Approaches where direct engagement is not feasible









Approach
Kind
What it draws on
Limit




Proxy consultation
Engagement substitute
An advocacy organization, a group whose job is to speak up for others’ interests, speaks for the interests of the affected group
Works without access to the specific people a given deployment touches


Structured adversarial review
Engagement substitute
One person is given the explicit job of arguing the affected party’s interest inside the assessment, so that interest has a voice even when the affected person is not there to speak
What it has is an assigned advocate’s best argument, not the affected party’s own voice


Published research on comparable systems and groups
Evidence source
What other organizations and researchers have already documented about how similar tools affect similar people
Substitutes general findings for this deployment’s specific population


Complaint and appeal records
Evidence source
What people said when a comparable system’s outcome affected them enough to prompt a formal objection
Captures real grievance, but only from the people who took the harder step of filing one


Outcome analysis after deployment
Evidence source
Who was rejected, hired, or advanced once the system is running
Evidence of a different kind again, arriving only after the decision it might have informed has been made



A worker advocacy group that knows hiring discrimination patterns can raise concerns that a screened applicant would raise. It can do this without ever locating that applicant. A properly run TalentScreen assessment would have used structured adversarial review. Calloway’s did not.
No method in this group solves the underlying problem, and none should be presented as if it did. That holds for the engagement substitutes and the evidence sources alike.
An assessment that uses every one of these methods still has not consulted the people it assesses risk to. To suggest otherwise would be false. What the methods do is put a documented, defensible effort in place of the silence that an unreachable group would otherwise leave in the assessment. The honest record of an assessment names three things. It names the reachability analysis performed. It names which methods were used as a result. And it names what each one could not recover. It does not present a substitute as equivalent to the engagement it stands in for.







Figure 15.1: Figure 14.1. Assessment process flow



Read Figure 14.1 as the five components in sequence. Consultation from section 14.2 feeds risk identification directly. It does not sit outside the process. The figure does not show everything, though. In practice, the same reachability analysis and engagement methods can also revise other parts. They can revise the system description, the risks identified, the mitigation chosen, and the conclusion about residual risk. They do more than give one input to risk identification. The figure also does not show the loop from a documented decision back to section 14.6’s reassessment triggers. A decision made here is not a hard stop. It can reopen the same assessment later.
Without engagement, the assessment lacks an input that several later steps depend on.

title: 14. Risk Assessment and Management
text:
14.3 Risk scoring and prioritization
A risk score starts from two factors, likelihood and severity. Likelihood is how probable a harm is. Severity is how bad it would be. These two factors are only the starting pair. Many other factors can matter as much. These include exposure, scale, duration, and reversibility. They include how quickly a problem would be detected and the underlying uncertainty. They include which rights are affected and how harm is spread across a population. They also include the strength of controls already in place. Reversibility is whether a harm can be undone. In plain terms, these factors ask how many people a harm could touch, how big it could get, and how long it would last. They also ask which rights it would reach, and how sure the team is about its own answers.
A legal or rights-based red line is a limit that may not be crossed. A favorable score on some other factor cannot offset it.
The discipline that scoring requires is to resist the appearance of precision that numbers suggest. Take a risk labeled “likelihood 3, severity 4” on a five-point scale. That label is not a measurement. It is an estimate that people reached by thinking the risk through, and the number is only a label for that estimate. Multiplying the two numbers into a combined score is not a calculation that an ordinal scale supports. An ordinal scale puts items in order, and the gaps between its steps need not be equal. On such a scale, the step from one label to the next may be a bigger jump in real risk at the top than at the bottom. Multiplying the two labels treats those unequal steps as if they were equal. The calculation is supported only if that specific scale and operation have been validated for the purpose. So the resulting number works as a label for putting risks in order against each other. It is not a result of real arithmetic that can be trusted on its own.
The scale’s value is comparative, not absolute. It lets an assessment team rank one risk against another using a shared vocabulary. An assessment that reports a combined score has to report more. It must also give the reasoning behind each factor and the other considerations named above. Otherwise it has reported a number without the thinking that gives it meaning.
Prioritization is where scoring becomes useful. An organization has limited time and budget. A list of risks with no ranking gives it no way to decide what to address first. Forcing an explicit ranking surfaces a tradeoff that a flat list lets an organization avoid. If the highest-scored risk is addressed first, a lower-scored one waits. Naming that choice, with the reasons for it, is more honest than treating every identified risk as equally urgent. Treating every risk as equally urgent means that none receives the priority its own score says it deserves.
The hardest moment in scoring comes when a stakeholder group insists that every risk on the list is critical. This response is common. It deserves a direct answer, not a delay. The right answer is not always the same, though.
Some risks resist a single total ranking, for three reasons. First, a risk that a law or policy makes categorically unacceptable does not wait in line behind a risk that is only high-scored. Categorically unacceptable means never allowed, whatever its score. Second, two risks that touch different kinds of harm, such as a safety risk and a rights risk, can be incomparable instead of falsely tied. Incomparable means there is no fair way to rank one above the other. Third, risks that are jointly urgent or tightly dependent on each other may need to be addressed together instead of in a forced sequence. Tightly dependent means that fixing one depends on fixing the other. Ranking every risk into one ordered list in these cases would create the same false precision as a bare numeric score.
Once those cases are set aside, a claim that everything left is equally critical is a refusal to prioritize. It is not a risk assessment. Comparing what is left is the work that scoring exists to do. For that remaining set, the team does not overrule the stakeholder. It requires the comparison directly. It asks a forced-choice question. If only one of risk A and risk B could be addressed first, which one would it be, and why?
Suppose a stakeholder cannot answer that question for two risks that are not legally prohibited, not incomparable across harm types, and not truly tied. Then the stakeholder has not assessed them as equally severe. The stakeholder has declined to do the comparative work that scoring requires. The assessment process should surface that refusal. It should not accept an unranked list as though ranking had occurred.
Ranking also answers a narrower question than it can sound like. It orders remediation work, which is the work of fixing risks. It does not decide whether deployment is acceptable. A risk can cross a non-deployment threshold, a line past which the system must not be put into use. That happens when the risk is legally prohibited or exceeds the organization’s own stated risk tolerance, how much risk it has said it will accept. Such a risk does not wait its turn in the line of fixes. It blocks deployment, wherever it lands in the ranked order. A system can carry several such risks at once. Each one must be resolved before deployment, and none of them gets a place in a single priority line.







Figure 15.2: Figure 14.2. Risk scoring with prioritization



Read Figure 14.2 by comparing its two outputs, not by grid position alone. The grid on the left plots four named risks by likelihood and severity. The ranked list on the right orders those risks for remediation. Position on the grid and place in the ranked order are still not the same information. Two of the plotted risks, labeled A and B here, share a severity row but sit in different likelihood columns. Even so, the rank between them still needed an explicit, argued tiebreak, a stated reason for putting one ahead of the other. The figure does not show which risks a legal or policy prohibition excludes outright. That test is applied separately, before any risk reaches the grid or the list.

title: 14. Risk Assessment and Management
text:
14.4 Mitigation planning and control selection
Mitigation is where an assessment becomes action. Without it, the assessment remains a description of risk that nothing addresses. Mitigation is the step most often skipped in practice. Identifying and scoring risk feels like the substantive work. Assigning and verifying a control feels like an afterthought.
The first mitigation decision is which treatment to pursue, before any control is chosen. A team has several treatments to choose from. It can avoid the use entirely. It can redesign the system or narrow its scope. It can reduce the risk with a control. It can share or transfer part of the exposure, which means passing part of the risk to another party. It can accept the risk, that is, decide to carry it knowingly, within delegated authority, which is authority formally handed to the person deciding. For a system already deployed, it can retire the system. Adding a control to an otherwise unchanged design is one option among these. It is not the default. The mitigation component should record which option was chosen and why before it describes the control.
For each significant risk addressed by a control, the mitigation component then states what the control does. It states whether the control is technical and built into the system, procedural and followed by people, or contractual and written into an agreement. The component also states who owns operating the control. And it states how the control’s effectiveness will be verified. Effectiveness should not be assumed just because the control was assigned.
Organizations routinely collapse an important distinction. They use one word for everything a control does. A control should be named for what it does, and Table 14.4 names the choices.
Table 14.4. Control mechanisms







Mechanism
What the control does




Prevent
Prevents the event from happening at all


Deter
Deters the event by raising its cost


Detect
Detects the event after it has occurred


Contain
Contains the event before it spreads further


Correct or recover
Corrects or recovers from the event once it is detected


Compensate
Compensates for harm that the control could not prevent



One control can do more than one of these, depending on how it is implemented.
Chapters 11 and 12 name the same set of effects (reduce likelihood, detect, contain, intervene, correct, recover, verify) for generative and agentic risk specifically. The same vocabulary of named effects applies here, in place of a bare reduce-or-detect label invented for this one topic.
Consider a monitoring dashboard that flags disparate outcomes. It detects a disparity that has already occurred, which is valuable. But detection alone does not make the disparity any less likely to happen. That changes only if the dashboard is connected to a containment or correction step that acts on what it finds. A claim that a control reduces a risk, and does more than detect or contain it, needs evidence before it is recorded that way.
Retraining a model on a more representative population, one that better matches the people the system affects, may reduce a disparity risk. The risk goes down only if evaluation, meaning testing, against the affected population shows the improvement. Labels, objectives, sampling, features, thresholds, and the deployment context can all preserve or worsen a disparity despite a more representative training set.
An organization may assign a detecting or partially effective control and record it as though the underlying risk had been fully reduced. If it has no evaluation evidence, it has documented a false sense of the system’s real exposure.
Every proposed control needs a feasibility test before it is recorded as the assessment’s answer. Feasibility includes the cost constraint that Chapter 17 develops in full. A control that nobody can afford to operate at the volume and pace the deployment requires will lapse in practice. It lapses quietly, while the documentation continues to describe it as active. An assessment that names an infeasible control has produced paperwork, not mitigation.
The mitigation component should therefore force a second question. The first question is whether a control addresses the risk in principle. The second is whether the organization will run it at the scale the deployment demands. A control that fails the second test needs to be replaced before the assessment is considered complete. It should not be flagged as a future improvement while the risk it was meant to address stays unaddressed.
A replacement may not be available. If no feasible control brings the risk within tolerance, the honest outcome is one of four. The team can redesign the system, narrow its scope, delay deployment, or reject the proposed use. The assessment must not record an infeasible control as though feasibility were someone else’s problem to solve later.
crumbs: 15  14. Risk Assessment and Management

title: 14. Risk Assessment and Management
text:
14.5 Residual risk acceptance
Residual risk is what remains once a control is applied. Nearly every control leaves some, because complete elimination of a risk is rare. An assessment that claims complete elimination should be read with skepticism.
The residual risk acceptance component asks three questions, and the assessment must answer all three explicitly. Who accepts the risk that remains? On what basis? How is that acceptance documented?
The “who” is not free-floating. Chapter 13 sets out a three-lines structure, a way of splitting risk duties across three groups. In it, the first line is the business or use owner, and the second line is an oversight function. The business or use owner accountable for the underlying decision holds first-line acceptance authority for risk within its delegated tolerance, the amount it is authorized to accept. If the second line must agree, that agreement is a control on the acceptance. The second line does not become the acceptor.
Residual risk above a stated tolerance escalates to a higher authority. That authority may be an executive, a governance body, or the board, whichever one the organization’s own delegation, its formal handing out of authority, assigns. The person running the assessment does not accept it just because they happen to be running the assessment. Some residual risk cannot be lawfully accepted at all, no matter who signs, because the law does not allow anyone to accept it. An assessment that treats acceptance as always available skips a question that comes first. That question is whether the remaining exposure is lawful to carry, meaning whether the law allows the organization to keep running with it.
A properly authorized acceptance is a record, not only a signature. It records the stated basis and any conditions attached. It records the monitoring that checks those conditions hold. It records an expiry or review date, by which the acceptance must be revisited instead of assumed to run forever. An assessment may identify residual risk but record no named, properly authorized acceptance that meets this standard. Then that risk is unaccepted. In practice, this is an acceptance that nobody made and nobody can be held to.
A control sometimes verifies something narrower than the requirement it was meant to serve. In other words, there is a gap between what a test checks and what the requirement demanded. That gap does not disappear once testing ends. It belongs in the residual risk component and should be named there as residual risk. It should not be left as an unstated gap between what the requirement says and what the control covers. Suppose Chapter 7’s testing already showed that the control checks less than the requirement asks. An assessment that carries the control forward as though it fully satisfied the requirement has claimed a completeness that the underlying work does not support.
Unaccepted residual risk is a risk with no recorded decision. It is not yet a settled legal liability, which is a legal responsibility for harm that has already been established. The distinction still matters, even though the practical stakes are similar either way. A risk with no accountable acceptor is not a risk the organization has decided to bear. The organization has not gotten around to deciding about it.
An incident that later makes the risk real will first raise the question of who accepted it. The absence of an answer tends to look like the liability the assessment never formally established. An assessment with no answer to that question has failed at the one component every other component exists to support.
crumbs: 15  14. Risk Assessment and Management

title: 14. Risk Assessment and Management
text:
14.6 Reassessment triggers
An assessment is not a one-time document. Treating it as one is the failure that let Calloway extend TalentScreen to a second job family without redoing any work. Calloway’s first assessment had been done correctly for a different population.
Reassessment triggers name in advance which changes require the assessment to be redone. They stop an organization from assuming that a system approved once stays adequately assessed forever. The list is organized by what changed. It is not treated as seven interchangeable items.
Model and data triggers cover a material change to the model or version deployed. They cover a change to training or fine-tuning data or its labels. For a generative system, they also cover a changed prompt, retrieval corpus, or grounding source. Fine-tuning is extra training that adapts a model to a task. A prompt is the instruction given to a model. A retrieval corpus is the body of documents the system looks things up in. A grounding source is a source the system’s answers are tied to. Chapter 11 shows that a prompt change can materially change observed behavior without touching the model’s weights. Weights are the numbers inside a model that training sets.
Use and population triggers cover an extension to a new population or use case that the original assessment never covered. That was Calloway’s own gap. They also cover a shift in the makeup of the affected population, even without a formal decision to extend the system.
Agentic-specific triggers fire on a change to an agent’s granted permissions, tool access, or action scope. An agent’s action scope is the range of actions it is allowed to take, and its permission scope is what it is allowed to reach. Chapter 12 explains that permission scope is itself a design choice that carries risk. It is not a one-time setting.
Dependency triggers apply to any system class, not only agentic systems. A dependency is something the system relies on. A vendor is a company that sells or licenses a tool. A change to a vendor, a purchased model, an API, a subagent, or an orchestration configuration can shift the system’s risk. This is true whether the system is predictive, generative, or agentic. An API is a connection that lets one piece of software use another. A subagent is a smaller agent that a larger agent calls on. An orchestration configuration sets how the parts of a system work together.
Evidence and performance triggers cover several events. One is a control that failed. Another is a monitored performance or harm threshold that was crossed. A third is a near miss, which did not cross a threshold but showed that one was closer than assumed. These triggers also cover a complaint or appeal. They cover new evidence bearing on a risk the assessment already named, whether it comes from research, an audit, or a comparable incident elsewhere. And they cover a failure in the evidence itself.
An evidence failure can take three forms. A traceability matrix entry may be marked as met, meaning recorded as satisfied, without adequate support. A traceability matrix links each requirement to the evidence that it is met. A retention period may have lapsed, so the records were already gone by the time anyone needed to check a claim against them. A retention period is how long records are kept. Or a logging gap may leave a risk the assessment relied on unable to be checked at all. A risk decision that rests on unverified or since-invalidated evidence is no more sound than one that rests on a stale model (Chapter 15). A stale model is one that is out of date.
Context triggers address a change in the applicable law, standard, or regulator expectation that affects the system’s duties or risk. This applies whether or not the change moves the system’s classification tier under Chapter 3’s factors. Context triggers also cover a material change to the organization’s own structure or workflow around the system. And they cover a security threat that has become newly relevant to the system’s operation.
Elapsed time is the last and most general trigger. A fixed calendar interval does not by itself demand a full assessment. But a population, a regulatory environment, and a model’s real-world performance can all drift, which means change slowly. They can drift with no single event marking the moment. So elapsed time calls for a risk-based review interval, shorter for higher-tier systems. It does not call for an undifferentiated full rerun on a fixed schedule for every system alike.
An incident trigger needs its own caution. It is tempting to reassess only the component the incident exposed. Chapter 10 explains that a lookback and root-cause analysis can reveal a shared cause that reaches beyond the single system where the incident surfaced. A lookback is a review of earlier events. A root-cause analysis traces a problem back to the underlying reason it happened. A reassessment that stops at the exposed component can miss the adjacent-system and portfolio-level exposure that the incident was evidence of. Adjacent systems are other systems that share parts or causes with the one where the incident happened. Portfolio-level means across all of the organization’s systems.
Without triggers defined in advance, assessments go out of date with no event to mark it. Suppose an organization governs a system under a year-old assessment. That assessment no longer describes the system’s actual population, regulatory exposure, or performance. The organization does not enjoy a lighter compliance burden. It is governing a system that its own assessment no longer describes.
Calloway’s extension to the logistics job family was a case of this kind. It reached a new population that TalentScreen’s original fairness testing had never covered. Fairness testing checks whether a tool treats different groups fairly. What let the extension proceed on an assessment written for a different population entirely was the absence of a defined trigger, not any single person’s oversight.
Table 14.1 groups these triggers by what changed. It names the immediate action each family calls for. It also states the reassessment scope. Triage means sorting problems so the most urgent is handled first. A validity review is a check of whether the assessment still holds true. Blast radius means how far an action or failure could reach. A bare list of trigger names does not tell a team what to do when one fires.









Trigger family
Examples
Immediate action
Reassessment scope




Model and data
Model or version change; training or fine-tuning data or label change; for a generative system, a changed prompt, retrieval corpus, or grounding source
Pause the affected change pending review if the system is already live
The changed component plus any downstream effect on risk already identified


Use and population
Extension to a new population or use case; a shift in the affected-population distribution without a formal extension decision
Confirm the new scope and who authorized it
System description, risk identification, and mitigation, since a different population can change all three


Agentic-specific
Change to an agent’s granted permissions, tool access, or action scope
Confirm the change against the permission-scope standard Chapter 12 requires
The action-scope and blast-radius analysis specifically


Dependency (any system class)
Vendor, purchased model, API, subagent, or orchestration configuration change
Verify the controls the assessment relied on are still actually in place
The dependency’s role in every risk that assumed its prior behavior


Evidence and performance
Control failure; a crossed performance or harm threshold; a near miss; a complaint or appeal; new external evidence; an evidence failure such as an unverified traceability entry, a lapsed retention period, or a logging gap
Triage and contain where a threshold has already been crossed; where the trigger is an evidence failure, treat the underlying risk as unverified until the evidence is restored
The specific risk and control the evidence bears on


Context
Change in applicable law, standard, or regulator expectation, whether or not it moves the Chapter 3 classification tier; organizational or workflow change; a newly relevant security threat
Route to legal or governance review as applicable
Classification, duties, and any control the changed context affects


Elapsed time
A risk-based review interval is reached, shorter for higher-tier systems, not a fixed cycle uniform across every system
Run a documented validity review
Targeted or full, decided by the validity review’s own findings rather than assumed in advance



Table 14.1. Reassessment triggers grouped by what changed, using the same families as section 14.6. The grouping is this book’s own synthesis. It is not a validated or universally observed set. After an incident that exposes one component, the default is the lookback across adjacent systems described in section 14.6. The default is not to reassess only the exposed row. “Nothing visibly changed” does not mean “no trigger fired.” The elapsed-time and use-and-population rows can both fire with no single distinct event marking them. Read the table against the TalentScreen case. Calloway’s extension satisfied the use-and-population row. No discrete failure had to occur first for that trigger to fire.
