title: 14. Risk Assessment and Management
section: Case in focus: the assessment that was never run twice
text:
Case in focus: the assessment that was never run twice
TALENTSCREEN · Hypothetical, following the running cases
This continuing fictional scenario illustrates the reassessment-trigger failure that section 14.6 describes. It does not report an event that happened at any real organization. Every fact below is invented for teaching purposes, including the contract term, the audit cadence, and the complaint. The audit cadence is how often audits happen.
Calloway’s first impact assessment for TalentScreen was written when the tool was licensed for manufacturing floor hiring. It followed the five-component structure described above. Measured against its own scope, it was competent work. It named the disparate-impact risk. It assigned a bias-audit control, which this hypothetical’s vendor contract specified on an annual cadence. A bias audit is an independent check of whether a tool’s results differ unfairly across groups. The assessment also documented residual risk acceptance from the head of talent acquisition. The head of talent acquisition accepted the risk that the annual cadence left a gap between audits, during which drift could go undetected.
The consultation methods described in section 14.2 were not part of Calloway’s assessment practice at the time. As a result, the assessment made no structured attempt to hear from the applicants the tool screened. It did not even include a documented analysis of whether a channel to them was possible. There was no proxy consultation with an advocacy organization. No one was assigned the job of arguing an applicant’s interest in a structured adversarial review. The assessment reasoned entirely from the vendor’s own audit data and Calloway’s internal hiring statistics. No channel existed through which an affected applicant’s perspective could enter the process, even in the limited, substitute form described above.
Eighteen months after the manufacturing floor deployment, Calloway’s logistics division adopted TalentScreen for its own hiring. No new assessment was opened. The reasoning, reconstructed after the fact, was that the tool itself had not changed. That reasoning missed the use-and-population trigger that section 14.6 names. An extension to a new population is a reassessment trigger whether or not the underlying model changed at all. The reason is that the fairness testing in the original assessment characterized the manufacturing applicant population, not the logistics one. A stable model does not guarantee stable performance across a population that the original testing never included.
The gap surfaced only when a complaint under the logistics deployment prompted an internal review. A complaint is one of the evidence sources section 14.2 names, and here it arrived after deployment, not before. The review found a disparity in the logistics population. The manufacturing-floor bias audit had never been positioned to catch it, because that audit covered a different population entirely.
No one at Calloway made an explicit decision to skip reassessment. The organization had no defined trigger that would have forced the question. So the absence of a redone assessment was not a decision that anyone made and could be held to. It was the default outcome of not having asked.
A real, documented analogue to the audit duty that Calloway’s fictional vendor contract invents is New York City’s Local Law 144. Local Law 144 requires an employer or employment agency that uses a covered automated employment decision tool to do three things. The employer must obtain an independent bias audit within the year before use. It must publish a summary of the results. And it must give candidates and employees notice of the tool’s use. A tool of this kind is called an AEDT, short for automated employment decision tool. The employer, not the vendor, remains responsible for compliance (checked 2026-09-12).
The comparison is instructive where it differs from Calloway’s hypothetical. Local Law 144’s duty runs to the deploying employer by law. In Calloway’s case, the duty came from a clause in the hypothetical’s vendor contract.
A Title VII disparate-impact analysis is a separate legal question. It asks whether a facially neutral practice causes a disparate effect without job-related justification. A facially neutral practice is one that looks neutral on its face. The audit result alone does not resolve that question one way or the other.
The four-fifths rule, which some bias audits report against, is a rule-of-thumb administrative benchmark. The rule compares each group’s selection rate with the highest group’s rate. Four-fifths means 80 percent, so the rule flags a group whose selection rate falls below that share of the highest group’s rate. The EEOC’s own Uniform Guidelines describe it as an aid to enforcement, not a legal definition of disparate impact. The EEOC is the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the federal agency that enforces employment discrimination law. Passing the four-fifths rule does not by itself establish that a practice is lawful.
A governance program should treat the Calloway scenario as a teaching device for the reassessment-trigger failure. It should treat a real regulator’s published requirements, cited above, as the minimum the law requires for a covered deployment in that jurisdiction.
A correctly completed audit still leaves several things undone. A bias-audit result does not by itself validate that the screened criteria are job-related. It does not provide a required accommodation, which is an adjustment that removes a barrier so a person can take part. It does not satisfy Local Law 144’s separate notice requirement. The law does not create a general right to appeal an AEDT result. Any recourse channel beyond notice comes from another law, a policy, or the organization’s own governance design. Recourse means a way to challenge a result. The audit result also does not monitor human overrides. A human reviewer may override the tool’s recommendation in a way that brings back the same disparity the audit measured. A control this narrow needs the fuller acceptable-use and monitoring controls that Chapter 13 develops. Acceptable-use controls are rules about how a tool may and may not be used. It should not be treated as a complete fairness program on its own.

title: 14. Risk Assessment and Management
text:
Summary
An impact assessment needs five components at minimum. They form a management spine, not a complete, legally sufficient assessment. The five are system description, risk identification, mitigation, residual risk, and a documented decision with named accountability. Risk identification draws on Chapter 1’s harms taxonomy and Chapter 3’s classification factors. Assessment focus then shifts by system class. Predictive systems center on error and disparity. Generative systems center on content and misuse. Agentic systems center on action and scope. A legally required assessment type adds its own required elements on top of the spine.
Some stakeholders cannot be reached by standard methods. This is a real methodological gap, not a solved problem. A documented reachability and safety analysis comes first. Direct and representative engagement comes next where that analysis allows it, through worker representatives, advisory panels, and civil-society organizations. Proxy consultation, structured adversarial review, published research, complaint records, and post-deployment outcome analysis stand in for engagement. They do so in a specific and limited way, and only where real engagement is not feasible.
Risk scoring combines likelihood and severity as a structured comparative estimate, not a precise measurement. Prioritization forces the explicit tradeoff that a claim of “everything is critical” is designed to avoid. That holds once legally prohibited and truly incomparable risks are set aside. A marked red line separates risks that no score can make acceptable from risks that scoring can compare.
Mitigation turns assessment into action. Every significant risk gets a named control, an owner, and a verification method. Each control is named for its mechanism, which is prevent, deter, detect, contain, correct, recover, or compensate. A bare reduce-or-detect label is not enough. A claimed risk reduction rests on evaluation evidence, not assumption. Every control is also tested against the feasibility that a real operating budget imposes.
Residual risk acceptance requires a named, properly authorized acceptor and a documented basis. The first line accepts risk within delegated tolerance. Risk above that tolerance is escalated, following the roles in Chapter 13. Unaccepted residual risk is a risk that nobody has decided to bear.
Reassessment triggers cover several kinds of change. They are model and data changes, use and population changes, agentic-specific changes to permissions and tools, and dependency changes that affect any system class. They also include evidence and performance changes, legal and organizational context changes, and a risk-based elapsed-time review. An incident trigger defaults to a lookback across adjacent systems, not only the exposed component. Without triggers, an assessment goes out of date with nothing to mark it. It governs a system that has already changed out from under it.

title: 14. Risk Assessment and Management
text:
Review questions
COMPREHENSION

Name the five components of an impact assessment and explain what is missing from an assessment that identifies risk and assigns controls but records no named acceptance of residual risk.
Explain why assessment focus differs across predictive, generative, and agentic systems, and give the specific risk category each class centers on.

APPLIED

A workshop stakeholder insists that every risk on an assessment’s list is equally critical. Describe the specific question this chapter would put back to that stakeholder, name one category of risk where that question would not apply, and explain why the question still forces a comparison for everything outside that category.
For a proposed control, describe how to name its actual mechanism, prevent, deter, detect, contain, correct, recover, or compensate, rather than defaulting to a reduce-or-detect binary, and explain what evidence a claim that the control reduces a risk needs before it can be recorded that way.

SPOT THE RISK

An organization extends a purchased screening tool to a new population without opening a new assessment, reasoning that the tool itself has not changed. Identify the reassessment trigger this reasoning misses and explain why “the tool did not change” does not answer it.

COMPARE AND DECIDE

Compare proxy consultation through an advocacy organization against post-deployment outcome analysis as methods for accounting for an unreachable stakeholder population, and state what each recovers that the other does not.

RUNNING CASE

TALENTSCREEN Using the case in focus, explain why Calloway’s first assessment could be competent on its own terms while still leaving the organization exposed, and identify the specific trigger that should have forced a second assessment before the logistics deployment proceeded.


An assessment is only as good as the record it leaves behind. A control, a residual risk decision, and a reassessment trigger all depend on documentation specific enough to be tested, not just asserted. The assessment process hands the next stage of work a specific set of artifacts, the documents and records it produces, not a general impression that an assessment happened.
The first artifact is the scoped system record, which describes the system and its limits. The second is the engagement record. It names the reachability analysis performed and what it recovered. The third is the risk register, with its uncertainty and red-line determinations. The register is the list of identified risks. The fourth is the set of control specifications and their test evidence. The fifth is the residual-risk acceptance, with its authority, conditions, and expiry. The sixth is the monitoring plan, which says how the system will be watched over time. The seventh is the set of reassessment triggers for this specific system. The last is the complaint and recourse channel that affected people can use.
The next chapter turns to the documentation discipline that makes each of those artifacts specific enough to survive an audit instead of being only claimed. It also takes up a harder problem that agentic systems pose. The log of such a system, which is its record of events, must reconstruct not just what happened but under whose authority.

title: 15. Documentation and Evidence
text:
What you will be able to do
This is a constructed scenario, meaning a made-up one, and it continues the running cases. A regulator asked Northfield Health to demonstrate that MedAssist’s sepsis alert had performed within its validated bounds. A regulator is a government body that enforces rules. Sepsis is a dangerous reaction to infection. MedAssist is the model, the AI system, that warns staff when a patient is getting worse. Its validated bounds are the limits within which it was tested and shown to work. The regulator asked about the community hospital where a delayed alert contributed to the incident in Chapter 10. Northfield’s governance team went looking for the record. The governance team is the group that oversees how the organization governs its AI.
They found that the requirement the model had been built against had no acceptance criteria attached to it. The requirement read, “the model shall flag deteriorating patients with clinically acceptable sensitivity.” Acceptance criteria are the tests a result must pass to count as good enough. Sensitivity is the share of truly sick patients that an alert catches. Nothing said what “acceptable” meant.
Everyone who had worked on MedAssist believed the requirement had been met, because the model had performed well in the testing everyone remembered. No one could produce the record. No one could show what “acceptable” meant. No one could show what threshold had been tested against it, or when that test had last been rerun for the community hospital population specifically. A threshold is the cutoff a result must reach to pass.
The belief was probably correct. For the regulator’s purposes, it was also unusable. A regulator who asks to see evidence cannot act on an organization’s confidence in its own memory. It can only act on what the organization can produce. Some regulations require the record to exist independently of the underlying practice. Under such a regulation, a missing record is its own separate problem, whether or not the practice itself was sound.
Documentation discipline is what turns confidence into evidence. It has four parts. The first is requirements specific enough to test. The second is a traceability matrix, a table that links each requirement to the safeguard and the proof behind it. The third is a model card, a short document that describes what a model is for and how it performs. A skeptical reviewer reads a model card differently from the way its author intended. The fourth is logging, meaning automatic records of what a system did. The records must be detailed enough to reconstruct a decision or an action months after the fact.
Agentic systems, AI systems that take actions on their own using tools, make the logging problem harder. That harder version of the problem is part of the same discipline. Reconstructing what happened is a different task from reconstructing who is answerable for it.

title: 15. Documentation and Evidence
text:
Write a requirement specific enough to test, and distinguish a weak version of a requirement from a strong one on sight
Build a traceability matrix that connects a requirement to its control (the safeguard meant to meet it) and its evidence. Use it to answer whether a requirement is satisfied or only addressed on paper
Read a model card critically. Treat an omission or a vague section as an unresolved evidence question to raise. It is not an incidental gap, and it is not a settled fact about what happened
Specify logging that can reconstruct a decision or an agentic action. Include the authority chain (the record of what permission an agent acted under), which a decision log alone cannot supply. Then separate that chain from the question of who is legally and organizationally accountable

title: 15. Documentation and Evidence
text:
15.1 Writing testable requirements
A testable requirement needs five elements in its normative statement, the sentence that says what must happen. These elements make the requirement verifiable, not aspirational. The first is the actor or system the requirement binds. The second is the behavior required of it. The third is the operating conditions and the population the requirement applies to, meaning the group of cases it covers. The fourth is a measurable criterion. The fifth is a method for verifying that criterion.
The requirement’s record carries more fields. These fields help manage the requirement. They do not help test it. A stable identifier lets people reference and trace it. A source records where the requirement came from. A priority says what happens when it competes with another requirement for resources. An owner and a status complete the record. The status says whether the requirement is currently met, partially met, unverified, or not applicable. A requirement that will be reused or revised also carries a version and its dependencies on other requirements.
Northfield’s sensitivity requirement had no measurable criterion and no verification method. That makes it a statement of intent, not a weaker version of a complete requirement. Nothing in it could show whether the intent was met.
Measurability alone does not make a requirement sound. A number attached to a requirement is only as good as the evidence that produced it. Three examples are a clinical threshold (the cutoff a result must reach), a testing cadence (how often the test is repeated), and a population boundary (which patients the requirement covers). Each needs justification from clinical evidence, applicable regulation, and the system’s own validation record. A precise-sounding number on the page is not justification.
Here is a weak version of Northfield’s requirement. It reads, “the model shall flag deteriorating patients with clinically acceptable sensitivity.” It sounds specific because it names a metric, sensitivity. But it names no threshold and no population. Two reviewers applying the same words in good faith could reach different conclusions about whether a given result satisfies it. Nothing in the requirement resolves the disagreement. “Clinically acceptable” carries real meaning to a clinician. That meaning was never turned into something a test can check against.
A strong version states the threshold and the population together. It also traces each number to where it came from. For example, it reads, “the model shall achieve sensitivity of at least [the threshold established in the device’s own validation record] for sepsis onset within [the detection window that record specifies], measured per hospital site, retested on [the cadence the record’s monitoring plan requires]”. Device is the term a medical regulator uses for the regulated product. A validation record is the written record of the testing that showed the system worked. Sepsis onset is the moment the condition begins. A detection window is how long after that moment an alert still counts as catching it in time. A monitoring plan is the written plan for watching the system after release, and it is what sets the cadence. The bracketed form is deliberate. A real requirement fills each bracket from a specific clinical or regulatory source. It records that source in the requirement’s evidence field. A requirement that states a number with no traceable origin has replaced one unverifiable claim with a more convincing-looking one.
A single sensitivity threshold is also not the whole of what a real acceptance decision needs. A clinical alert can hit a sensitivity target and still fail in other ways. It can produce an unusable false-positive burden, meaning too many false alarms. It can show poor calibration, meaning its stated risk levels do not match what happens to patients. It can change how staff work in a way that makes clinicians tune it out. A complete requirement pairs sensitivity with the complementary measures that the specific decision calls for. These include specificity, the share of healthy patients the alert correctly leaves alone. They include positive predictive value, the share of alerts that turn out to be right. They also include calibration and alert burden, which is the load the alerts place on the staff who receive them. A complete requirement does not rest on one metric alone.
What makes the strong version strong is that it can fail a test against a stated, sourced criterion. It is not strong because it contains numbers. The weak version cannot fail, because nothing was specified in enough detail to fail against. A requirement that cannot fail a test has not constrained anything.

title: 15. Documentation and Evidence
text:
15.2 Traceability
A traceability matrix is a table that links each requirement to its control and its evidence. The control is the safeguard meant to meet the requirement. The evidence shows that the control works. The matrix answers three questions that a requirements list alone cannot. Is anything addressing this requirement? What specifically addresses it? Has that thing been verified to work, by whom, and as of when? Table 15.1 shows what a matrix with real rows looks like for two requirements of FAIRLEND, Meridian’s credit system.
The two rows below use terms from credit law and from testing. An adverse action notice is the notice sent to a person who is denied credit. Regulation B is a credit rule, and the code number beside it in the table says where that rule is written down. A factor-ranked output lists the reasons for a decision in order of importance. A sampling protocol is a written plan for how a sample is drawn and checked. A tolerance is how much difference a check will allow before the result counts as a mismatch. Q2 of a year means its second quarter, April through June.
Table 15.1. Traceability matrix for two FAIRLEND requirements










ID
Requirement
Control
Evidence
Status




FL-014
Adverse action notice must state the creditor’s actual principal reasons for a denial, per Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.9
Explanation module generates factor-ranked output at denial time
Sample of 50 denial explanations reviewed in Q2 2026; no sampling protocol, tolerance, or comparison method against the model’s actual decision logic was recorded
Unverified. Evidence exists but does not establish that the stated factors are the actual principal reasons


FL-015
Explanation must be understandable to a layperson, not merely technically accurate
Explanation module output reviewed against a plain-language readability standard
Readability scoring on the same 50-sample set; no comprehension or usability testing with actual readers was performed
Unverified. A readability score measures grade level, not whether a reader actually understood the explanation



Neither requirement can be marked “met” from the evidence recorded. The reason differs for each.
FL-014 turns on what Regulation B demands. Regulation B implements the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, a United States credit law. Regulation B requires that an adverse action notice state the creditor’s actual principal reasons for the decision. Generic categories do not meet the rule. Factors that only influenced a score somewhere in the process do not meet it either. A factor-ranked output is evidence of compliance only if a defined sampling protocol shows that the ranked factors match those actual reasons. The FL-014 row as recorded specifies neither the sampling frame (the pool the sample comes from) nor the comparison method. Its status is therefore unverified rather than met (checked 2026-09-13). A date marked checked is the day the source was last confirmed.
FL-015 fails for a different reason. A readability score measures whether text is written at an appropriate grade level. It does not show whether an actual layperson understood the text. Readability is a proxy, a stand-in measure. A matrix that lets a proxy substitute for the comprehension evidence the requirement calls for has confused what was tested with what was required.
A control sometimes checks something narrower than its requirement. Chapter 7 established that the gap between them must be recorded, and not folded into a plain “met” status that says nothing about the gap. The traceability matrix is where that recording happens. An organization reading only the control column would believe both requirements satisfied. Only the evidence column, read against what each requirement demands, reveals that neither one is.
Table 15.1’s status column is deliberately cautious. It marks a requirement met only where the evidence plainly supports it. A requirement’s status feeds the risk decisions described in Chapter 14. A residual risk acceptance is a formal decision to live with the risk that remains after the controls are in place. An unverified requirement cannot support such an acceptance the way a fully verified one can.
A residual risk acceptance record should name the specific matrix entries it relies on. Then a later change can trigger the reassessment that Chapter 14 already requires. Without that link, the change sits unnoticed in a matrix nobody revisits. The trigger might be a change to a requirement’s status, a control that stops working, or a sampling protocol that proves inadequate.
Table 15.1 shows only the columns needed here. A matrix for a live system usually tracks more. It records the system and data version each row applies to. It records the assessor and the verification date. Where a gap has been formally accepted and not only recorded, it records an exception and its expiry. An exception is an approved, written permission to fall short of the requirement for a set time, and its expiry is the date that permission runs out. Expiry and reassessment live in that residual-risk record. They are not duplicated here.

title: 15. Documentation and Evidence
text:
15.3 Model cards
A model card is a short document that describes a model. At minimum, it should cover five things. Intended use states what the model is meant to do and, as important, what it is not validated for. Validated means tested and shown to work. Training data describes what the model learned from and what populations that data represents. Performance and evaluation results report how the model performed and against what benchmark, meaning against what standard test or reference point. Limitations name known failure modes and the conditions under which performance degrades. Maintenance information states who owns the card, how to report an issue, and when it was last updated.
The original model card framework covers a broader set of categories. These include intended users, factors (the conditions and groups that change how a model performs), ethical considerations, and quantitative analyses disaggregated by subgroup. Disaggregated results are broken out for each group instead of averaged together. A deploying organization is the organization that puts a model to use. It should add whichever of those categories a specific system’s risk profile calls for. It should not treat this five-category core as exhaustive.
A model card is not the only document that this evidence standard reaches. It describes one model. A system built from several models, or one operating under a specific legal regulation, typically needs more. It needs a broader system card or the fuller technical documentation that a regulation like the EU AI Act requires. A system card describes a whole system rather than a single model. Technical documentation is the full written record of how a system was built and tested. The EU AI Act is the European Union’s law regulating AI. These documents come on top of the model card, not instead of it.
Each section exists to answer a specific question that a deploying organization needs answered before relying on the model. A card missing a section has left that question unanswered rather than implicitly answered favorably.
Reading a model card adversarially means reading it as a skeptical reviewer would. The reviewer treats what the card omits or leaves vague as an unresolved evidence request. An omission is neither a neutral gap nor a settled fact about what happened.
A card with no limitations section does not reveal why the section is missing. Limitations testing might not have been done. It might have been done and not published. Or it might have been left out by an author who did not think to include it. A reviewer cannot tell which from the card alone. What the reviewer can do is ask directly. Was limitations testing performed? If so, can the protocol and the disaggregated results be produced?
A vague limitations section raises the same kind of question. An example is a section stating that the model “may perform differently across subgroups” without naming which subgroups or by how much. Vagueness settles nothing. It does not by itself establish that unfavorable testing occurred and was withheld. Treating vagueness as proof of a hidden bad result substitutes suspicion for evidence. That is the same substitution an unsourced number makes when it stands in for justification.
The useful move is the same in both cases. A reviewer should request the protocol and the disaggregated results. The reviewer should compare the evaluation population against the intended deployment population. If the answer is a refusal, or the material is unavailable, the reviewer should record that as its own finding. The reviewer should not infer what it means.
A thin performance section prompts its own follow-up. Suppose it reports only an aggregate accuracy figure, one overall number with no breakdown by group. The question is the one that Chapter 6 applies at selection. What is the performance broken out by the specific populations this deployment will serve? An aggregate figure can hide a disparity, just as a fairness metric chosen without scrutiny can.
The table that follows uses a few terms the sections above do not. Provenance is the record of where something came from and how it changed over time. A runtime environment is the setup of software and hardware a model runs inside. A dependency is another piece of software or data the model relies on. A subgroup is a group of people whose results can be reported separately. A misuse review is a check of the ways a system could be used wrongly or harmfully.
Table 15.2. Model card sections and the question each one should answer








Section
What it should establish
Question to ask when it is missing or vague




Intended use
What the model is validated to do, and what it is not validated for
What specific uses were tested, and what happens if this deployment falls outside them


Training data
What the model learned from and what populations that data represents
Does the training population match the deployment population, and if not, in what way


Performance and evaluation
How the model performed, against what benchmark, disaggregated by relevant subgroup
Can the disaggregated results be produced, not only the aggregate figure


Limitations
Known failure modes and the conditions under which performance degrades
Was limitations testing performed, and can the protocol and results be produced


Provenance and version
Which model version the card describes and how it relates to earlier versions
Does this card match the version actually deployed, and what changed since the last version


Maintenance and ownership
Who owns the card, how to report an issue, and when it was last reviewed
Who is the current owner, and when was the card last checked against the current model


Security, misuse, and legal restrictions
Known misuse risks and any legal or licensing restriction on use
Has a misuse review been performed, and what does the license actually permit


Deployment dependencies and monitoring
What the model assumes about its runtime environment, and how it is monitored once deployed
What happens to the card’s claims if a dependency changes, and who is watching for that



Table 15.2 is a checklist to run against any model card. It applies whether the card has the five-category core or the fuller original framework. A section that looks thorough still gets its question. The point of reading adversarially is to ask the question. It is not to assume that a section which looks complete has already answered it.

title: 15. Documentation and Evidence
text:
15.4 Audit trails and logging
A decision may need to be reconstructed months later. An affected individual may challenge it. A regulator or an internal review may ask about it. So the organization must capture information at the time of the decision that nobody expects to need until they suddenly do.
Table 15.3 lists the five items a log needs at minimum, and the further items that reconstruction may need depending on the system and the regulation it operates under. Section 15.5 develops the authorization decision for agentic systems specifically.
Table 15.3. Audit log items, minimum and conditional








Item
What it records
When needed




Input
The input the system received
Minimum


Model and configuration version
Which model version processed the input, and the configuration, the set of settings the model ran with
Minimum


Output
The output produced
Minimum


Human override
Any override, meaning a person changing what the system decided, and the reason given for it
Minimum


Timestamp
When each of the other items occurred
Minimum


Policy or tool version
The policy or tool version in force at the time
Where reconstruction needs it


Reviewer or approver
Who reviewed or approved the decision
Where reconstruction needs it


Error or exception record
Where the system failed to complete normally
Where reconstruction needs it


Correlation identifier
A shared label that ties together the related entries of a request spanning multiple systems or a multi-step agentic action
Where reconstruction needs it


Authorization decision
The authorization decision behind an action
Where reconstruction needs it


Integrity record
That the log itself has not been altered after the fact
Where reconstruction needs it



A log missing the model version cannot show which version’s known limitations applied to a specific decision. That matters when a limitation is discovered after the fact. The organization then needs to know which past decisions the limitation might have affected.
Capturing “the input” does not mean storing it in full regardless of what it contains. Some inputs carry personal, privileged (legally protected from disclosure), or otherwise sensitive material. For such inputs, the logging design should record a masked, hashed, or reference form that is enough to support reconstruction. A masked form hides the sensitive parts, a hashed form is a short code that stands for the original without revealing it, and a reference form points to where the original is kept. The design should not default to full-content capture as the only way to meet the requirement. Access to any unmasked original should itself be controlled and separately logged.
Retention, meaning how long the logs are kept, is in real tension with privacy obligations. The same records that let an organization reconstruct a decision months later often contain personal data. Privacy regulation pushes organizations to minimize and delete that data promptly. The tension does not resolve to a single rule of thumb. It resolves to a retention schedule. The schedule comes from the specific law a system falls under and from the specific purpose each category of record serves.
The EU AI Act sets a concrete floor for a high-risk system once its high-risk obligations take effect. A high-risk system is a category the Act defines for riskier uses of AI. The Act does not leave retention for each organization to decide. The amended timetable is the revised schedule for when the Act’s rules start to bind. An annex is a numbered list attached to the end of a law, and the two annexes named below each cover a different set of high-risk uses. Under the amended timetable, the Annex III high-risk rules apply from 2 December 2027. The Annex I product-related high-risk rules apply from 2 August 2028.
A provider is the organization that supplies the system, and a deployer is the organization that uses it. From the applicable date, a provider must retain the automatically generated logs under its control for at least six months. It must keep them longer where other applicable Union or national law requires it. Union law here means the law of the European Union. A deployer carries a separate retention duty for the logs under its own control. A provider separately must retain the system’s technical documentation. The period is ten years after the system is placed on the market or put into service (Articles 18, 19, and 26, checked 2026-09-13). A system is placed on the market when it is first made available for use. It is put into service when it is first put to its intended use.
A privacy regulation such as the GDPR, the European Union’s data protection law, points the other way. It favors keeping personal data no longer than the purpose for retaining it requires (Article 5). An organization under both obligations needs a schedule that treats operational logs, audit evidence, and technical documentation as separate categories. Each category has its own minimum and its own justification. The schedule should not apply one plausibility test uniformly to everything the system produces. A plausibility test here means a single rough guess about how long a record seems worth keeping.

title: 15. Documentation and Evidence
section: 15.5 Reconstructing agentic action: sequence and authority
text:
15.5 Reconstructing agentic action: sequence and authority
Agentic systems make the reconstruction problem harder, because two things must be reconstructed and they are different things.
The first is the action sequence. It records the observable state available to the agent at the time, meaning everything the agent could see when it acted. That state includes its inputs, its retrieved context (information it looked up), and its prior tool results. The sequence also records the action the agent selected and what it invoked, meaning which tool or service it called. This is the same kind of information that a decision log captures for a predictive or generative system. For an agentic system, that information extends to a chain of actions instead of a single output.
The second is the authority chain. A sequence log does not automatically capture it. The authority chain records what authorization the agent acted under. That authorization is a decision more than a single fact. Reconstructing it means recording the elements the decision depended on, and Table 15.4 lists them.
Table 15.4. Elements of the authority chain







Element
What it records




Principal
Which principal requested the task. A principal is the party that asks the agent to act, and it can be a person or a software service


Policy
What policy governed the decision to grant or deny the task


Scoped credential
What credential was issued. A scoped credential is a digital pass that allows only a defined set of actions, and its scope is that set of actions


Registered agent identity
Which identity the credential was issued to. A registered agent identity is the name under which the organization recorded the agent, and it was established under Chapter 12’s registration requirement


Constraints and validity window
The credential’s constraints and its validity window, the period during which it works


Delegation
Whether a supervising agent delegated the task to a subordinate one under a narrower scope than the one it held itself



How that credential evidence is represented depends on the architecture. A policy-enforcement system checks each request against the organization’s rules. It can record the decision itself at the point where enforcement happens. The record holds who asked (the subject), what they asked to reach (the resource), and what they asked to do with it (the action). It also holds the surrounding circumstances (the context), which version of the rules applied (the policy version), and what was allowed or refused (the outcome). It can hold all of that with no separate credential object at all. A system built on OAuth-style token exchange, a standard way of passing permissions between systems, instead records an issued token, its scope, and its validity. A token is a kind of digital credential. A hop is one step in a chain of delegation, where one party passes a task to the next. A fresh credential at a given hop is required only where the architecture’s own policy calls for one. It is not a general rule.
The chain must record the scope in force at the moment of the action, not at the moment the agent was registered. Scope can be narrowed, widened, or suspended after registration (Chapter 12). A log that checks only the registration-time scope will misstate what the agent was authorized to do when it acted.
A sequence log with a complete authority chain answers one question. It shows who was authorized to act and under what scope. It does not by itself answer who is accountable for the outcome. Authorization (whether the action was permitted), causal contribution (how much a given party brought the outcome about), and legal or organizational accountability (who has to answer for it) are different questions. An agent’s registered identity answers the authorization question in technical terms. It is not a person or a legal entity capable of answering for the outcome.
Establishing accountability means mapping the technical chain back to the human and organizational roles that Chapter 13 defines. The chain’s parts are the principal, the delegation, the credential, and the action. The mapping answers three questions. Who owned the decision to deploy the agent with this scope? Who is the designated risk owner if the action causes harm? Who had the authority to prevent it? A designated risk owner is the named person the organization makes responsible for a given risk.
A complete authority chain is necessary evidence for that mapping. It is not the mapping itself. Treating a fully recorded chain as proof of who is answerable skips the step that connects a technical record to an accountability decision.
Multi-agent architectures, which use several AI agents working together, make the distinction between sequence and authority acute. The chain from a human principal to the agent that executes an action can run through several intermediate hops. A supervising agent may delegate to a subordinate one, and that one may delegate again. Each hop must be recorded independently. The record includes whatever credential, token, or policy record the architecture issued or checked at that hop. It also includes the hop’s scope and validity window. A hop missing that record breaks the chain at that point. That leaves an unanswerable gap between the principal who authorized the work in general terms and the specific agent that took the specific action under challenge.
Registration creates an identity that a log can reference. The authority chain records that identity in use at the moment of a specific action. It records the policy decision and the credential, which were verified and not just asserted.
Preventive enforcement is what stops an out-of-scope action before it happens, meaning an action outside the set the credential allows. It consists of the policy decision and the runtime recheck at the resource the agent calls. The resource is the system, tool, or store of data the agent is trying to reach. A runtime recheck is a second check made when the action is attempted. Preventive enforcement does not itself depend on the log.
Monitoring (Chapter 9) is the separate, ongoing check that compares what already happened against what was authorized. It can do that checking only if the data already exists in the log it monitors. A monitoring function built to compare actions against permission scope needs that data. It has nothing to compare against if the log never captured the policy decision and the scope in force at the moment of each action. The log design therefore decides whether that monitoring, and the accountability mapping that Chapter 13 requires, can run at all.






Figure 16.1: Figure 15.3. Authorization chain from principal request to acting agent, and where accountability is established




Figure 15.3 shows two paths side by side. Read them together instead of reasoning about a missing hop in the abstract. On the broken path, the principal and the acting agent have complete records. The supervising agent’s delegation step has a gap. The chain stops being followable at that gap. For reconstruction purposes, the chain is broken however complete the two recorded ends look. Even the complete path answers only the first of the figure’s two questions, who was authorized. The accountability step at the end of that path names who is answerable. Skipping that step, not a missing hop, is the more common failure in practice.

title: 15. Documentation and Evidence
text:
15.6 Evidence for regulators
Demonstrable compliance differs from believing that an organization complies. Northfield found this out when its confidence in MedAssist’s validated sensitivity produced no record a regulator would accept.
Demonstrable compliance means a specific document, a specific test result, or a specific log entry exists and can be produced on request. It is tied to the specific requirement and the specific time period a regulator is asking about. Believing you comply means the organization’s staff are confident the underlying work was done. That confidence may well be true. Northfield was in that position, correct in substance but unable to prove it.
Three separate questions are involved, and keeping them separate matters. Did the system satisfy the substantive requirement? Did the organization create and retain the evidence that a specific law or policy requires it to keep? Is the evidence that exists sufficient for the regulator or decision-maker asking about it?
Some regulations treat the second question as its own independent obligation. The EU AI Act’s documentation and logging duties, described in section 15.4, are examples. Under such a regulation, a missing record can itself be a violation, however the first question would have come out. A missing record can also foreclose the organization’s ability to answer the third question favorably, even when the underlying practice was sound.
The traceability matrix, the model card, and the logging are part of governance itself, not paperwork layered on top of it. They let an organization answer all three questions instead of only the first one. Northfield’s experience shows what happens when only the first question has a good answer.

title: 15. Documentation and Evidence
section: 15.7 Automating documentation and versioning governance artifacts
text:
15.7 Automating documentation and versioning governance artifacts
Documentation can be generated automatically from development artifacts that already exist. Examples are a model’s training configuration, its test suite results, and its deployment manifest. The test suite results are the outcomes of the tests run on the model. The deployment manifest is the file that lists how the model is set up for release. Generated documentation can be more reliable than documentation written separately after the fact, but only under specific conditions. First, the source data feeding the generator has to be correct. Second, the mapping from source to document has to be validated. Third, the generator itself has to be versioned and reproducible. A person still has to sign off that the generated section is complete and means what it appears to mean.
Automation without those conditions does not remove error. It changes what kind of error occurs and how far it spreads. A faulty generator or a stale mapping can spread the same wrong number into every document it produces. A single transcription error never reaches that scale.
Consider a model card’s performance section. Generating it directly from the test suite’s output means no one transcribes the numbers into a document later. That removes the error the Northfield example illustrates, a record that no longer matches what was tested. The fix works only if the pipeline generating that section is under the same change control (the formal process for approving changes) and review as every other governance artifact.
Governance artifacts are maintained objects, not one-time deliverables. They need ongoing upkeep. A requirements template ages as the systems it is applied to change, meaning it slowly stops fitting them. A template last revised before agentic systems existed will produce weak requirements for agentic risk. This is the weakness that the testability standard in section 15.1 warns against. The weakness comes from the template, which never prompted for a scope-specific acceptance criterion, a test tied to the limits of what an agent may do. It does not come from anyone writing a weak requirement.
A risk taxonomy, the organization’s classified list of risk types, ages the same way. A threshold set once, with no defined review cycle, ages the most invisibly of all. A threshold never announces that the conditions it was calibrated under no longer hold. Each of these needs a named owner and a scheduled review. Chapter 14’s reassessment triggers apply the same discipline to an individual system’s assessment. Here it applies to the governance program’s own tools, not to any single system the tools are used to review.
Updating a template, a taxonomy, or a threshold does not by itself update the systems already governed under the version being replaced. A governance program needs a migration step alongside the update. The step should identify which live systems the change affects and tell their owners. Without that step, a revised tool sits next to assessments and requirements that were never brought forward to match it.

title: 15. Documentation and Evidence
section: Case in focus: one requirement, three paths to evidence
text:
Case in focus: one requirement, three paths to evidence
MEDASSIST · FAIRLEND · TALENTSCREEN · Hypothetical, following the running cases
A related transparency goal runs through all three running cases, but the concrete legal requirement differs in each domain. Credit and medical alerting both give the affected person, or the clinician acting on their behalf, a route to a specific explanation of the individual outcome. Employment works differently. TalentScreen is the applicant-screening tool that Calloway purchased. Its governing rule, New York City’s Local Law 144, requires a bias audit and advance notice before the tool is used. A bias audit is a check of whether the tool treats groups of people unfairly. The rule does not require an individualized explanation to a rejected applicant.
Tracing the transparency goal across all three domains shows how differently it gets satisfied, and through what different mechanisms. The mechanism depends on whether the system was built internally (the build path) or purchased (the buy path).
At Northfield, MedAssist generates its sepsis alert internally. The explanation requirement has direct evidence behind it, and Northfield controls that evidence end to end. The model’s feature contributions, which show how much each input pushed the alert up or down, are logged at alert time. A clinician-facing summary is generated from those contributions. Northfield’s own validation team tested the summary for comprehensibility against a sample of nursing staff before deployment. The traceability matrix entry for this requirement cites Northfield’s own test data. If a regulator asks for the underlying evidence, Northfield can produce it directly. Northfield built the pipeline the evidence came from.
At Meridian, FAIRLEND’s adverse action explanation is also built internally. It follows the factor-ranked output that Regulation B’s reasons requirement calls for, as traced in section 15.2. The evidence chain looks similar to MedAssist’s in structure. It is internal test data, internally controlled and directly producible. The complication lies in the evidence’s adequacy, not its source. Section 15.2 showed that the evidence for FL-014 and FL-015 falls short of what each requirement demands. The matrix records that gap explicitly. It does not resolve it.
At Calloway, TalentScreen’s explanation to a rejected applicant is a requirement that Calloway’s own governance program has adopted. Local Law 144 itself does not compel it. Calloway also did not build the capability. It is a feature of the purchased tool. The evidence for whether it satisfies that internal requirement is whatever the vendor is willing to supply.
Calloway has no visibility into TalentScreen’s internal architecture. Neither Northfield’s feature-contribution log nor Meridian’s factor ranking is a record of a model’s internal reasoning either. Both are outputs the model produces alongside its decision. They are useful evidence, but not a window into how the model arrived at the decision. What Calloway lacks, and Northfield and Meridian have, is any output of that kind to evaluate directly. The evidence available instead is vendor-supplied documentation that describes the explanation feature in general terms.
Reading that vendor documentation adversarially is one path to better evidence. It applies the approach of section 15.3 to a vendor artifact instead of a model card. It is not the only path available to a purchasing organization. Calloway can test the explanation feature’s outputs directly against known cases, without needing architectural visibility. It can negotiate audit and data-access rights into the vendor contract. It can commission an independent evaluation. It can validate a sample of explanations with actual rejected applicants, instead of assuming the vendor’s general description covers comprehensibility. It can track complaint volume against the feature over time.
None of these closes the evidence gap entirely. Pressing a reluctant vendor for stronger evidence remains necessary regardless, and that is Chapter 16’s subject. Still, a purchasing organization is not limited to accepting whatever the vendor is willing to supply.

title: 15. Documentation and Evidence
text:
Summary
A testable requirement’s statement needs five elements. These are an actor, a required behavior, operating conditions and population, a measurable criterion, and a verification method. The requirement’s record also carries an identifier, source, priority, owner, and status. These fields serve management, not testability. A weak requirement differs from a strong one in whether it names a specific, sourced threshold and population. The strong one is precise enough to fail a test.
A traceability matrix connects each requirement to its control and its evidence. Its evidence column, not its control column, reveals whether a requirement is met, unverified, or only addressed on paper. Any gap that Chapter 7’s testing showed must be recorded explicitly and not folded into a plain pass. A requirement’s status then feeds directly into the residual risk decisions that Chapter 14 describes.
A model card’s sections each answer a specific question. Reading a card adversarially treats an omission or a vague section as an unresolved evidence request that generates a follow-up question. It does not treat the gap as proof of what caused it.
An audit trail must capture, at minimum, the input, the model and configuration version, the output, any override, and a timestamp. These items support reconstruction months later. The specific system and regulation require additional fields. The law that governs each category of record sets its retention. One example is the EU AI Act’s six-month logging floor and ten-year documentation duty for covered systems. A single plausibility test, one rough guess applied to everything alike, does not set retention.
Agentic systems require reconstructing two distinct things. The action sequence shows what happened. The authority chain shows what was authorized. That includes the policy decision, the credential, and the scope in force at the moment of action, not at registration. A multi-agent delegation chain breaks at any hop that is not independently recorded. A complete authority chain establishes who was authorized to act. It does not by itself establish who is accountable for the outcome. Accountability requires mapping the chain back to the human and organizational roles that Chapter 13 defines.
Demonstrable compliance means having created the evidence that a specific law or policy requires. It is a separate question from both substantive compliance and believing you comply. A regulator’s inquiry tests whether the organization keeps these three questions distinct.
Documentation generated automatically from development artifacts can be more reliable than documentation written separately after the fact. That holds only when the source data, the mapping, and the generator itself are under the same review as every other governance artifact. Governance artifacts also age. Templates, taxonomies, and thresholds need a named owner and a review cycle. Chapter 14 applies the same discipline to an individual system’s assessment, and here it applies to the program’s own tools.

title: 15. Documentation and Evidence
text:
Review questions
COMPREHENSION

Name the elements a testable requirement’s normative statement needs, distinguish them from the fields a requirement’s record carries for management purposes, and explain what specifically was missing from Northfield’s original sensitivity requirement.
State the three questions a traceability matrix answers that a plain requirements list cannot.

APPLIED

A model card includes a limitations section stating the model “may perform differently across subgroups” with no further detail. Explain why this vagueness cannot by itself establish that unfavorable subgroup testing occurred, and state the specific follow-up question a reviewer should ask instead of inferring one.
Specify the fields an audit log needs at minimum to reconstruct a contested decision six months later, name one additional field a regulated agentic system might need beyond that minimum, and explain why the model version field matters independently of the output field.

SPOT THE RISK

A multi-agent system’s log records the human principal’s initial authorization and the acting agent’s final action, but not the intermediate supervising agent’s delegation step. Explain why this chain is broken for reconstructing what happened despite both ends being fully recorded, and why a complete chain would still not, by itself, tell you who is accountable.

COMPARE AND DECIDE

Compare the evidence available for a build-path explanation requirement against a buy-path one, and name at least three specific actions, beyond reading vendor documentation adversarially, that a purchasing organization can take to strengthen its evidence.

RUNNING CASE

MEDASSIST FAIRLEND TALENTSCREEN Using the case in focus, explain why a shared transparency goal produces three different legal requirements and three different kinds of evidence across the three systems, and state specifically what TalentScreen’s governing rule requires.


Documentation proves what an organization has already done. The next chapter addresses evidence that depends on a third party. Gaps in that evidence can come from limited visibility, weak contracts, supplier dependencies, or an outright refusal to disclose.

title: 16. Third-Party, Vendor, and Supply Chain Governance
text:
What you will be able to do
This constructed scenario continues the running cases, the example organizations that recur from chapter to chapter. Calloway Industries did not build TalentScreen. It licensed the resume-screening and candidate-ranking tool from a vendor, which is a company that sells software to other organizations. Licensing the tool did not by itself settle who would bear the cost if a disparate-impact claim under Title VII ever arrived. Title VII is a US law that prohibits discrimination in employment. A disparate-impact claim says a hiring practice harms one group more than others, even without any intent to do so.
An employer’s own use of a hiring tool typically remains its own exposure, whoever built the tool. Exposure means the risk of being held responsible. How far that exposure also reaches the vendor depends on the claim, the jurisdiction whose law applies, the facts, and what the contract assigns.
Governing a purchased or licensed system differs from the discipline Part II developed for a system an organization controls end to end. It brings three new demands.
First, it requires due diligence, which is a careful check of a vendor before and during a purchase. The vendor’s interests are not identical to those of the deploying organization, the organization that puts the system to use. The vendor also supplies much of the evidence. That evidence needs independent scrutiny before anyone can trust it.
Second, it requires contract terms. Those terms either serve governance or leave the organization exposed by omission, which means exposed by what the contract left out.
Third, it depends on a supply chain, which is the series of parties that build and pass along the system. The chain runs from a base model through fine-tuning, adapters, and integration to deployment. A base model is the large general model that everything else builds on. Fine-tuning is extra training that adapts it to a task. An adapter is a small add-on module that changes how the model behaves. Integration is building the model into a product. Deployment is putting that product to use. Along this chain, the deploying organization’s visibility typically runs out well before its legal responsibility does. Visibility means how much the organization can see into each part.

title: 16. Third-Party, Vendor, and Supply Chain Governance
text:
Structure vendor due diligence as a risk-based inquiry, one whose depth matches the risk at stake, with open, specific, and limitation-focused questions as one technique within it. Record what a declined question establishes without assuming why it was declined
Evaluate vendor-supplied evidence, including a vendor bias audit, which is a test of whether a system treats groups differently. Question its methodology, independence, and scope instead of accepting its stated result
Draft contract provisions that serve governance, with defined variables in place of vague placeholders. Identify where procurement leverage, which is bargaining power in the buying process, exists both before and after signature
Assess a supply chain’s obligation and visibility at each layer as two separate attributes. Identify what a model developer’s own policy terms quietly pass on to an organization’s own product
crumbs: 17  16. Third-Party, Vendor, and Supply Chain Governance

title: 16. Third-Party, Vendor, and Supply Chain Governance
text:
16.1 Due diligence as structured inquiry
Due diligence is a risk-based process, not a single conversation. The depth of the check matches the risk the system carries. It starts before a vendor is even contacted. That early work defines the intended use, which is what the system is sold and bought to do, the roles the law assigns to each party, and the affected people. It also defines the system’s criticality and the evidence a decision will require. Criticality is how much depends on the system working.
Inside that process, one effective interview technique asks three kinds of question in order. Open questions come first. They let the vendor’s own framing reveal what it considers important. Specific questions come second. They pin down the details the open answers surfaced. Limitation questions come last. They name what the vendor is least likely to volunteer. This sequence is not the whole of due diligence.
An open question might ask the vendor to describe the system’s intended use cases and the populations it was developed and tested against. Suppose the open answer names a population. A specific question then asks for the disaggregated performance, which means the results broken out by group. The groups should be the specific demographic groups this deployment will serve. The aggregate figure, the single overall number the vendor’s marketing material leads with, does not answer that question. A limitation question asks what the system has failed to do correctly in the past twelve months. It also asks what use cases the vendor explicitly declines to support.
Material limitation questions are the ones large enough to affect the decision. They belong early enough in the process that a vendor’s answer, or refusal to answer, can still change it. Asked only once relationship momentum has built, meaning both sides already expect the deal to go ahead, the same questions make declining look like the harder path. A due diligence sequence built to make refusal costly for the vendor is a negotiation tactic, not a governance control. The sequence above is meant to surface information. It is not meant as leverage over the vendor’s incentives.
Due diligence closes with a decision, not a completed questionnaire. The accountable risk owner, the person answerable for the risk, makes that decision. The owner draws on the legal, security, privacy, and technical review that the system’s risk tier, the level of risk assigned to it, calls for. The owner can reject the relationship or require remediation, which means having the vendor fix what the review found. The owner can also approve the relationship with named conditions and an expiry date, or escalate it to a higher level of the organization for decision.
Contracting, onboarding, monitoring, incident response, and exit follow from that decision. They do not substitute for it. Sections 16.5 and 16.10 develop each.
crumbs: 17  16. Third-Party, Vendor, and Supply Chain Governance

title: 16. Third-Party, Vendor, and Supply Chain Governance
text:
16.2 Assessment dimensions
Due diligence assesses at least four dimensions, and Table 16.3 states what each one asks. A weak or unclear answer on any one is itself a finding. It is not automatically a signal of what the vendor is hiding.
Table 16.3. The four core assessment dimensions







Dimension
What it asks




Provider
Who the vendor is, how long it has operated, and what its financial stability suggests about long-term support


System
What the system does, what data it was built on, and how it performs across the populations it will encounter


Documentation
Whether a model card, a technical specification, or an equivalent document exists at all


Compliance
What regulatory obligations the vendor has already assessed against the deployment’s jurisdiction and sector



A model card is a short document that describes what a model is for, how it was built, and how it performs.
On the provider dimension, an unclear answer is a real gap in the evidence for a support and continuity decision. On the system dimension, the answer sometimes stays in marketing terms instead of technical specifics. That leaves the question open. It does not tell you which explanation accounts for the vagueness. The cause could be an unflattering technical answer, an incomplete internal understanding, or an unpracticed sales process. On the documentation dimension, if no model card or equivalent document exists, its absence is itself the finding. It is not a gap to route around.
A fuller review is proportionate to the system’s risk tier. It also covers data provenance, which is where the data came from. It takes in security and resilience, privacy, safety and accessibility, and the design of human oversight. It covers subprocessors, which are companies the vendor hires to handle data for it, and other dependencies. It extends to incident history, intellectual property and licensing terms, and business continuity, which is the vendor’s ability to keep operating after a disruption. It also covers exit and portability, which is the ability to leave and take your data with you.
A review limited to the four core dimensions should say so explicitly. Otherwise it implies a completeness it does not have.
crumbs: 17  16. Third-Party, Vendor, and Supply Chain Governance

title: 16. Third-Party, Vendor, and Supply Chain Governance
text:
16.3 Vendor resistance
A vendor’s interests are not identical to the deploying organization’s. Due diligence has to account for that gap without assuming it resolves in one direction. An unanswered question shows an evidentiary gap, which means the evidence a decision needs is missing. It is not proof of what caused the gap. The record, which is the written file the organization keeps on the vendor, should reflect that distinction.
The first useful move is to separate two kinds of request. One touches a genuine trade secret. The other does not. A trade secret is business information that a company keeps private because it gives the company an edge. Architecture and training methodology mean how a model is built and how it was trained. Whether disclosing either would expose a protected trade secret depends on the applicable law and the specific facts. There is no fixed, universal boundary. Some jurisdictions and some architectures make the claim strong.
Pressing past a well-founded trade-secret claim is rarely productive unless the deploying organization offers an alternative. One alternative is a nondisclosure agreement, a contract that binds the reader to keep information secret. Another is a clean-room review, in which a few approved reviewers inspect protected material under strict controls. A third is an independent assessor bound by confidentiality.
Other information sits differently. Disaggregated performance figures, documented failure modes, which are the ways the system is known to fail, and known limitations do not require disclosing how the system works internally. A vendor that declines to share information of that kind has left the deploying organization with an unresolved evidentiary gap. That is true whatever the vendor’s actual reason for declining.
What an organization needs from a vendor depends on the system’s risk tier and use. A short, fixed list understates it. Disaggregated performance, documented failure modes, and known limitations are usually part of that evidence. A consequential deployment typically needs more. That includes intended-use scope, version history, and training and evaluation provenance. It includes security and privacy posture and human-oversight design. It also includes incident history, monitoring and change-management practices, subcontractor dependencies, and applicable licensing and support terms.
Specific follow-up questions carry the inquiry further when a vendor first declines a broader request. If a vendor calls an audit’s methodology proprietary, meaning the vendor treats it as its own private business information, the follow-up is narrower. It asks whether the audit’s date, sample size, and metric names can be shared without the underlying calculations. If a vendor declines to share training data, the examples the model learned from, the follow-up asks for less. It asks whether the vendor will share the demographic composition of that data at a summary level. Neither follow-up discloses methodology.
Suppose a vendor keeps declining even a narrowed, non-proprietary request. The underlying question is still unresolved. The record should state that as an unresolved gap. It should not state it as proof the vendor was hiding an unfavorable result. The deploying organization does not need to know why the information was withheld to decide whether it can proceed without it.
Some gaps are disqualifying. They should be named that way directly, not negotiated around indefinitely. Take a vendor that will not disclose any disaggregated performance data at all, for a system deployed in a context that Chapter 3’s classification would place at a meaningful risk tier. That vendor has left the deploying organization with no basis for the risk assessment Chapter 14 requires. Proceeding anyway means proceeding on an unverified assumption, not on governance.
Whether a specific gap is disqualifying depends on the system’s risk tier. It also depends on what alternative evidence, if any, can substitute for what the vendor withholds. The discipline is to decide this in advance. Otherwise a team may rationalize acceptance after the fact, because a deployment deadline has already created momentum toward proceeding.
Every declined question should be documented, not discarded. The record of what a vendor would not answer is itself evidence. Chapter 15 anticipates the situation where a later challenge asks what the organization knew and when. Compare two records. One says, “The vendor declined to answer this and we proceeded on the following alternative basis”. The other shows no sign that the question was ever asked. The first is a materially different record than the second. A documented gap is evidence that the question was asked. It is not, on its own, a substitute for the answer.






Figure 17.1: Figure 16.1. Due diligence sequence




Figure 16.1 has two branches, not only the decline branch. An answer is not itself acceptance. The affirmative path, where the vendor answers, still runs through verification. It then reaches the same decision point that a decline eventually reaches by a different route.
