A proposed control specifies human review of every system output. What cost consideration should be raised before accepting the control as designed? What should the response be if the control turns out to be unaffordable at production volume?

SPOT THE RISK

A governance program reports a high volume of completed reviews with a near-zero rejection rate. Using the distinction between process metrics and outcome metrics, identify what this pattern might signal. Then name the additional evidence, beyond the rejection rate itself, that would confirm or rule it out.

COMPARE AND DECIDE

A system is continuously monitored after deployment. State the specific conditions that must hold before that monitoring justifies a lighter predeployment gate. Then describe a case where excellent monitoring would not justify the lighter gate.

RUNNING CASE

TALENTSCREEN Using the case in focus, explain why applying a uniform review process across all three of Calloway’s systems produced a bypass. Identify the specific design change that addressed it. Also say what further evidence a real program would still want before concluding the fix fully worked.


The laws and regulations that a governance program works under keep changing. The final chapter explains how to govern durably under that uncertainty. Durable governance keeps working as the rules change.

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
text:
What you will be able to do
The European Union delayed the high-risk obligations of its AI Act in July 2026. The AI Act is the EU’s law on artificial intelligence. Its high-risk obligations are the duties it places on the AI systems it classes as high risk. The law itself sets out which systems those are. Chapter 2 traced this delay and the two planning risks it exposes. Those risks threaten any organization that treats a regulatory date as fixed.
Colorado, a US state, ran a sharper version of the same pattern. It repealed, meaning cancelled, the entire framework that had set its original compliance date. It then enacted a replacement law.
These facts form a pattern, and it will repeat. A governance program built to a fixed regulatory calendar will keep meeting this same failure, on some regulation, indefinitely, because the pattern is structural. It is not tied to any one law.
The aim is a program that survives the pattern instead of getting lucky on a single date. What carries forward is the discipline, not a snapshot of law.

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
text:
Explain why a governance program built around fixed compliance dates fails. Use a real regulatory delay to show the mechanism rather than to give an abstract warning.
Run horizon scanning, which means watching for coming legal change, as a routine discipline. It has four parts. They are choosing sources, setting a schedule, sorting items by urgency (called triage), and turning each change into a tracked internal change request.
Design a classification and mapping structure that survives regulation change. It builds directly on the inventory and classification work of Chapter 3.
Name the obligations that stay stable beneath any specific regulatory framework. Describe what the AI governance field asks of the people who practice it.

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
text:
18.1 Why compliance calendars fail
A compliance calendar treats a regulatory date as the plan itself. A sound plan treats the date as one input that may move. The EU delay shows two ways the calendar approach fails.
The first failure is over-investment. The organization treats the date as immovable. It spends budget and attention finishing certification work, which is the formal proof that a system meets the rules. That work is measured against harmonizing standards, the technical standards a product is checked against. In the delay’s own telling, those standards were the reason the date moved. While such a standard is unfinished, there is nothing settled to check a system against. Work finished early against an unready standard often has to be redone when the standard changes.
The second failure is under-investment. The organization treats the date as already moved before the law changed. It then runs no active preparation during the gap between the proposed delay and its enactment. During that gap, the original date remained the legally operative one, meaning the date in force, whatever everyone expected to happen to it.
Colorado’s sequence makes the same point more clearly, because the date moved more than once. SB24-205, a Senate Bill, set a compliance date of 1 February 2026. SB25B-004 moved it to 30 June 2026. A stipulated stay, a pause in a court case that the parties to it agree to, then suspended enforcement before that date arrived. While that pause held, the duties the law set were not enforced.
SB26-189 then replaced the entire framework, effective 1 January 2027. An effective date is the date a law starts to apply. A statute is a law passed by a legislature. The new bill stripped out the risk management program and impact assessment requirements. Those requirements had been the compliance spine of the earlier statute, meaning the part most of the compliance work hung on. A risk management program is a standing process for finding and reducing risk. An impact assessment is a written study of a system’s effects.
An organization that built to either of the first two dates built toward obligations that a later date changed again. An organization that built the risk-management architecture the original statute required built infrastructure that a documentation-and-disclosure regulation does not ask for. A documentation-and-disclosure regulation is one whose main demands are records and telling people what a system does. Two years of preparation produced compliance readiness for a law that never took effect in the form the organization prepared for.
The EU failure and the Colorado failure share one root cause. Each treats a regulatory date as if it had the certainty of a plan. A date is only one changeable input into a plan. A plan built correctly treats the date as the best current estimate of when an obligation takes effect. The estimate can be revised the moment new information arrives.
The underlying governance work goes on its own schedule. That work is the inventory, the classification, the risk assessment, and the documentation. It goes forward whichever specific date currently governs. The date decides when the work must be finished.

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
text:
18.2 Horizon scanning
Horizon scanning is the routine that keeps a governance program from being surprised by changes like those in section 18.1. Its structure is the one every other governance process uses. It has defined sources and a cadence, which is a set schedule for checking them. It has a triage step. It also has a translation step, which turns what is found into something the rest of the program can act on and eventually close.
The process also needs a named owner and a defined set of roles. Table 18.1 names the roles and the part of the work each one owns.
Table 18.1. Horizon-scanning roles







Role
Responsibility




Scanning owner
Collects the information.


Qualified analyst
Assesses the information’s status and whether it applies.


Legal counsel
Owns the authoritative legal interpretation where one is needed, meaning the reading of the law that the organization will stand behind. That way the first person who read the source does not decide what it means.


Owners of the affected systems
Assess the impact.


Business owners, the managers responsible for the work those systems support
Assess the impact as well.


Authorized decision-maker, someone the organization has put in charge of this kind of call
Approves the resulting action.


Assurance, an independent check
For a material change, which is one that matters to the organization, validates that closure happened. It does not accept a status update at face value.



Source selection means choosing a specific, finite set of places where regulatory change will appear before it reaches general news coverage. There are five, and Table 18.2 lists them. A docket is the public file of items in a case or a proceeding. A jurisdiction is a place with its own laws, such as a state or country. Litigation means a court case.
Table 18.2. The five horizon-scanning sources







Source
What it is




The relevant regulator’s own rulemaking docket
The regulator’s public file of the rules it is working on.


A legislative tracking service for each jurisdiction where the organization operates
A service that follows bills as they move through a legislature.


The bulletins of industry associations
The notices a trade body sends its members.


A small number of standards bodies, for the frontier obligations that attach to the most advanced AI models
Bodies that write the technical standards an industry agrees to use.


The court docket for any litigation testing an obligation already in force
The public file of that court case.



The standards bodies’ work decides when a conformity presumption, a rule that treats a product as compliant if it follows an agreed standard, becomes available at all. The court docket is the source that would have surfaced Colorado’s stipulated stay directly, rather than the later docket that replaced the statute the stay had paused.
Reading whatever a general news feed happens to surface is not horizon scanning. It is reacting to whatever a search algorithm ranked as top news, weeks after the docket entry that mattered was filed.
Each source record should also hold the source’s own authoritative text. It should hold the publisher, the version, the status, the date, and a stable locator as well. A stable locator is a reference that keeps pointing to the same document. A secondary summary of a rule is not the same kind of evidence as the rule itself. Section 18.3 sets the mapping card out in full and shows why this matters when a source feeds one. A mapping card holds one regulation’s own test for whether that regulation applies to a given system.
Cadence is a risk decision, and no universal fixed interval fits it. No single schedule catches every kind of change with enough lead time to matter. A final rule is a regulator’s finished rule, as opposed to a proposed one. A security directive is an order from an authority requiring security steps to be taken. A court order, a final rule, a security directive, and a supplier’s contract notice do not arrive on the same clock as a legislative tracking service. Provider, supplier, and vendor all mean the outside company that supplies a system.
The right design sets a service level for each source and each obligation. A service level is a target for how quickly the organization notices and acts. The design uses automated alerts where an authoritative source provides them. It uses scheduled review for slower-moving sources. It uses event-driven escalation for court orders, final rules, incidents, and provider notices. A provider notice is word from the supplying company that something has changed. Escalation means sending the issue up to the people who must decide. Checking every source on the same calendar ignores how fast each source moves.
Triage means sorting items by how urgently they need action. It is more than a two-way split between what to watch and what to act on immediately. Two cases show why. A proposal’s own lead time, the time before it would take effect, can be shorter than the time a response would need. A signed law can also turn out not to apply to the organization, the actor, the system, the territory, or the date at all. An actor here is a party in a legal role, such as the maker or the user of a system.
A workable triage scores each item on the authority of its source and on its legal status, meaning how far it has got toward being law. It also scores applicability, meaning whether the law reaches this organization at all, and how likely the item is to take effect as written. Triage then scores the item’s lead time, its impact if it takes effect, and its reversibility, how easily a step taken now could be undone. It scores what else depends on the item and the actual decision deadline.
Triage then assigns the item to one of several states, not only two. The states are watch, analyze, prepare, implement, challenge, pause, and close. Challenge means contest it. A proposed bill can land in prepare rather than watch when it has a short statutory lead time and a high probability of passage. A statutory lead time is the time a law itself allows before its duties take hold. A signed law that does not reach the organization’s own actors or systems can close without ever becoming an active change request. A change request is a tracked internal task for responding to a change.
Translation connects horizon scanning to every other part of the governance work. A regulatory change that clears triage becomes a tracked change request. The request carries, at minimum, its owner, scope, source, legal status, applicability analysis, and decision. It also carries implementation evidence (proof that the change was actually made), validation (a separate check that it works), and a closure date. Chapter 15 already set out this same kind of record for requirements in general. A tracked request differs from a fact noted in an email and left to whoever remembers it when the next audit runs.
Some problems must not stall silently. A missed deadline escalates. So does a conflicting authority, a source the organization cannot get hold of, a failed control, or scope that stays unclear. The responses available, depending on what the escalation finds, are a restriction, a pause, a rollback, seeking relief (asking the authority to ease the obligation), or retiring the system. A restriction cuts back what the system is allowed to do.
Closure records what the change revealed. When the case shows that the source list, the cadence, or the mapping structure missed something, closure updates it. The outcome is not filed away unexamined.
The change record must also reach the rest of the program. It does not end at the horizon-scanning desk. A change that alters a system’s applicable duties needs the same authority Chapter 17 gives to a target-model change. A target-model change is a change to how the governance work itself is set up. A change that starts in a supplier’s own notice, rather than a regulator’s, needs the handling Chapter 16 set out for suppliers. A supplier-initiated change is one the supplier starts rather than the regulator. An organization that has both need not unify them into a single schema, which is a fixed layout for a record. Keeping the two record types separate, each cross-referencing the other, is a reasonable working choice.
The Colorado sequence illustrates the complete lifecycle, not only the translation step. First, a well-run horizon-scanning practice opens a change request when SB25B-004 passes. The source is the bill text and its enactment date. The applicability is the organization’s Colorado-covered systems. The decision is to prepare toward the amended date.
Second, the practice revises that request at the stipulated stay. The record states that enforcement was suspended while the underlying obligation was not yet repealed. The decision is to pause implementation while keeping the assessment work already done.
Third, the practice closes the original request and opens a new one when SB26-189 is enacted. The record states that the prior statute was repealed and replaced. Applicability is analyzed again against the new statute’s different duties. The decision is to rebuild the change record from the new statute’s text instead of carrying the old one forward.
Each version is dated, retained, and tied to the same underlying system records. A later question about what the organization believed it had to comply with, and when, then has an answer. The answer traces to a specific source and decision, not to memory.

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
text:
18.3 Regulation-agnostic design
Regulation-agnostic design means a design that does not depend on any single regulation. Chapter 3 set out the mechanism this section extends. One shared fact record, describing what a system is and does, supports one mapping rule for each applicable regulation. Each regulation’s own mapping rule is kept on its own mapping card. Each regulation’s own dated trigger, which is the condition that makes its rules apply, is evaluated against those facts independently. No jurisdiction’s conclusion is fed into another’s rule as if it were itself a fact.
Sections 18.1 and 18.2 add the case this mechanism was built for. A regulation’s own trigger is not a fixed input. It is itself subject to delay, amendment, or full repeal and reenactment, as in Colorado’s sequence. Colorado’s statute, New York City’s Local Law 144, and every other regulation that might apply to the same system each define their own covered objects, actors, triggers, exclusions, and duties. The New York City law is a city law rather than a state or national law. Covered objects are the things a law applies to. Each regulation can also change on its own schedule, without the others moving at all.







Figure 19.1: Figure 18.1. Regulation-agnostic mapping architecture



Read Figure 18.1 as three connected structures, not one. The first is a fact record that never states a legal conclusion. The second is a set of independent mapping cards, one for each applicable regulation. Each card runs its own dated legal trigger against the same shared facts. The third is a change-handling structure. It treats a legal change and a system-fact change as two separate kinds of event. Both feed the same later steps of analysis, decision, and closure.
When a regulation changes, only that regulation’s mapping card is updated. The change may be a delay, an amendment, or a full repeal and reenactment, as in Colorado. The fact record does not change because the law changed. It describes what the system does and to whom. It does not say what any particular law currently calls that.
A change in the system’s own facts is the other way into the change-handling structure. Examples are a new population, an added capability, or a different deployment location. That second entry exists to force one step. Every regulation’s mapping card is re-evaluated against the new facts. An old classification is not assumed to still hold.
Chapter 2’s point about regulatory machinery applies here too. A mapping card’s trigger test has to be built from the regulation’s own words, whether in the statute or in an annex. It must not be built from a paraphrase. An annex is an attached schedule or list that forms part of a law. Building the test that way means someone has to have read the specific provision the card points to. A card built from a paraphrase gives the wrong answer as soon as the regulation’s own text differs from the short in-house wording the organization uses.
Each mapping card should be a dated, versioned artifact with its own legal-review and next-review fields. That lets an organization answer, months or years later, which obligations applied to a given system under a given regulation on a given date. The horizon-scanning record of section 18.2 and the mapping structure set out here together are built to answer that question without reconstruction from memory.

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
text:
18.4 What stays stable
Regulations use different words for similar things. One may call a document a data protection impact assessment, another an AI impact assessment, and another may not name it at all. A data protection impact assessment is a written study of the risks of a data use. Beneath this vocabulary, a small set of reusable governance capabilities recurs across many of the frameworks the earlier chapters examined.
These capabilities do not recur as identical legal duties. A specific regulation may require a capability in full. It may require only a narrower piece of it. It may permit the capability without requiring it, or omit it entirely. This section names the capabilities themselves. It does not claim that every regulation demands each one alike. There are seven.
Table 18.3. Seven recurring governance capabilities









Capability
Chapter
What it is
How regulations treat it




Know what you have
Chapter 3
An inventory, a list of an organization’s AI systems. It is useful whichever regulation asks for one.
Several of the regulations covered earlier require it directly.


Assess before deploying
Chapter 14
An impact or risk assessment. It is good practice even where no specific statute names it.
Several frameworks require one in some form.


Test for disparate effect
Chapter 7
Checking whether a system affects some groups of people worse than others, which is fairness testing.
Several frameworks for consequential decisions ask a version of this question. Not every applicable regulation imposes a testing duty of its own.


Document
Chapter 15
The evidence discipline, which produces a record.
Several regulations ask an organization to produce that record on demand. Some regulations require less documentation than others.


Oversee
Chapter 8
A human review point, a place where a person checks what the system decided.
It appears under several frameworks that govern automated decisions about people. The scope of required oversight varies by regulation and by use case.


Monitor
Chapter 9
Ongoing monitoring of performance and drift, the gradual change in how a system performs over time. It answers whether a system still behaves the way its initial assessment assumed.
Few regulations mandate monitoring in that specific form. A well-run program benefits from it regardless.


Respond
Chapter 10
The incident process the notification duties assume is already in place.
Several regulations place a notification duty, a duty to tell someone what happened, on an organization after a breach or a serious incident. Notification triggers, deadlines, and recipients differ by regulation.



Consequential decisions are decisions with major effects on people. The disparate-effect question may be named algorithmic discrimination, disparate impact, or an equal-opportunity standard. Those are three different legal names for versions of the same question.
These seven capabilities overlap across frameworks. A program built on the whole set can survive a regulation changing its name for a requirement, changing its threshold, or changing its entire enforcement architecture. Enforcement architecture means the whole arrangement by which a law is enforced. The inventory, the assessment, the testing, the documentation, the oversight point, the monitoring, and the incident process stay useful infrastructure. They do so whichever regulation’s vocabulary currently describes them.
This is a claim about what the capabilities make available to an organization when a regulation changes. The book has no documented finding about how organizations that held Colorado’s replaced statute fared.
Such a program loses the specific vocabulary and the specific threshold when a regulation changes. The mapping structure in section 18.3 is built to absorb both. The program keeps the underlying capability the vocabulary was describing. That holds provided the new regulation’s own trigger is checked against the capability and is not assumed to match the old regulation’s.

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
text:
18.5 The profession
What this field asks of its practitioners is a specific, uncommon combination of four qualities. It does not ask for any one deep specialization.
The first quality is technical literacy without technical expertise. The practitioner understands how a model is built, tested, and deployed. That is enough to ask a developer a real question and to recognize an answer that dodges it. The practitioner does not need to be able to build the model personally.
The second quality is legal literacy without legal training. The practitioner understands how an obligation is structured and habitually reads a statute’s own text, not a secondary summary of it. That is enough to spot an issue and gather the relevant facts. It also means being able to draft a candidate mapping rule for section 18.3’s structure. The draft does not become authoritative on its own.
Spotting the issue and gathering the evidence are different activities from giving the authoritative legal interpretation. A mapping rule needs a named, qualified legal owner. It needs a documented review before it governs a live system. It needs a clear path for sending a disputed reading up for decision, and a way to appeal that decision. It must not rest on whichever practitioner drafted it first.
The third quality is the skill to tell real risk from theater, activity that looks like governance without reducing risk. Chapter 17 named this distinction. It now applies to an entire regulatory landscape, not to one program. The practitioner has to be able to tell a real new obligation from a compliance vendor’s marketing about one.
The fourth quality is standing to say no. It is the rarest of the four, and no amount of technical or legal literacy substitutes for it. It is not a personal trait that some practitioners happen to have. It is an authority the organization has to hand over in writing. The written grant needs its own scope, its own review, and its own escalation path. It has to exist before the moment it is needed. Then a business sponsor can hear that a deployment will not proceed as designed from someone the organization has agreed in advance can say so. A business sponsor is the manager whose budget and goals the deployment serves. The sponsor does not discover, in the moment, that no one clearly can.
Where the discipline is heading remains unsettled on more than one axis. The first axis is US federal law. The United States Senate stripped a proposed decade-long moratorium on state AI enforcement from a 2025 budget reconciliation bill by a vote of 99 to 1. A moratorium is a ban on acting for a set period. Federal preemption means federal law overriding state law. The vote is the clearest available evidence that senators divide on federal preemption for reasons other than which party they belong to. An organization operating across US states therefore cannot assume that federal action will simplify the current patchwork of state law on any predictable timeline.
The second axis is Colorado itself. Its rulemaking on the replacement statute was still in progress as of 13 September 2026. Rulemaking is the process of writing the detailed rules under a statute. The Attorney General’s public comment period on the draft rules was open, and a revised draft of those rules had not yet appeared. Colorado, whose sequence is the central example here, has not finished settling its own rules.
Either of these two developments may have resolved by the time a reader arrives. The account of that development here should then be read as a demonstration of the horizon-scanning discipline of section 18.2. The account does not claim that the landscape has stopped moving.

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
text:
18.6 From compliance to advantage
Chapter 4 argued that a governance program’s cost is best justified when it stops a system that should never have been built. Left alone, such a system can eat a year of engineering time before someone finally asks whether it should exist. Governance that instead spends its effort documenting the right system after the fact protects the organization’s evidentiary position, which is its ability to prove what it did and why. It does not prevent the more expensive failure that a wrong system produces in the first place.
This is the book’s rationale for where governance’s value concentrates. It is not a demonstrated finding independent of the argument that produced it. Stating it plainly as a rationale is worth more than dressing it in the language of competitive differentiation, the claim that governance puts a company ahead of its rivals. The evidence available to the book does not support that language. No rigorous, generalizable finding establishes that AI governance produces a market advantage that can be told apart from ordinary risk avoidance. A reader who wants that specific claim should look elsewhere for it.

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
section: Case in focus: three systems, three years later
text:
Case in focus: three systems, three years later
MEDASSIST · FAIRLEND · TALENTSCREEN · Hypothetical, following the running cases
Northfield, Meridian, and Calloway are the invented organizations in the three running cases. MedAssist’s community hospital gap was the delayed alerts for sepsis, a dangerous reaction to infection. The gap was between two sites, a community hospital and an academic center. Chapter 10 traced the delays to three parallel contributing factors spanning testing, monitoring, and process. The gap prompted the remediation described earlier. Northfield then tried to demonstrate compliance under Chapter 15’s evidence discipline. That effort showed that the underlying acceptance criteria, the standards a system must meet to be accepted, had never been written down. Northfield has since written them.
Does performance for the community hospital population now match performance at the academic center? Or does the record only look cleaner than before? That question cannot be answered from outside Northfield’s own ongoing monitoring. Northfield’s governance function cannot answer it with full confidence yet either. A single remediation cycle is not a demonstrated pattern across the population the original gap affected.
FairLend had a boundary dispute between AI governance and model risk management, the existing practice of controlling the risks of the models an organization uses. Chapter 13 traced the eighteen-month process. That dispute resolved into the working division of authority that the chapter described. The division has held for the deployments that have gone through it since.
Chapter 13 itself acknowledged that some future case will eventually fall on the boundary and not cleanly on one side of it. Whether the division holds in that case remains untested. Meridian has not yet had one.
TalentScreen’s governance program now runs a properly tiered process across all three of Calloway’s systems in that composite case, one put together from more than one situation rather than drawn from a single one. A tiered process gives each system a level of oversight that fits its risk. Chapter 17 described the program’s sequencing failure and correction. What Calloway has not yet done is extend the same tiered discipline to whatever it adds to its portfolio next. The argument there was that a target operating model earns nothing by existing on paper for a system count that has already grown past it. A target operating model is the planned way the governance work is organized.
Calloway’s inventory, per Chapter 3’s original finding, was incomplete the first time anyone looked for shadow AI, meaning AI tools used without the organization’s knowledge. This book gives no reason to believe that a single look ever finds everything. Calloway’s next inventory sweep is not guaranteed to find nothing new either.
None of the three organizations has reached a finished state, and none should expect to. A governance program that considered any of these three resolved would be showing the theater Chapter 17 warned against. It would treat seeing no problem right now as proof that there is no problem.

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
text:
Summary
Compliance calendars fail because a regulatory date is a changeable estimate and not a plan. Over-investing against a date treated as fixed comes from the same mistake as under-investing against a date treated as already moved. The EU’s 2026 delay and Colorado’s repeal-and-reenactment sequence show a pattern the legal record documents. What any specific organization did in response is inference, not observed finding.
Horizon scanning turns the underlying risk into a manageable operating discipline with a named owner and defined actors. Its sources are selected for where change appears first. Its cadence is set by risk and source volatility, which is how often and how fast a source changes. It does not use one fixed interval. Its triage step scores authority, applicability, probability, lead time, and reversibility, and it sorts items into more than a simple watch-or-act split. It also translates what clears triage into a tracked, dated change request. The request is carried through implementation, validation, and closure.
Regulation-agnostic design keeps a stable, regulation-neutral fact record separate from each regulation’s own independently evaluated mapping card. A regulation change touches only that regulation’s card. No regulation’s own legal conclusion, such as a “high risk” label, is treated as another regulation’s input.
Beneath any specific regulation’s vocabulary, a set of reusable governance capabilities recurs, though not as identical legal duties. They are knowing what you have, assessing before deploying, testing for disparate effect, documenting, overseeing, monitoring, and responding. Any given regulation may require, permit, narrow, or omit each one. A program built on this capability set is positioned to keep that infrastructure useful when a regulation’s name, threshold, or entire enforcement architecture changes.
The field asks its practitioners for four qualities. The first is technical literacy without technical expertise. The second is legal literacy without legal training, kept separate from authoritative legal interpretation and backed by a qualified legal owner. The third is the skill to tell real risk from theater. The fourth is the standing to say no, which is a delegated authority granted in advance and not a personal trait.
The direction of the discipline remains unsettled on more than one axis. This book’s own argument is that governance earns its return primarily by preventing the wrong system from being built in the first place. The book states this as a rationale. It does not present it as a demonstrated business case, because the evidence does not yet support one.

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
text:
Review questions
COMPREHENSION

Explain the shared root cause behind over-investing against a regulatory date treated as immovable and under-investing against a date treated as already settled before it is law.
Explain why horizon-scanning cadence should follow source volatility and risk, not a single fixed interval. Then describe two triage states, beyond watching only or acting only, that a proposal or a signed law might legitimately be assigned to.

APPLIED

A system’s fact record shows an employment use case with a given autonomy, scale, and affected population. Explain why that record should not itself store a conclusion such as “high risk.” Then explain what changes, and what does not change, in the system’s governance record when a regulation governing that use case is repealed and replaced with a different framework.
Using the reusable governance capabilities named in section 18.4, identify which chapter of this book originally established each capability. Then explain why a specific regulation might require, permit, narrow, or omit any one of them rather than imposing an identical duty.

SPOT THE RISK

A governance program treats a proposed but not yet enacted regulatory delay as though compliance work against the original date can stop immediately. Identify what is at risk in that decision and what a properly run horizon-scanning triage step would have done differently.

COMPARE AND DECIDE

Compare classifying a system separately under each applicable regulation against classifying it once and maintaining a mapping to each regulation’s obligations, for an organization operating across multiple jurisdictions whose laws change independently of each other, and state which approach this book favors and why.

RUNNING CASE

MEDASSIST FAIRLEND TALENTSCREEN Using the case in focus, explain why none of the three organizations’ governance programs should be described as finished. Then explain what risk that description would create if a governance program believed it.


Every chapter in this book has argued, in its own subject, for the same underlying discipline. Know what a system is before deciding what to do about it. Assess before deploying. Design controls in proportion to what is at stake. Keep the evidence that lets the organization demonstrate, not just believe, that it did these things. The specific laws this book has cited will have moved again by the time it is read. That discipline is what was meant to survive the move.

title: Appendix A: Technique Reference
text:
The chapters apply several general information-gathering and analysis techniques without teaching them from first principles. This appendix is a pointer to what each technique is, when a chapter uses it, and where to look for a fuller treatment, not a substitute for learning any of them properly. Ordinary versions of most techniques assume a cooperative subject, and governance work frequently does not have one. Two techniques get real, worked treatment in their chapters instead of a pointer here for exactly that reason, consulting stakeholders who cannot be reached (Chapter 14, section 14.2) and questioning a vendor who has reason not to answer (Chapter 16, section 16.3). Look there, not here, for those two.
Affinity grouping. Sorting a large number of individually generated ideas, findings, or complaints into a smaller number of natural categories by inspecting them for similarity, not by imposing a category scheme in advance that the raw material might not actually fit. Use it after a brainstorming session or an open-ended survey has produced more individual items than a group can usefully discuss one at a time. See Chapter 3’s shadow AI discovery, where individually reported tools have to be grouped before they can be classified. For further reading, see any general text on qualitative data analysis.
Benchmarking. Comparing a system, a metric, or a process against a defined reference point, either an industry norm, a prior version of the same system, or a stated target, to establish whether a result is good, typical, or concerning. Use it when a number needs context to be interpretable on its own. See Chapter 7’s testing thresholds and Chapter 9’s drift baselines. For further reading, see any general text on quality measurement or statistical process control.
Brainstorming. Structured group generation of options or possibilities before evaluating any of them, deliberately separating idea generation from idea judgment so early criticism does not suppress options a group would otherwise have surfaced. Use it when a risk list, a use case list, or a set of candidate controls needs to be wide before it needs to be right. See Chapter 3’s inventory discovery and Chapter 14’s risk identification. For further reading, see any general text on group facilitation or creative problem solving.
Checklist review. Verifying a deliverable or a decision against a predefined, fixed list of required elements, catching omissions a less structured review would miss. It suits anything with a stable, enumerable set of requirements, such as a documentation package or a release gate. See Chapter 8’s deployment readiness review and Appendix C’s templates generally. For further reading, see any general text on quality assurance methods.
Decision matrix. A table scoring a small number of candidate options against a fixed set of weighted criteria, producing a total score per option that makes the basis for a comparison explicit instead of leaving it implicit in a group’s unstated intuitions. A weighted total is only as sound as the assumptions behind it. It assumes the scales across criteria are comparable and that a high score on one criterion can offset a low score on another. That assumption does not hold for a legal, safety, or rights requirement, which a low overall score should never be allowed to outweigh. Use it whenever more than two options are genuinely under consideration, the criteria that matter can be named in advance, and normalized scales are used. Run a sensitivity check to confirm the ranking survives reasonable changes in the weights. Apply any non-negotiable constraint as a gate before scoring, not by folding it into the score itself. See Chapter 6’s model selection factors and Chapter 13’s operating model comparison. For further reading, see any general text on multi-criteria decision analysis.
Document analysis. Extracting information from existing written material, policies, contracts, model cards, prior incident reports, rather than generating new information through interviews or observation. Use it before a live consultation whenever the timeline allows, since a question already answered in an existing document should not consume a stakeholder’s time, but do not let it delay input that is urgent on its own terms. An affected person’s immediate concern, an incident still unfolding, or a decision on a short deadline should not wait on a document review that could run in parallel instead. See Chapter 15’s evidence discipline and Chapter 16’s model card interrogation. For further reading, see any general text on qualitative research methods.
Facilitated workshop. A structured group session, run by a neutral facilitator, that brings multiple stakeholders together to reach a shared output, a classification scheme, a risk register, a target operating model, in one coordinated session instead of through separate interviews later reconciled by hand. Use it when the output requires agreement across roles, not aggregation of separate opinions. See Chapter 13’s operating model design and Chapter 17’s requirements gathering. For further reading, see any general text on group facilitation technique.
Five whys. A root cause technique that asks “why” repeatedly against a stated problem, each answer prompting the next why, until the questioning reaches a cause the organization can actually act on rather than a symptom one level removed from it. A single chain of whys tends to find one cause, but an incident, especially one involving people, process, and a system together, more often has several interacting contributory factors. Framing the technique as a search for the one root cause can end the inquiry too early. Or it can land on an individual’s action as the answer, when the actual conditions that made that action likely deserve equal attention. Use it when an incident’s immediate cause is obvious but its underlying cause is not. Treat multiple branches as a normal outcome, not a failure of the technique, and direct the questioning at conditions and system design instead of at assigning blame to a person. See Chapter 10’s incident investigation. For further reading, see any general text on root cause analysis, including fishbone or cause-and-effect diagramming as a related technique.
Focus group. A moderated group discussion with a small number of participants selected for a shared characteristic relevant to the question, used to surface reactions, concerns, or usability problems that individual interviews might not reveal through group dynamics alone. Use it when the goal is understanding a shared experience, not gathering independent facts. See Chapter 8’s pilot feedback and Chapter 17’s rollout evaluation. For further reading, see any general text on qualitative research methods.
Gap analysis. Comparing a current state against a defined target state and naming the specific, itemized distance between them, rather than describing either state in isolation. It fits whenever a target has been defined and the question becomes what stands between here and there. See Chapter 17’s current-to-target sequencing. For further reading, see any general text on organizational change management.
Interview, structured and semi-structured. A one-on-one or small-group conversation using a prepared set of questions, asked consistently across participants in a structured interview or adapted in response to what a participant says in a semi-structured one. Use a structured interview when comparability across participants matters most; use a semi-structured one when depth on an individual participant’s specific situation matters more than strict comparability. See Chapter 3’s inventory interviews, Chapter 14’s stakeholder consultation, and Chapter 17’s requirements gathering. For further reading, see any general text on interview technique in applied research.
Observation. Watching how people actually perform a task, in its ordinary setting, instead of asking them to describe it afterward, on the reasoning that a description of a workflow and the workflow itself frequently diverge without anyone intending to mislead. Use it whenever a workaround or an informal practice is suspected but has not been reported. See Chapter 17’s requirements gathering from what people do when a process becomes inconvenient. For further reading, see any general text on contextual inquiry or ethnographic method.
Peer review. Having a person with comparable expertise, but no direct authorship stake in the work, examine a decision, a document, or a finding before it is finalized. The reasoning is that a second qualified reader catches errors the original author’s own familiarity with the material makes hard to see. Reach for it when a finding will be relied on downstream, a classification decision, a risk score, an audit result, and a single unreviewed judgment carries more consequence than the added time a second reader costs. See Chapter 17’s discussion of a second reviewer disagreeing with the first as an outcome metric for whether classification is accurate. For further reading, see any general text on quality assurance in professional practice.
Prioritization scale. A method for ranking a list of items, risks, requirements, findings, into a small number of tiers by relative importance, forcing an explicit comparison instead of leaving every item marked equally important. A ranking assumes the items compared are the kind of thing capacity can trade off against each other. That is not true of a legal, safety, or rights duty, which the organization has no discretion to deprioritize regardless of where it lands on the list. Exclude those items from the ranking exercise, and treat them as required, not just highly ranked. Use it whenever the remaining, genuinely discretionary list is longer than an organization’s capacity to act on all of it at once, which is nearly always. See Chapter 14’s forced risk-ranking tiebreak and Chapter 15’s requirement priority field. For further reading, see any general text on requirements prioritization technique.
Process mapping. Diagramming the sequence of steps a workflow actually follows, including decision points and handoffs between roles, to make a process visible and discussable instead of implicit in individual habit. A map limited to steps and handoffs omits the evidence, controls, exceptions, and ownership a governance process also needs; add those elements before treating the map as complete. Use it before redesigning any workflow, so the redesign changes a documented reality rather than an assumed one. See Chapter 17’s control and workflow design. For further reading, see any general text on business process modeling.
RACI matrix. A table assigning, for each significant activity, exactly who is Responsible for doing the work, who is Accountable for the outcome, who must be Consulted before a decision, and who merely needs to be Informed after one. It resolves the ambiguity that produces both duplicated effort and dropped responsibility. “Exactly one accountable person per activity” is the matrix’s own operating convention rather than a universal organizational rule. It needs reconciling with a governing body’s oversight accountability, an executive’s ultimate accountability, and a control or assurance function’s independent accountability for checking the work, none of which a single RACI row is built to represent on its own. Use it whenever more than one role could plausibly own a task and the organization has not yet said which one does, alongside whatever governance and assurance accountability already sits above the activity level. See Chapter 13’s incident-response responsibility assignment. For further reading, see any general text on project or program governance.
Risk matrix. A grid plotting likelihood against severity, used to compare and prioritize risks on two dimensions simultaneously instead of collapsing them into a single combined score that hides which factor is driving a risk’s position. The ordinal categories a matrix typically uses, low, medium, high, compress a wide range of actual likelihood and severity into a small number of bins. This can rank two meaningfully different risks identically, or place a low-probability, catastrophic risk in the same cell as a frequent, minor one. Calibrate what each category actually means before using it, and treat a cell placement as a starting point for judgment rather than a finished conclusion. Set an explicit non-compensable threshold, too, such as any risk to life or an irreversible rights harm, that a matrix position alone cannot downgrade. Use it whenever a risk list needs comparison, not only enumeration, alongside a stated uncertainty about where a given risk actually falls. See Chapter 14’s risk scoring. For further reading, see Cox, “What’s Wrong with Risk Matrices?”, Risk Analysis 28(2), 2008, on the technique’s known ranking and categorization limits.
Sampling. Examining a subset of a population, selected either randomly or purposively, when examining the full population is impractical. Random selection on its own does not guarantee a representative or statistically defensible estimate. It requires a clearly defined sampling frame that actually covers the population of interest, a known or estimated probability of inclusion for each unit, and a stated plan for handling nonresponse or missing cases. Where the frame or response pattern is uneven, it also requires weighting to correct for it, together with a reported margin of uncertainty rather than a single point estimate presented as exact. Use random sampling, built this way, when the goal is a defensible estimate across the whole population; use purposive sampling when the goal is understanding specific, known cases of concern, and do not present a purposive sample’s findings as population-representative. See Chapter 9’s sampling-with-adjudication approach to delayed ground truth. For further reading, see any general text on sampling methodology in applied statistics.
Stakeholder mapping. Identifying every person or role with a genuine stake in a decision or a system, and characterizing each by their level of influence over the outcome and their level of interest in it. This lets engagement effort be allocated deliberately, not defaulted to whoever is easiest to reach. Influence and interest alone systematically underweight a person or group who is significantly affected by a system’s outputs but holds little organizational power over it. A mapping that stops there tends to concentrate engagement effort on internal stakeholders who are easy to reach, rather than on the people the system actually affects. Add the population’s expected impact, any heightened vulnerability, relevant rights, and the practical barriers a given group faces to participating at all. Use those added dimensions to correct engagement effort toward low-power, high-impact groups, instead of away from them. Use it at the start of any consultation effort, before deciding who to interview, survey, or convene. See Chapter 14’s stakeholder consultation and Chapter 17’s requirements gathering from developers, business owners, and reviewers. For further reading, see any general text on stakeholder analysis method.
Survey and questionnaire. A structured set of questions distributed to a larger group than an interview practically reaches, trading the depth of an individual conversation for coverage across a wider population. It fits when a finding needs to be established across a population instead of illustrated through individual cases. See Chapter 17’s training completion and rollout feedback collection. For further reading, see any general text on survey design.
SWOT analysis. A structured inventory of an initiative’s internal Strengths and Weaknesses alongside external Opportunities and Threats, used to surface a rounded picture before a decision rather than only the factors that first come to mind. Use it sparingly, only where a genuinely rounded picture, not a risk list alone, is what the decision requires. See Chapter 13’s operating model selection. For further reading, see any general text on strategic planning method.
Timeline reconstruction. Assembling a dated, sequential record of what happened, decision by decision and event by event, from logs, messages, and documents produced at the time rather than from participants’ later recollection of the order events occurred in. Use it for any incident investigation or post-mortem where the sequence of decisions matters as much as the decisions themselves. See Chapter 10’s incident documentation requirement that decisions be captured with timestamps as the response unfolds. For further reading, see any general text on incident investigation method.
Traceability matrix. A table linking each requirement to the specific evidence that demonstrates it was met, making a status claim checkable against a named artifact rather than asserted on memory. Use it wherever a later reviewer, internal or regulatory, will ask an organization to demonstrate rather than simply state that a requirement was satisfied. See Chapter 15, section 15.2, for this book’s full treatment. For further reading, see any general text on requirements management.
Voting and ranking techniques. Methods, including simple ranked voting and weighted-point allocation across a fixed budget, for converting a group’s individual preferences into a single prioritized list without one person’s opinion silently dominating the outcome. As with a prioritization scale, exclude a legal, safety, or rights requirement from the vote entirely rather than letting a group’s preference ranking decide whether the organization does something it has no discretion not to do. Use it, for the genuinely discretionary remainder of a list, after brainstorming has produced more candidate items than the group can act on and a shared ranking is needed to choose among them. See Chapter 13’s operating model decision process. For further reading, see any general text on group decision-making method.

title: Appendix B: Regulatory Quick Reference
text:
The EU AI Act: tiers and obligations
This appendix is a snapshot, not a living document. Every entry below was checked against the primary source named against it, current as of 12 September 2026. Regulatory dates move. A reader consulting this appendix more than a few months after publication should treat every date here as a starting point for a horizon scan rather than as a current fact, per the discipline Chapter 18, section 18.2 describes. Where a date or status could not be confirmed against a primary source, this appendix says so instead of printing an unverified figure.
The Act regulates by risk tier and allocates duties by role, established in Chapter 2. It sets out four tiers, presented below in descending order of obligation.
Unacceptable risk (Article 5). Prohibited outright are social scoring of natural persons, certain forms of biometric categorization and untargeted facial recognition database scraping, emotion inference in workplaces and schools, and exploitation of vulnerabilities. The 2026 Digital Omnibus added two more to the list, AI systems generating non-consensual sexually explicit deepfakes of identifiable people and AI-generated child sexual abuse material. The social-scoring prohibition reaches any deployer, public or private, not public authorities alone.
High risk (Article 6, Annexes I and III). The Act’s most detailed obligation set applies here, requiring a risk management system, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency to deployers, human oversight, and accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity. These obligations fall primarily on providers, with a narrower set on deployers. Annex III lists standalone high-risk use cases directly, including employment, creditworthiness, and law enforcement contexts this book’s running cases inhabit. Annex I covers high-risk AI embedded in products already regulated under EU product safety law.
Limited risk (Article 50). Article 50 attaches transparency duties to specific systems and actors, not to a residual bucket covering everything outside the other tiers. Providers and deployers must disclose that a person is interacting with an AI system, label synthetic content, and disclose deepfakes and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest.
Minimal risk. Everything else, unregulated by the Act’s risk tiers, though general-purpose AI model obligations under Chapter V apply regardless of the risk tier of any downstream system built on such a model.

One standard, covering the quality management system obligation, cleared CEN-CENELEC’s own internal approval in mid-2026, which is a necessary step toward Official Journal citation but is not the citation itself. Do not treat a standard’s internal publication by a standards body as equivalent to its legal effect under the Act; only Official Journal citation confers the presumption.

title: Appendix B: Regulatory Quick Reference
section: EU AI Act conformity assessment routes
text:
EU AI Act conformity assessment routes
A high-risk system reaches the market through one of two routes. Internal control lets a provider self-assess conformity against the Act’s requirements and issue its own declaration, available for most Annex III use cases where a harmonized standard has been applied or where the provider can otherwise demonstrate the requirements are met. Third-party conformity assessment, through a notified body, is required for biometric identification systems and for products already subject to third-party assessment under other EU product law, such as medical devices. A provider using internal control still bears full legal responsibility for the system’s conformity; the absence of third-party review changes who checks the work, not what work must be done.

title: Appendix B: Regulatory Quick Reference
text:
United States: federal landscape
No single, complete federal AI statute has been enacted as of this appendix’s check date. Federal AI policy operates through executive action and agency guidance, not legislation. Executive Order 14365 set federal AI policy direction. Litigation testing its interaction with state law, including a challenge to Colorado’s now-superseded statute, produced a stipulated stay of enforcement rather than any ruling on the merits. No US court has ruled on the merits of a challenge to a state AI law as of the check date. A proposed decade-long moratorium on state AI enforcement was removed from a 2025 reconciliation bill by a 99 to 1 Senate vote. That is the clearest evidence available that federal preemption of state AI law is contested on grounds other than party. A discussion draft addressing preemption of state authority over AI model development specifically, without a bill number as of the check date, was released in mid-2026 by members of the House. Whether it has since been introduced as a numbered bill should be checked directly, not assumed either way.
NIST, an agency and not a legislature, has published the closest thing to federal technical guidance. See below.

title: Appendix B: Regulatory Quick Reference
text:
NIST AI Risk Management Framework
The AI RMF (NIST AI 100-1, published January 2023) organizes risk management into four functions, each with named categories, and the table below holds each function’s purpose and categories.
The four AI RMF functions and their categories








Function
Purpose
Categories




Govern
Cultivates an organizational culture and structure for AI risk management
Policies and processes, accountability structures, workforce diversity in AI risk roles, organizational commitment to trustworthy AI characteristics, mechanisms for external stakeholder feedback, and policies addressing third-party and supply chain risk


Map
Establishes the context needed to frame risk correctly
Understanding the deployment context, categorizing the AI system, documenting its capabilities and intended benefits and costs, mapping risks and benefits across system components, and mapping impacts to individuals, groups, and society


Measure
Applies quantitative and qualitative methods to analyze and track risk
Identifying appropriate methods and metrics, evaluating the system for trustworthy characteristics including validity, safety, and fairness, tracking identified risks over time, and gathering feedback on how well the measurement approach itself is working


Manage
Allocates resources to the risks the first three functions surfaced
Prioritizing and acting on risk, applying strategies to maximize benefit and minimize harm, managing third-party risk specifically, and documenting and monitoring risk treatments over time



A companion Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, published July 2024) maps these same four functions to risks specific to generative systems, including confabulation, harmful content generation, data privacy leakage through model outputs, and intellectual property concerns among others. Both documents remained the current, unrevised versions as of this appendix’s check date. NIST has stated the framework is under revision as part of a federal AI policy initiative, so a reader should check for a newer version before treating either document’s exact category list as final.

title: Appendix B: Regulatory Quick Reference
text:
ISO/IEC 42001: clause structure
ISO/IEC 42001:2023, the AI management system standard, follows the common high-level structure shared across ISO management system standards, making it straightforward to integrate into an organization already certified to a standard such as ISO 27001 or ISO 9001. Its numbered clauses proceed, in order, through Scope, Normative references, Terms and definitions, Context of the organization, Leadership, Planning, Support, Operation, Performance evaluation, and Improvement. An Annex lists specific AI management controls and objectives, covering policies related to AI, internal organizational roles, resources dedicated to AI systems, impact assessment, and the AI system life cycle. It also covers data governance for AI systems, information provided to interested parties, use of AI systems, and third-party and customer relationships.
The European Commission and its Joint Research Centre have stated that ISO/IEC 42001, while a useful foundation for an AI management system, is not aligned in objective with the specific quality management system the EU AI Act requires. ISO/IEC 42001 requires an AI system impact assessment covering individuals, groups, and societies, but its certification is not designed to satisfy the Act’s system-specific technical documentation and quality management provisions. An organization certified to 42001 has not thereby satisfied the Act’s quality management obligation, though the certification’s processes substantially overlap with what the Act separately requires.
