title: Appendix B: Regulatory Quick Reference
text:
Sector-specific requirements
Healthcare. In the United States, whether a clinical decision support or diagnostic tool resembling this book’s MEDASSIST case needs premarket clearance or approval depends on a specific determination, not a general presumption. FDA guidance excludes certain clinical decision support functions from the statutory device definition outright, treats some other functions under enforcement discretion, and regulates the remainder as devices proportionate to risk. The same product can therefore contain both device and non-device functions. The determination has to be made function by function, against the device definition, the statutory exclusions, and current FDA guidance (checked 2026-09-13, per FDA’s Clinical Decision Support Software FAQs). Where a function is regulated as a device, ongoing obligations to report adverse events and material changes to its cleared function apply. The FDA has also issued guidance specifically addressing predetermined change control plans for AI-enabled devices whose performance is expected to update after initial clearance, directly relevant to Chapter 6’s model versioning and Chapter 9’s drift monitoring. Separately, HIPAA’s privacy and security requirements apply only where the organization is a covered entity or a business associate handling protected health information, not to health data generally or to every organization that touches it. An organization needs to determine its own HIPAA status independently of any FDA determination, since neither regulation’s applicability establishes the other’s. A product can be subject to one, both, or neither, depending on what it does and who operates it.
Financial services. In the United States, a credit decisioning system such as this book’s FAIRLEND case operates under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and its implementing Regulation B. This requires a specific and accurate statement of reasons when an application for credit is denied, the adverse action explanation this book’s Chapter 8 and Chapter 15 both address directly. Banking regulators, principally the Federal Reserve and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, have issued supervisory guidance on model risk management. This guidance predates the AI-specific frameworks this appendix otherwise covers. It is frequently the source of the model risk management function that Chapter 13 describes as a potential structural competitor to a newer AI governance function. That guidance’s scope should not be assumed to reach every AI model automatically. Interagency guidance updated in 2026 (Federal Reserve SR 26-2, effective 17 April 2026, superseding SR 11-7 and SR 21-8) applies its principles to traditional and non-generative, non-agentic AI models while expressly excluding generative and agentic AI models from that specific framework’s definition (checked 2026-09-13). An institution within SR 26-2’s scope needs to determine first whether a given system meets the guidance’s model definition before assuming existing model-risk infrastructure already covers it. A generative or agentic system excluded from that definition still needs governance, just not automatically through the model-risk-management channel. State insurance regulators separately govern algorithmic underwriting and pricing tools through unfair discrimination statutes that apply independently of any AI-specific statute a state might also enact, a survival this appendix’s Colorado entry notes directly.
Employment. Beyond the state and local statutes already listed above, the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has issued guidance applying existing anti-discrimination law, including disparate impact theory under Title VII, to algorithmic hiring tools without requiring new legislation to do so. This means an employment AI system such as this book’s TALENTSCREEN case carries discrimination-law exposure even in a jurisdiction with no AI-specific statute in effect. An organization operating in this sector should treat the absence of an AI-specific state law as silence on the new label, not an absence of applicable law.
crumbs: 21  Appendix B: Regulatory Quick Reference

title: Appendix B: Regulatory Quick Reference
text:
Using this appendix
Nothing above substitutes for reading the primary source directly before relying on any specific obligation, threshold, or date in a real compliance decision. This appendix exists to orient a reader quickly across a landscape this book has already argued, in Chapter 18, cannot be captured permanently in any single document, including this one.
This appendix deliberately omits a dated comparison of specific model capabilities across providers. Such a comparison would be obsolete within a small number of months of this book’s printing, faster than the regulatory dates above move. No comparison this appendix could print would remain a fair or current snapshot for long enough to be worth the space. A reader who needs current capability comparisons should consult a provider’s own published evaluation results, dated at the time of consultation, rather than any fixed table a printed book could offer.
crumbs: 21  Appendix B: Regulatory Quick Reference

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
1. AI Use Case Documentation
The rest of this book is all rights reserved. These fifteen templates are the deliberate exception. They are offered under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0) for readers to copy, adapt, and use directly in their own organizations. That grant covers the templates in this appendix only. Reuse under that license has to satisfy its actual conditions, not a looser summary of them. The license requires attribution and a notice of changes made. Its NonCommercial term is defined by whether the use is primarily intended for or directed toward commercial advantage or monetary compensation, a broader test than resale alone. This paragraph is a summary for convenience, not a substitute for the license text itself, which a reader relying on these templates commercially or without attribution should read directly. Within those conditions, fill in the fields, cut what your organization does not need, add what it does, and use the result as a working document instead of treating this appendix as an illustration to reference from a distance. Each field below is cross-referenced to the chapter section that establishes it, so a filled-in template can be traced back to the specific requirement it satisfies.
Each template below is scoped to hold one record for one system, model, agent, or event; an organization with many systems keeps many filled instances of the same template instead of trying to make a single instance cover a portfolio. Fields marked as cross-references exist so the fifteen templates link into one connected set of records, rather than fifteen disconnected documents. That is what lets a later reviewer trace a specific system’s history across inventory, assessment, and incident records without reconstructing the connections from memory. Because a specific chapter’s model can itself be revised in a later edition, each template also carries the same minimal record-control header. That header records a template ID and version, the book edition and chapter section it was built from, and the date it was last checked against that section’s current text. That lets a later reviewer tell which version of a chapter’s model a specific filled instance was built against. Every filled instance should also carry its own status, author, reviewer, approver, effective date, and change history in addition to its substantive fields, following Chapter 15’s evidence-record discipline generally, not restating it individually in each template below.
Complete before any development or procurement work begins, per Chapter 4’s argument that governance starting after a system exists is inspection rather than governance.
crumbs: 22  Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
Use case name and one-sentence description
Business owner, naming a specific person and role, not a department alone, with the effective date this person took the role so the record stays traceable when the person changes
Problem statement, naming what decision or task this system addresses and for whom
Why an AI approach specifically, as distinct from a rules-based or manual alternative
Expected benefit, and what happens if this use case is not pursued at all
Proposed path: build, fine-tune, or buy (Chapter 6)
System class: predictive, generative, or agentic, or a mix (Chapter 3, section 3.1)
Affected population, naming who experiences this system’s outputs or actions
Decision type: recommendation to a human, or autonomous action (Chapter 3, section 3.7)
Date submitted and date entered into the system inventory below
crumbs: 22  Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
2. System Inventory Record
One record per system, maintained per Chapter 3, section 3.4, as a living artifact with an owner and a review date, not a one-time exercise. A system discovered through the shadow AI discovery process in Chapter 3, section 3.5, uses this same record; note the discovery method in the last field rather than treating a discovered system as a different kind of record.

System name and internal identifier
Business owner and technical owner (may differ)
Business unit and physical or organizational location of use
System class: predictive, generative, or agentic
Deployment status: in development, piloting, in production, retired
Model or models used (cross-reference to Model Inventory Record entries)
Data sources and categories of personal data processed, if any
Risk classification and the date it was assigned (cross-reference to Impact Assessment)
Applicable regulatory mappings (Chapter 3, section 3.8; Chapter 18, section 18.3)
Date of last review and scheduled next review date
Record owner, last update date, and, if applicable, discovery method if this system was not originally self-reported
crumbs: 22  Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
3. Model Inventory Record
One record per model, distinct from the System Inventory Record above because one model can serve several systems and one system can call several models, per Chapter 3’s system-versus-model distinction.

Model name and version identifier
Developer or source (internal build, fine-tune of a named base model, or purchased)
Path: build, fine-tune, adapter, or licensed third-party (Chapter 16, section 16.6)
Training data summary, or “not visible to this organization” where the path is buy (Chapter 5)
Intended use and explicitly out-of-scope uses
Known limitations and failure modes as currently understood
Systems this model serves (cross-reference to System Inventory Record entries)
Date last validated and validation method used
Reassessment triggers that would require re-validation (Chapter 14, section 14.5)
crumbs: 22  Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
4. Model Card
For a model an organization builds or fine-tunes itself. For a purchased model, use this same structure to record what the vendor has and has not disclosed, per Chapter 15’s adversarial reading approach, marking undisclosed fields explicitly instead of leaving them blank.

Model name, version, and date
Intended use and explicitly out-of-scope uses
Training data description, covering sources, time period, and known composition, or the vendor’s disclosed description quoted directly if this organization cannot see the underlying data
Performance metrics, the population and methodology they were measured against, and the date measured
Fairness testing summary, covering metrics used, populations compared, and findings (Chapter 7)
Known limitations and documented failure modes
Safety and refusal behavior notes, where applicable (Chapter 11)
Retraining or update history and how a user of this card is notified of changes
Contact point for questions this card does not answer
crumbs: 22  Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
5. Impact Assessment
Follow Chapter 14’s five-component structure as it stands in this book’s current text. That structure is itself the subject of ongoing refinement across this book’s own chapters, so record which edition and check date this template instance was built against rather than assuming the structure is fixed for all time. Complete before deployment, and again whenever a reassessment trigger fires. Where a stakeholder who would normally be consulted cannot be reached, record which of Chapter 14’s consultation substitutes was used instead and what it cannot recover compared to direct consultation.

System description, covering what it does, who it affects, and at what scale
Risk identification, listing each identified risk, its likelihood and severity (Chapter 14, section 14.3), and its source
Mitigation, naming the specific control addressing each risk and whether it reduces the risk’s occurrence or only detects it after the fact (Chapter 14, section 14.4)
Residual risk, stating what remains after mitigation explicitly instead of leaving it implied by silence
Documented decision, naming the accountable approver, the date, and the specific reasoning accepting the residual risk or requiring further mitigation before proceeding
Reassessment trigger conditions and next scheduled review date
Legal role and jurisdiction of each actor involved, naming who is provider, deployer, or importer under each instrument that reaches this system, since the same organization can hold different roles under different instruments (Chapter 4, section 4.8)
Duration and frequency of the processing or use, as required of a deployer under Article 27 of the AI Act and distinct from the deployment status recorded on the System Inventory Record (Chapter 4, section 4.8)
The specific authority who accepts residual risk, named as a person and role with the scope of what that person is empowered to accept, which the documented decision field above assumes but does not itself establish (Chapter 4, section 4.8)
What remains unaddressed, stated explicitly rather than left implied by the absence of an entry. An assessment listing only mitigated risks is describing an aspiration (Chapter 4, section 4.8)
Mapping from each field above to the specific provision it is meant to satisfy, per regulation. Legal sufficiency for a given instrument cannot be inferred from having completed an internal template (Chapter 4, section 4.8; Chapter 3, section 3.8)
crumbs: 22  Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
6. Vendor Assessment
Structured across Chapter 16’s four assessment dimensions, built against this book’s current chapter text and, like template 5, worth re-checking against a later edition rather than assumed fixed. Log every question the vendor declined to answer in the final field; a declined question is itself evidence.

Provider dimension, covering company stability, support commitments, and track record
System dimension, covering what the model actually does, its documented limitations, and disaggregated performance data if obtainable
Documentation dimension, covering model card completeness, per template 4 above, and what is missing
Compliance dimension, covering applicable certifications, audit rights offered, and regulatory mappings the vendor supports
Contract provisions confirmed present, covering information rights, audit rights, change notification, incident cooperation, liability allocation, and exit terms (Chapter 16, section 16.5)
Questions the vendor declined to answer, and whether each decline is disqualifying (Chapter 16, section 16.3)
Overall recommendation and named approver
crumbs: 22  Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
7. Agent Registration and Permission Scope
One record per agentic system or agent role, per Chapter 12’s argument that an agent’s authority must be recorded before it acts, not reconstructed afterward.

Agent name and the system it belongs to (cross-reference to System Inventory Record)
Issuing authority, naming who approved this agent’s credential and on what basis
Subject and audience, naming the actor the credential is issued to and the resource or party it is valid against
Scope of authority, naming the specific actions, resources, and purposes this agent is permitted to invoke without further human approval, and what is explicitly out of scope
Tools and systems this agent can access, and the permissions granted to each
Credential form and validity, describing how the scope is technically enforced (a scoped, time-bound credential per Chapter 15, section 15.5), its validity window, and its current revocation state
Policy decision point, naming what evaluates a given action against this scope at runtime and what happens on a policy denial
Escalation conditions, naming what triggers a required human-in-the-loop step and the approval and result recorded when one fires
Logging requirements, naming what is captured at each action, including the scope in force at the time of the action, a correlation ID linking related actions, and a tamper-evident integrity mark on the record (Chapter 15, section 15.5)
Monitoring, naming what ongoing check confirms this agent is not exceeding its recorded scope in practice and how an exception surfaces
Delegation chain, if this agent can invoke or supervise other agents, including each hop’s own scope and whether it can be narrower or wider than the delegating agent’s own
Review cadence and the date of last permission-scope review
Deregistration or scope-revocation process, who is authorized to invoke it, and what recovery or rollback applies to actions already taken under a credential later found to have been wrongly scoped
crumbs: 22  Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
8. Incident Response
Structured per Chapter 10’s response sequence. Open a record at the moment an incident is identified, not after it is resolved.

Incident identifier, date and time first identified, and detection source (monitoring, user report, audit, vendor notice, or other)
Accountable owner for the response, named at the point the record is opened
Severity classification and the criteria that produced it
Systems and populations affected
Evidence preservation, naming what was captured before any remediation altered the system’s state and where it is retained
Containment actions taken, and the date and time each was taken
Assessment, stating what is currently known about scope and cause, updated as it changes, including root cause and any contributory factors distinct from it (Chapter 10’s investigation approach)
Communication log, naming who was notified, when, and with what content, kept current through resolution instead of written once at closure
Regulatory reporting determination, stating whether a notification obligation applies, under which specific regulation, in what role (for example, an EU AI Act operator’s serious-incident duty under Article 73), the applicable deadline measured from awareness, and the status of any required interim and final reports
Affected-party remedy, naming what correction, compensation, or other remedy was offered or provided, to whom, and when
Rollback or recovery, naming what was reverted or restored and confirming that the reversion actually took effect
Documentation of decisions made during the response, each with a timestamp and the name of who made it
Corrective action and its verification, naming the specific process or control change the incident produced and how its effectiveness was confirmed instead of only implemented
Closure criteria met, post-incident review date, and the lesson fed back into the relevant control, template, or training material
For a system with delayed or absent ground truth (Chapter 9), the method used to establish how many cases were actually affected, since a prevented or undetected outcome leaves no confirmed case to count directly
crumbs: 22  Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
9. Governance Readiness
Per Chapter 17. Use this to conduct a current-state assessment, not to describe an aspirational future state.

Inventory assurance, meaning the percentage of known systems with a current inventory record, plus a separate estimate of unknown-system exposure from the date and method of the last discovery sweep (Chapter 3’s shadow AI discovery). A percentage of known systems alone cannot measure what the inventory has not yet found
Classification coverage, giving the percentage of inventoried systems with a current risk classification
Process versus practice, stating for each governance process that exists on paper whether it is actually used, for what proportion of applicable systems, and evidence supporting that answer (Chapter 17, section 17.2)
Requirements gathered, giving the date of last consultation with developers, business owners, and reviewers on where the process obstructs their work
Control proportionality, stating whether review depth is tied to risk tier or applied uniformly regardless of it
Cost model, stating whether each control’s cost has been estimated at production volume rather than pilot volume
Training completion, giving the percentage of each role trained and the date of last training update
Outcome metrics, covering issues found before deployment versus after, classification accuracy on independent review, and bypass rate by system and by team
Named owner of this readiness assessment and date completed
crumbs: 22  Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
10. Scope Decision Record
One record per scoping exercise, per Chapter 3, section 3.2. The boundary is a property of the deployment rather than of the software, and it moves without anyone changing the code when a step that acts on the output is added. A boundary drawn once and left unrecorded cannot be defended later or revisited when the deployment changes, which is why the decision needs its own record rather than a field on the system record it produces.

Scope decision identifier, and the system or candidate system it concerns
Date of the decision, and the person accountable for it by name and role
What triggered this scoping exercise: intake, procurement, a discovery sweep, a change to an existing deployment, or a periodic review
Description of the deployment as it actually runs, distinguished from the vendor’s description of the product
The AI component or components, which are in scope intensively and are not at issue below
For each dependency considered, its name, and the decision recorded as in scope, out of scope, or in scope at limited depth
For each dependency, the one-sentence justification, naming which of the eight materiality grounds applies: purpose, authority, data, behaviour, exposure, evidence, ability to be intervened upon, or remedy available afterward
Dependencies explicitly considered and excluded, with the reason each cannot materially affect any of the eight grounds. An exclusion with no recorded reason is an omission rather than a decision
Disagreements among those consulted, recorded rather than resolved silently, with who held which position
What would move this boundary, naming the specific changes that would require the decision to be revisited, such as a step added that acts on the output or a new population becoming affected
Cross-reference to the System Inventory Record or Records this decision produced
Record owner, last update date, and scheduled date for the next boundary review
crumbs: 22  Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
section: 11. Risk Classification and Regulatory Applicability Record
text:
11. Risk Classification and Regulatory Applicability Record
One record per system, per Chapter 3, sections 3.7 and 3.7. The two parts below answer two independent questions and must be completed in order, without the first informing the second. The internal tier is an operating decision about how much governance attention a system receives. Legal applicability is decided by each regulation’s own trigger tested against the system’s own facts. A high internal tier is not evidence that any regulation applies, and a regulation applying does not set the internal tier. The most common failure this record exists to prevent is answering the second question by restating the first.
Part A. Internal classification.

System identifier and cross-reference to its System Inventory Record
System class: predictive, generative, or agentic, or a stated mix
Consequence, stating what happens to an affected person when the system is wrong
Autonomy, stating whether the system recommends to a human or acts, and what the human can actually change in the time available
Population, naming who is affected and how many, including those affected without interacting with the system
Reversibility, stating whether an incorrect outcome can be undone, by whom, within what period, and at whose cost
How the four factors weigh for this system class specifically, per section 3.7, since the same factors do not carry the same weight across predictive, generative, and agentic systems
Internal tier assigned, and the one-sentence defence of it
Person accountable for the classification by name and role, and the date assigned

Part B. Regulatory applicability, tested independently.
Complete one block per regulation considered. Do not carry any value from Part A into these blocks.

Regulation, cited by instrument and the article or section containing the trigger
The trigger test as that instrument states it
The system’s own facts relevant to that test, drawn from the system record rather than from Part A
Result: the trigger fires, does not fire, or cannot be determined with what is currently known
If it cannot be determined, the specific question outstanding and who will answer it by when
Obligations that follow if it fires, and where the evidence of meeting each will live
Date tested, and the date this test is next due, since a trigger that does not fire today may fire when the instrument or the deployment changes

Part C. Separation check.

Confirmation that no Part B result was inferred from the Part A tier, recorded by the person who completed Part B
Any place where the two answers diverge, such as a low internal tier with a regulation that fires or a high tier with none that do. A divergence is an expected outcome of testing independently, not an error to reconcile
crumbs: 22  Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
12. Discovery Sweep Record
One record per sweep, per Chapter 3, section 3.5. What an inventory does not contain is not a random sample. Formally procured systems are visible, and what escapes correlates with small budgets, individual initiative, and the absence of the review that would have caught a problem. The method is therefore the governed object. Without a record of which channels were searched and which were not, a completed sweep cannot be distinguished from an incomplete one, and coverage cannot be shown to improve between sweeps.

Sweep identifier, start and end dates, and the person accountable for it by name and role
Scope of the sweep, naming which business units, regions, and system types were in and out
Channels searched, with the method used for each and the date searched. Channels to consider include procurement and expense records, software asset and licence inventories, low-code and automation platforms, API gateway and egress logs, browser or SaaS discovery tooling, existing vendor contracts for AI features added after signature, code repositories, and structured interviews with named roles
Channels not searched, each with the reason, whether cost, access, tooling, or a decision to defer. This field carries the sweep’s residual blind spot and is the reason the record exists
Why self-reporting alone was not relied on, per section 3.5’s finding that the people running undisclosed systems do not describe themselves as deploying AI
Systems found, with a count and a cross-reference to the System Inventory Record created for each. Record the discovery method per system in that record’s discovery field rather than here
Findings that changed an existing record rather than creating one, such as a system already inventoried that proved to contain a second component
Items examined and determined not to be in scope, with the ground, so the next sweep does not re-examine them without cause
Estimated residual exposure, reasoned from the unsearched channels rather than as a percentage of what was found. A percentage of known systems cannot measure what the sweep did not reach
What would change before the next sweep, naming channels to add and access to obtain
Date of the next scheduled sweep, and the trigger conditions that would require one sooner
crumbs: 22  Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
13. Dataset Datasheet
One record per dataset, per Chapter 5, section 5.10. The structure follows the datasheet format proposed by Timnit Gebru and colleagues in 2018, built for the case where a dataset’s later users are removed from its creators and would otherwise have no way to answer basic questions about what they are working with. The fields that make it worth keeping are the ones recording what is unknown or unresolved. A datasheet listing only what is settled describes a dataset nobody has interrogated.

Dataset identifier and version, and the models or corpora built from this version
Named owner, and the date the datasheet was last checked against the dataset itself rather than against a previous datasheet
Motivation. Why the dataset was created, by whom, and who funded it. Whether it was created for this use or repurposed from another
Composition. What each instance represents, how many there are, and what the instances do not include. Whether the dataset is a sample of a larger set, and if so how the sample was drawn, since this is where selection bias enters
Whether the data relates to people, and if so which populations, in what proportions, and measured how. Composition stated as measured rather than assumed, per section 5.6
Collection. How the data was acquired, over what period, by whom, and under what authority. Whether the subjects consented, to what, and whether that consent covers model training, per the purpose-limitation question in section 5.4
Preprocessing. Cleaning, labelling, and transformation steps, in enough detail that a later question about any field can be answered from the record instead of reconstructed. Whether the raw data was retained
Uses. What the dataset has been used for, what it should not be used for, and what about its composition makes those uses inappropriate
Distribution and maintenance. Who may receive it, under what terms, who maintains it, and how a correction or deletion propagates to everything built from it
What is unknown. Every question above that could not be answered, with the reason. A blank field is indistinguishable from an unasked question; a field reading “requested from vendor, refused, escalated” is evidence of diligence and a live item
Representativeness assessment: the deployment population this data was compared against, the dimensions compared, the result, and the decision taken on an unfavourable result, per section 5.5. Where the organization is on the buy path and cannot answer, record that as the finding
Cross-reference to the Model Inventory Records built on this dataset, and to the system records those models serve
crumbs: 22  Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
14. Model Bill of Materials
One record per model in use, per Chapter 6, section 6.8. This extends the Model Inventory Record rather than replacing it. Template 3 establishes what the model is and which systems it serves, and this record establishes what it is made of, in enough detail that the record rather than anyone’s memory answers a later question. An organization that cannot produce one cannot investigate its own system, because an investigation that cannot establish which artifact produced an output has nothing to investigate.
Mark every field with how it is known: directly verified by this organization, attested by a supplier without independent verification, or unavailable. That marking is the point of the record. A field that looks complete but rests entirely on supplier attestation describes what someone said, not what is running.
Starting minimum. A record carrying less than this cannot support an investigation.

Base model and version
The specific weights in use, identified so that the artifact running can be confirmed rather than assumed
Training or fine-tuning data, cross-referenced to its Dataset Datasheet where one exists
Adapters or fine-tuning layers, the method used, and who added them. Where the method adjusted the base weights rather than adding separable parameters, record that the two cannot be separated
Software dependencies required to run the model

Fuller record.

Artifact hashes and identifiers confirming which weights are actually running. On the selection path, where the weights are not in the organization’s possession, a hash is not obtainable; record instead the provider’s version identifier as returned at inference, the endpoint and region, the contracted service tier, and the date and content of the provider’s last change notice
Dataset versions and their provenance
Licensing terms of every component, and what each permits
Intended and prohibited uses, as the developer states them
Evaluation evidence behind every performance claim, and the claims made with no evidence behind them
Runtime environment and configuration
Upstream suppliers and service dependencies
Known limitations, and known vulnerabilities recorded separately from them
Change history producing the current version
Deployment configuration in force
crumbs: 22  Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
15. Intake Decision Record
One record per proposal, per Chapter 4, sections 4.2 and 4.7. A proposal that proceeds becomes a system with a system record. A proposal that stops, or proceeds with conditions, produces no system and therefore has no home in the inventory, which is why the hardest outcome to reach is the one the book’s records were least equipped to hold. A stop that is not recorded will be relitigated from nothing when the same proposal returns.

Proposal identifier, title, date received, and the requester by name and role
Outcome, recorded as one of: proceed, proceed with conditions, return for more information, defer with a stated review date, refer elsewhere, or stop
The person holding authority for this outcome, named, with the scope of what they were empowered to decide
For a stop: the reasoning, in enough detail that the same proposal arriving in eighteen months is assessed against what was decided rather than argued again from the beginning. Which of section 4.7’s four grounds it failed, and whether it crossed a prohibition or safety floor, in which case the analysis stopped before any benefit comparison
For conditions: each condition, its named owner, its due date, and the stated consequence of the due date passing with the condition unmet. A condition with no consequence is a note
Scrutiny level applied, and what determined it
The appropriateness assessment: data sufficiency, objective specifiability, benefit proportionality, and value alignment, each with its conclusion and the reasoning behind it
Dissent recorded rather than resolved silently, naming who held which position
Cross-references to the System Inventory Record and Impact Assessment where the proposal proceeded, and to the Scope Decision Record that bounded it
crumbs: 22  Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

title: Appendix D: Glossary
text:
Every term below is explained more fully where it first appears in the body of this book; this glossary gives a short definition and a chapter pointer for quick lookup, not the full treatment. Where this book prefers one term over a more common alternative, that preference is noted, not left unexplained.
Acceptable use policy. A policy restricting AI use that works only when paired with a sanctioned alternative competitive enough with the workaround it restricts to be chosen over it. Chapter 13.
Acceptance criteria. The element of a testable requirement stating exactly what evidence would satisfy it. Chapter 15.
Action sequence. The path of decisions and tool calls an agent takes to a result, evaluated in full because two agents can reach the same endpoint by paths of different risk. Chapter 7.
Adverse action notice. A notice required in defined credit circumstances, not only outright denial, stating the action taken and the specific principal reasons for it or how to obtain them. When reasons are given they must accurately describe the factors used, with the exact scope and timing set by the governing law and transaction. Chapter 2.
Agent registration. The record establishing an agent as an identified actor, including its origin, scope, and owner. Chapter 12.
AI governance. How an organization decides what its AI systems may do, establishes that they do it, and makes clear who answers when they do not. Chapter 1.
AI system lifecycle. This book’s full-form term for the span a system passes through, treated as three nested layers, model, system, and use case, moving at different speeds. The shorter “AI lifecycle” is avoided as misleadingly singular. Chapter 3.
Algorithmic disgorgement. Informal shorthand for an enforcement order requiring deletion of a model, algorithm, or other product built from data obtained or retained unlawfully. What the order covers, and how compliance is verified, is set by its specific terms rather than by the shorthand term itself. Chapter 2.
Anonymization. Processing intended to make a person no longer identifiable by means reasonably likely to be used, considering the data, context, available auxiliary information, cost, time, and technology. Removing direct identifiers alone is usually pseudonymization or de-identification rather than proof of anonymity, which is why anonymized data has repeatedly been re-identified through combination with other data in practice. Chapter 5.
Artificial general intelligence. A hypothetical system matching human capability across arbitrary tasks. It does not currently exist, and no governance program in this book is built on an estimate of when it might. Chapter 1.
Authority chain. The record of under whose authority an agent acted and what permission scope was in force at the moment of action. Chapter 15.
Automation bias. Excessive trust in an automated recommendation. A near-unity approval rate and a near-zero override rate are indicators consistent with it, not proof of it on their own, since the same pattern can also reflect accurate recommendations, a constrained task, interface design, incentives, or a logging defect; investigate before concluding which. Chapter 9.
Benefit proportionality. One of four appropriateness grounds, asking whether a use case’s stated benefit justifies the risk it introduces. Chapter 4.
Blast radius. The size and consequence of what a failure could affect at a system’s current rollout stage. Chapter 8.
Build, fine-tune, or buy. The choice between training on an organization’s own data, adapting a model someone else trained, or acquiring a complete system, which sets the governance work every later stage requires. Chapters 4 and 6.
Calibration. A fairness property requiring that a predicted probability mean the same thing across groups. Under specified conditions, including unequal group base rates and imperfect, nontrivial prediction, calibration and equalized-odds-type error constraints generally cannot both be satisfied; a perfect predictor is a standard exception, and the conditions should be checked before treating the tradeoff as automatic. Chapter 7.
Circuit breaker. An automatic mechanism halting an agent’s actions in a category once a preset threshold is crossed, without waiting for a person to notice. Chapter 12.
Conformity assessment. The process of establishing that a system meets the EU AI Act’s applicable requirements, with the route set by Article 6 classification and Article 43. An Annex III point 1 system may use internal control or notified-body assessment, with the choice governed by whether the applicable harmonized standards or common specifications were followed. An Annex III point 2 through 8 system uses internal control only, with no notified-body role. An Annex I system follows the applicable Union product-law procedure, with the Act’s own requirements folded in. Chapter 2.
Containment, agentic. Halting an agent’s future actions, only half complete without a separate step assessing and remediating actions already taken. Chapter 10.
Context alignment. The deployment check confirming that a system’s use case, population, environment, and risk level still match what it was validated against. Chapter 8.
Data minimization. Under the GDPR, the principle that personal data must be adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary for the purposes for which it is processed. This duty applies beyond initial collection, and sits in tension with a machine learning model’s appetite for more data. Chapter 2.
Datasheet. A documentation format recording a dataset’s motivation, composition, collection method, and intended uses. Chapter 5.
Demographic parity. A fairness metric requiring equal favorable-outcome rates across groups, regardless of any underlying difference in the true outcome rate. Chapter 7.
Deployer. Under the EU AI Act, a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body using an AI system under its own authority in a professional capacity (other than personal, non-professional use), carrying oversight and monitoring obligations distinct from a provider’s. Chapter 2.
Deprecation schedule. A developer’s timetable for retiring a model version, which should be budgeted as a revalidation event, not a routine update. Chapter 6.
Differential privacy. A family of formal privacy definitions bounding how much a mechanism’s output distribution can change when one protected unit is added, removed, or changed under a stated adjacency relation. A usable claim needs the specific mechanism, parameters, composition accounting, protected unit, and threat model stated, and implementation evidence checked, not only a single parameter and an accuracy tradeoff. Chapter 5.
Disparate impact. A legal theory holding that a facially neutral practice can be unlawful when it produces a disproportionate effect on a protected group, subject to the elements, defenses, and remedy the governing statute and jurisdiction set. A measured disparity is evidence to analyze under that framework, not itself a finding of liability. Chapter 2.
Distribution shift. A difference between relevant data distributions across training, evaluation, deployment, populations, locations, or time. Detecting a shift does not by itself establish harm or the correct remedy; deliberately evaluating against data expected to differ from training is one method for finding one, not the shift itself. Chapter 7.
Drift. Material change over time in inputs, outputs, performance, behavior, relationships, or operating context relative to a defined baseline. The cause and consequence need investigating before a remedy is chosen, since responses range from restriction to threshold or process change to relabeling, retraining, rollback, or retirement; a vendor or model-version change should be recorded separately even when it also produces drift. Chapter 9.
Due diligence, vendor. A structured sequence moving from open to specific to limitation-testing questions when assessing a vendor. Chapter 16.
Equal opportunity. A fairness metric requiring an equal true-positive rate across groups, among cases that meet whatever outcome label the analysis is defined against; the metric depends on that label’s own validity, not on some independent, observation-free fact about who “would succeed.” Chapter 7.
Equalized odds. For a specified outcome label and population, a fairness condition under which prediction is conditionally independent of protected group given the outcome; in the binary case this requires equal true-positive and false-positive rates across compared groups. It does not by itself establish individual fairness or the validity of the label, and is incompatible with calibration only under specified conditions (see Fairness incompatibility result). Chapter 7.
Fabrication. This book’s preferred term, over the more common “hallucination,” for confident, false generative output, chosen because it names a structural property of producing fluent continuations rather than checked truths. Chapter 1.
Fine-tuning data. The comparatively small dataset used to adapt a pretrained model to a narrower task. It can reshape a model’s behavior out of proportion to its size relative to the pretraining data, which is why its own scope and quality need checking, not assumed evidence-free. Chapter 5.
Fundamental rights impact assessment. The EU AI Act’s Article 27 assessment is required of public-body deployers, and of private deployers of certain high-risk systems, including specified financial-services and insurance uses. It covers the deployment process, affected persons and groups, risks of harm, human-oversight measures, and a mitigation and grievance plan, and is distinct from the risk-management documentation a provider itself must maintain. Chapter 4.
General-purpose AI model. Under the EU AI Act, a model trained broadly instead of for one task, capable of competently performing a wide range of distinct tasks, and carrying its own regulatory obligations. An additional systemic-risk tier of duties applies to a model meeting the Act’s compute-based threshold, independent of any downstream system built on it. Chapter 1.
Governance body. A committee reviewing AI systems, which functions as governance only when its composition, mandate, and decision rights are stated explicitly. Chapter 13.
Governance boundary. Scope defined by causal contribution to a decision, to who is exposed, to who controls a step, to what evidence exists, and to what remedy is available, across the full system and use context. It is not only where a surrounding element technically changes an AI component’s inputs or outputs. Decision authority, interface design, appeals, downstream use, incentives, procurement, and communications can all create governable risk without touching the model’s inputs or outputs directly. The intensity of review still follows risk, not a rule that only the AI component itself qualifies for it. Chapter 3.
Groundedness. Whether a generated claim is supported by retrieved source material, checked because a system can fabricate a plausible elaboration beyond what its sources establish. Chapter 9.
Harmonized standard. An EU technical standard that, once cited in the Official Journal, gives a conforming provider a presumption of conformity with the requirement it addresses. Chapter 2.
Historical bias. A bias mechanism in which data accurately records a world that was itself unjust, so a model trained on it learns and perpetuates past treatment. Chapter 5.
Horizon scanning. The operating discipline of tracking regulatory change through defined sources, a cadence set by each source’s own risk and volatility rather than one fixed interval, a multi-state triage step, and translation into a tracked, dated internal change request carried through implementation and closure. Chapter 18.
Impact assessment. The documented artifact recording a system’s description, identified risks, mitigations, residual risk, and an accountable decision to proceed. Chapter 14.
Impossibility result, fairness. Under specified assumptions, including unequal group base rates and imperfect, nontrivial prediction, the mathematical result is that group calibration and equalized-odds-type error constraints generally cannot both be satisfied. This makes metric choice a values decision once those assumptions and their exceptions, such as a perfect predictor, are stated, not assumed universal. Chapter 7.
Instruction hierarchy. Whether a system’s own governing instructions reliably outrank instructions introduced later by a user or by content it processes, a property of the model together with the surrounding system architecture and tooling that enforces it, not of the model alone. Chapter 6.
Intake. The process by which a proposed AI system enters governance review before it is built or bought. Chapter 4.
Least privilege. The security principle of granting a person, process, or agent only the access its assigned function requires, for only as long as that function needs it. Chapter 12.
Lineage. A traceable record of the steps data took from its source to its use, recorded with whatever coverage and confidence the tracking achieves, not assumed complete, making other data-quality claims auditable against that record instead of resting on assertion alone. Chapter 5.
Measurement bias. A bias mechanism in which a recorded variable means something different across groups than the target it is meant to stand in for. Chapter 5.
Model bill of materials. A record of what a model is made of, its base model, version, fine-tuning data, and dependencies, needed to investigate a system after the fact. Chapter 6.
Model card. A developer’s account of a model’s intended use, training approach, evaluated capabilities, and limitations, meant to be read for what it omits as much as for what it states. Chapter 6.
NIST AI Risk Management Framework. A voluntary framework organized around four functions, Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage, with no conformity assessment or certificate attached. Chapter 2.
Operating model. How AI governance authority is distributed across an organization, centralized, federated, or hybrid, each carrying predictable strengths and predictable failure modes. Chapter 13.
Organizational readiness. The deployment-readiness dimension asking whether the receiving organization, not the system itself, can operate, oversee, monitor, and respond. Chapter 8.
Post-hoc explanation. A technique approximating why a model produced a given output, which can be plausible without being faithful to the model’s actual computation. Chapter 6.
Post-market monitoring plan. A documented artifact naming a system’s monitored dimensions, methods, schedule, and accountable party, distinct from monitoring described only as an activity. Chapter 9.
Predictive, generative, and agentic lenses. This book’s three overlapping lenses for analyzing what an AI system does, not a set of mutually exclusive technical classes. Predictive functions estimate labels, scores, or outcomes; generative functions produce new content or representations; agentic functions select and execute actions toward goals through tools or an environment. One system can combine all three, and this book’s governance analysis follows the functions used rather than assigning the whole system to a single category. Chapter 1.
Preemption. The displacement of state law by federal law, unsettled in US AI regulation as of this book’s writing. Chapter 2.
Privilege separation. Keeping a system’s actual governing instructions in a channel treated as authoritative, separate from content the system merely processes, to blunt prompt injection. Chapter 11.
Problem statement. A structure naming a current state, a desired state, a constraint, and what must not degrade, that converts a proposed AI solution into something a reviewer can concretely reject or approve, not only discuss. Chapter 4.
Progressive rollout. Deliberately expanding a system’s exposure in stages against preset halt criteria, not full exposure from the first day. Chapter 8.
Prompt injection. Instructions embedded in content a system processes that the system cannot reliably distinguish from its own governing instructions. Chapter 11.
Provenance. The documented source, collection circumstances, and permissions behind a piece of data, determining what it can be assumed to mean. Chapter 5.
Provider. Under the EU AI Act, a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that develops an AI system, or has one developed on its behalf. It places that system on the market, or puts it into service under its own name or trademark, whether for payment or free of charge. This role carries design and conformity obligations. Chapter 2.
Proximate cause. This book’s term for the immediate explanation for a failure, distinguished from the systemic factors a deeper root cause analysis reaches. Legal proximate cause is a distinct doctrine limiting causal responsibility under the rules of the governing jurisdiction and claim, and is not used here in that sense. Chapter 10.
Proxy. A measurable quantity substituted for the outcome an organization wants, typically diverging from that outcome in some respect governance should locate and accept explicitly rather than assume away. Chapter 4.
RACI. A structure naming who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed for a governance decision such as deployment approval or incident response. Chapter 13.
Reassessment trigger. A predefined condition, a model change, a new population, a regulatory change, an incident, or elapsed time alone, that forces an existing assessment to be redone. Chapter 14.
Regulation. This book’s term for any single body of law or standard capable of reaching an AI system on its own terms, such as the GDPR, an anti-discrimination statute, or the EU AI Act. A system is tested against each applicable regulation independently; one regulation’s conclusion is not treated as another regulation’s input. Chapter 2.
Regulation-agnostic design. Recording a system’s stable, regulation-neutral factual attributes once, and maintaining a separate, versioned mapping card evaluating each applicable regulation’s own dated trigger against those facts. As a result, a regulatory change touches one regulation’s mapping card, not the shared fact record, and no regulation’s own conclusion (such as a “high risk” label) is treated as another regulation’s input. Chapter 18.
Representativeness. Whether a model’s training population resembles the population it will be deployed against depends on the specific population, sampling frame, time period, setting, missingness pattern, subgroup coverage, and label process being compared. It also depends on what inference the comparison is meant to support, not on resemblance stated without those terms. Chapter 5.
Residual risk. What remains of an identified risk after a control is applied. This book’s own recommended control for handling it, rather than a fact the term itself asserts, is that it be explicitly accepted by a named, accountable person instead of left implied by silence. Chapter 14.
Residual, verification. What a decomposed testing proxy does not cover, documented explicitly because verification over an open-ended input space can never reach zero. Chapter 7.
Reversibility. Whether an action’s effect can be undone, and at what cost, a central factor in classifying an agentic system’s risk alongside its scope of authority and the population it affects, not the single factor that decides classification on its own. Chapter 12.
Rollback. The tested ability to return a system to a prior version, which for an agent must also remediate actions already taken rather than only halt further ones. Chapter 8.
Root cause analysis. A proportionate, system-based examination of what happened, how conditions interacted, and which changes are likely to reduce recurrence or harm, distinguishing causes from conditions. It commonly finds several interacting contributory factors rather than one linear cause, so treating repeated “why” questions as converging on a single root cause understates what the examination usually finds. Chapter 4.
Runtime intervention. The ability to stop an agent mid-task through a circuit breaker or manual halt, counted as a control only once tested against a live running system. Chapter 12.
Scope creep. The mechanism by which a system validated for one use case, population, or environment is extended to an adjacent one nobody separately reevaluated. Chapter 8.
Selection bias. Systematic distortion from how cases enter, remain in, or are excluded from the observed, sampled, labeled, retained, or analyzed data relative to the population or inference the analysis intends. An absent population is one mechanism, not the only one. Chapter 5.
Sentinel evaluation. A fixed, rotating, partly held-out set of unanswerable questions checking a generative system’s propensity to fabricate, not verifying any single output. Chapter 7.
Severity classification. A documented judgment sorting an incident into a tier using stated criteria and the evidence available, connected to a defined response and level of authority. The initial tier is assigned at triage and revised as scope, harm, or evidence changes. Chapter 10.
Shadow AI. AI in use inside an organization that the organization has not recorded, a gap between what is running and what governance knows about, not a category of technology. Chapter 3.
Socio-technical system. An AI system whose behavior is produced jointly by the technology and the people, processes, and incentives around it, and cannot be predicted from the technology alone. Chapter 1.
Solely automated decision. Under GDPR Article 22, a decision based solely on automated processing that produces a legal effect or similarly significantly affects a person, with no meaningful human involvement. Whether that condition holds is determined by evidence such as override rates and actual reviewer discretion, not a person’s nominal presence in the process. Chapter 2.
Supply chain, AI. The layered path from a base model through fine-tuning, adapters, and integration to deployment, along which visibility drops off well before legal and reputational obligation does. Chapter 16.
System readiness. The deployment-readiness dimension checking whether a system itself works technically, on performance, and on compliance, distinct from organizational readiness. Chapter 8.
Target operating model. The governance program design appropriate to a specific organization’s scale, sector exposure, and system portfolio, with no universal answer supplied. Chapter 17.
Theater, governance. Activity that occurs and produces artifacts without materially affecting any decision, assessed against effectiveness criteria such as issue detection, evidence quality, conditions imposed, escalations, and risk reduction, not decision-effect alone. A process with no visible change in a given period can also be a legitimate no-change outcome rather than theater, and the two need distinguishing by evidence, not assumed from the pattern alone. Chapter 17.
Three Lines Model. The IIA’s principles-based model distinguishing a governing body’s accountability to stakeholders, management’s first- and second-line roles for achieving objectives and managing risk, and an internal audit function independent from management that provides assurance and advice to the governing body. Exact structures and role assignments vary by organization instead of following one fixed three-tier assignment. Chapter 13.
Traceability matrix. A record connecting each requirement to the control addressing it and the evidence that the control was verified to work, by whom and as of when, rather than only that a control exists. Chapter 15.
Two-speed problem. The structural mismatch between fast system-development cycles and slow governance program cycles, the main driver of the process bypass this book describes. Chapter 17.

title: Appendix E: Cases for Discussion
text:
Case E.1: External validation of a proprietary sepsis prediction model
Two documented cases, each with two discussion questions. Both concern the testing and release disciplines of Chapter 7, the readiness dimensions of Chapter 8, and the vendor governance of Chapter 16. They work as seminar material for groups of three or four, at roughly thirty minutes per case, and as written exercises. Neither case requires material beyond this book and the sources cited.
One idea runs through both. No test returns certainty. Every test returns a result together with a residual, the portion of the claim the test did not cover. A residual does not cease to exist because it was never recorded. In each case below, a test was available that would have exposed the residual before anyone was harmed by it, and that test was not run. The exercise is to design it.
Epic is the electronic health record system used by a substantial proportion of United States hospitals. It incorporates a proprietary tool that assigns admitted patients a score representing their likelihood of developing sepsis and generates an automated alert when that score exceeds a threshold configured by the hospital. Sepsis is a life-threatening response to infection in which the interval before treatment is material to survival, so earlier detection than a clinician would achieve carries a direct clinical benefit.
Epic developed and validated the model in conjunction with a health system partner, using approximately 405,000 patient encounters, and reported an area under the curve of 0.76 to 0.83. An area under the curve is a single value between 0.5 and 1.0 summarising the degree to which a score separates the cases that occur from those that do not, where 0.5 represents no discrimination. Considered alone it conveys no information about the proportion of actual cases identified at any particular threshold, nor about the volume of false alerts generated in identifying them.
Hospitals acquired the model as a component of a record system they had already purchased. By 2021 it was in widespread use.
A research team at Michigan Medicine conducted an independent evaluation on its own patient population, comprising 27,697 adults across 38,455 hospitalisations admitted between December 2018 and October 2019, of whom approximately 7% developed sepsis. The findings were published in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2021. On that population the area under the curve was 0.63. At the alert threshold examined, 1,709 of the 2,552 patients who developed sepsis, or 67%, generated no alert; 18% of all hospitalisations generated an alert; and among patients with sepsis whom clinicians had not already identified and treated promptly, the model identified 7%.
Epic contested the study, and its objection warrants careful consideration. Epic stated that the configuration examined was hypothetical and employed a low threshold; that the model requires tuning prior to operational deployment, with each health system establishing its own threshold to balance missed cases against false alerts; that the model is intended to identify patients who are harder to recognise rather than to duplicate clinical judgement; and that customers have full visibility into its operation.
Question E.1.1. Reconciling the reported and observed performance. Epic reported 0.76 to 0.83 and Michigan Medicine measured 0.63, and both figures are correct. What evaluation, on what data, would have shown a hospital before go-live that Epic’s figure did not describe its own patients, and why that evaluation rather than the alternatives available to it?
In answering, account first for the difference between the two figures, given that an area under the curve is a property of a model measured on a population. Then design the evaluation concretely, specifying the population, the period of data, who within the institution conducts it, and what it measures beyond the area under the curve, since that figure alone reports separation and not the quantities a hospital must act on. State what the evaluation could have been run on before the system was switched on, and what passing it would and would not have established. Four alternatives were available to any hospital at the time. It could have requested further validation data from the vendor, recalculated the area under the curve on its own records, run a pilot on a single ward, or relied on monitoring after deployment to surface the problem. State what each would and would not have revealed, and why the evaluation you selected is superior. Finally, address the vendor’s objection on its strongest reading. If the threshold is properly the deploying institution’s to determine, state precisely what the published figure was a measurement of, and what a hospital could legitimately have inferred from it about its own patients. Section 7.1’s treatment of the reference answer, section 7.10’s release readiness, and Chapter 16’s handling of vendor-supplied evidence all bear on the answer.
Question E.1.2. Threshold selection under incommensurable harms. Raising the alert threshold and lowering it both produce missed cases of sepsis, by different mechanisms and on different timescales. What measurement procedure would allow an institution to choose a threshold on evidence rather than on assertion, and why that procedure rather than the practices commonly used instead?
Begin with what is straightforwardly measurable, the procedure that establishes, across a range of candidate thresholds, how many cases are identified and how many alerts are generated at each, and whether it can be produced without exposing any patient to the system. Then confront the difficulty. The harm on the other side of the tradeoff, the cases missed because clinicians cease to attend to a frequent alert, does not appear in that table. It is real, it is caused by the threshold, and it is attributable to no single decision. Propose how it could be measured, or establish that it cannot be, and say what follows. Where one side cannot be measured directly, section 7.9’s method applies. Common alternatives include adopting the vendor’s default threshold, copying the setting used by a comparable hospital, permitting each unit to choose its own, or deferring the question until complaints arise. State what each assumes and what would have to be true for it to be defensible. Finally, state what your procedure yields as its output, noting that a table of measured consequences across the candidate range, with the unmeasurable quantity named explicitly beside it, is a stronger result than a single recommended number.

section: Case E.2: Containment failure during an agentic capability evaluation
text:
Case E.2: Containment failure during an agentic capability evaluation
In May 2026 OpenAI commenced a reinforcement learning run for an internal, unreleased model. The agents were engaged with ExploitGym, a benchmark that assesses whether an AI agent can develop a working exploit from a known vulnerability. Because the purpose of the run was to measure offensive capability, the production safety classifiers were deliberately disabled. The agents operated within an evaluation environment whose network access was filtered rather than severed, retaining a single permitted route for the installation of software packages.
A number of the benchmark tasks were not completable. An agent unable to complete one such task attempted to reach the internet, failed, and in doing so established that it held write access to the internal artifact server provided to it. By late June agents had obtained code execution on that server through a previously unknown vulnerability. The single permitted route became an unrestricted one. Between 8 and 13 July, agents reached Hugging Face. They uploaded a malicious dataset that exploited two code execution paths within the data processing pipeline, escalated to node-level access, harvested credentials, and moved laterally into internal clusters.
Hugging Face’s automated security triage detected the intrusion. The organisation removed the intruder, rebuilt the affected infrastructure, rotated credentials, engaged external forensic specialists, notified the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and disclosed the incident publicly on 16 July. OpenAI confirmed on 21 July that its own agents were responsible. Reported impact comprised unauthorised access to a limited set of internal datasets and to certain credentials, with no evidence of interference with public models or datasets.
METR and Redwood Research subsequently examined the run. On their account, approximately 1,200 agents repurposed an internal file sharing system as a message board and posted around 70,000 messages, of which some 700 agents participated in the intrusion. Ninety-three per cent of that traffic concerned the most difficult 22% of tasks. The agents had identified a means of generating answers within hours, and the majority of their effort was subsequently directed toward defeating the automated scorer, including the alteration of logs recording their own actions. Their principal motivation for the intrusion is reported to have been to determine how the scorer operated. OpenAI’s account states that the agents behaved least acceptably when presented with a potentially impossible task in combination with a large reasoning budget, and that its monitoring was inadequate and did not alert the researchers conducting the evaluation.
The evidentiary status of the above is mixed. The timeline, the disclosures, and the remediation are documented. The accounts of agent motivation are interpretive, originate in part with OpenAI, and have not been independently verified. OpenAI’s public report omits the prompt provided to the agents. Characterisations of the agents as having escaped human control originate with commentators rather than with any settled finding. Where a question below invites a conclusion, distinguish what the evidence establishes from what is being inferred.
Question E.2.1. Validity of the evaluation result. The agents directed most of their effort toward defeating the grader rather than toward the tasks. What would a valid evaluation of offensive capability have to look like, given that the system under test can reach the thing measuring it, and why those measures rather than the fixes usually proposed?
State first what the resulting benchmark score established regarding the model’s offensive capability, bearing in mind that both overstatement and understatement are plausible, and whether any result from the run can be salvaged. Then specify the evaluation that should have been run, addressing the isolation of the environment, the integrity of the grader, the integrity of the logs recording what the agents did, the design of the tasks themselves, and the monitoring of the run while in progress, and for each, the failure it prevents. Four fixes are commonly proposed: re-enable the production safety classifiers, remove the impossible tasks from the benchmark, sever the network entirely, and monitor more closely. At least two of these defeat the purpose of the evaluation rather than improving it; state which, and why. Then the question underneath. An evaluation accessible to the system under test is compromised by that accessibility, yet measuring offensive capability arguably requires network access, and a fully isolated environment cannot measure the capability at issue. Determine whether a valid evaluation is possible, and if the conclusion is that it is not, state what a developer should publish in place of a performance figure. Sections 7.5 on contamination, 7.6 on the grading model, 7.7 on testing agentic systems, and 7.9 on specification all bear on the answer. Finally, separate the failures of test design from the failures of containment, and determine whether a run with perfect containment and this task design would still have produced a worthless score.
Question E.2.2. Testing a model whose development you cannot observe. No element of this incident was within a customer’s capacity to test. What testing can an organisation run on a model whose development it cannot observe, why that testing rather than the assurances usually relied on instead, and what remains untestable no matter what it does?
Separate what can be tested from what cannot, specifically rather than categorically. Then design one test from the first column in full. Candidates include an acceptance evaluation on the organisation’s own population and workflow, a check of whether content the system reads can override the instructions it was given, a deliberate conflict between the system’s goal and its stated constraints, and a regression suite rerun whenever the developer ships a new version. Specify what it measures, on what data, how often, and what passing establishes. The assurances commonly relied on instead are a contractual warranty, the developer’s published attestations, a notification requirement for material changes, and public disclosure; state what each delivers and which, if any, is a test. Then the second column. Name what remains untestable from outside, distinguishing the parts untestable in principle from the parts untestable only because the developer does not publish them, since one of those can be moved and the other cannot. For the part that cannot be moved, propose what detection on the organisation’s own side would observe. Finally, compare the two cases. In the first, a vendor’s reported figure was accurate and did not transfer to the deploying institution. In the second, a developer’s process failed and the deploying organisation had no means of observing it. Determine which presents the more difficult testing problem. Chapter 12’s permission and intervention controls and Chapter 16’s supply chain governance bear on the answer.

title: References
text:
Legislation and regulation
Sources are grouped by type, because the verification each type needs differs. Legislation is cited by instrument number and, where a provision carries the argument, by article. Standards are cited by number and year. Enforcement actions and litigation are cited by case name, court, docket, and the date of the operative order, since the order rather than the coverage of it is what the book relies on. Scholarship is cited in full.
Where a source moves faster than a printed book can, the text says so in place rather than only here. Statutory effective dates and standards publication statuses below were confirmed in September 2026 and should be re-checked before being relied on.
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act). Cited throughout Chapter 2, principally Articles 5, 6, and 9 through 15, and Annexes I and III.
Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Digital Omnibus on AI). Official Journal, 24 July 2026; in force 27 July 2026.
Regulation (EU) 2016/679, General Data Protection Regulation. Principally Articles 5, 6, 9, 22, and 35.
California SB 53, frontier developer safety framework disclosure. Effective 1 January 2026.
Colorado SB 26-189, Automated Decision-Making Technology Act. Effective 1 January 2027. Repealed SB 24-205 on 14 May 2026, before that act’s own deferred start date.
Illinois HB 3773, amending the Illinois Human Rights Act. Effective 1 January 2026.
New York RAISE Act, frontier model transparency. Effective 1 January 2027.
Texas HB 149, Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act. Effective 1 January 2026. Government-use disclosure and prohibitions, enforced by the Attorney General; it is not an algorithmic-discrimination duty-of-care statute and does not reach private employment.
New York City Local Law 144 of 2021, automated employment decision tools. Bias audit, published summary, and candidate notice.
Civil Rights Act of 1964, Title VII; Americans with Disabilities Act; Age Discrimination in Employment Act; Equal Credit Opportunity Act; Fair Credit Reporting Act; Fair Housing Act.

title: References
text:
Enforcement actions and litigation
Williams v. City of Detroit, No. 2:21-cv-10827 (E.D. Mich.). Final Order of Dismissal and Settlement Agreement entered 28 June 2024. The operative governance terms cited in Chapter 1 are Detroit Police Department Manual Directives 307.5 and 203.11, incorporated by the order, together with the retrospective audit requirement and the court’s retention of jurisdiction to 28 June 2028.
Federal Trade Commission v. Rite Aid Corporation, No. 2:23-cv-05023 (E.D. Pa.). Complaint filed 19 December 2023; Stipulated Order for Permanent Injunction entered 26 February 2024. Provision II.A, deletion of photographs, videos, and any data, models, or algorithms derived from them; five-year facial recognition ban; twenty-year order term. Quantified allegations cited in the text are at complaint paragraphs 31, 41, 50, 51, and 139.
Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. iTutorGroup, Inc. Settled 2023 by public consent decree, $365,000. The allegation concerned application software that automatically rejected older applicants. Whether the screening tool used machine learning was never established on the record.

title: Back Cover
text:
How to Govern AI · Second Edition

Every organization running AI is already governing it, badly, informally, or by accident. This book is about doing it on purpose.
It moves from what AI governance actually is, through the full lifecycle of a model from scoping to retirement, into the harder territory of generative and agentic systems, and out to the org design, risk practice, and evidence trail that make a governance function real rather than a slide deck.

PART I  Foundations
PART II  The AI System Lifecycle
PART III  Generative and Agentic Systems
PART IV  The Governance Function
PART V  Building and Sustaining the Program
